item.title: EdenLive：世界状态交给程序、画面交给模型的实时生成式渲染器 ｜ EdenLive: Real-Time Generative Rendering from Any Visual Reference
item.description:
一句话：VAST 开源的 5B 实时生成式渲染器，单张 5090 上 720P 超 24FPS，端到端延迟百毫秒级。

要点：

  • 输入是「代理视频」（引擎或编码智能体渲染的简化画面）加目标首帧与文本提示，模型按参考的布局与运镜实时重绘成写实或指定画风。
  • 用视觉编码器把几何粒度差异很大的参考（2D/3D 代理、法线图、实拍视频）映射到共享特征空间，抑制参考外观泄漏进生成画面。
  • 蒸馏成少步分块自回归模型，服务端把程序模拟、参考编码与生成排成带一块前瞻的流水线；权重、推理代码与技术报告全部开源。

为什么值得看：这是「状态由上游程序维护、视觉由生成模型负责」这条路线目前最完整的可跑实现：世界状态可检查、可修改、可测试，交互还能挂到程序暴露的任意量上。做 AI 原生引擎时，可以直接照它的接口拆状态层与渲染层。

中文摘要：VAST 的 Project Eden 推出 EdenLive，一个面向交互应用的实时生成式视频渲染器。它把世界状态与视觉渲染解耦：上游程序（游戏引擎或编码智能体生成的代理画面）显式维护游戏逻辑与世界状态，EdenLive 只负责把简化参考视频、目标首帧和提示词渲染成高质量画面。这既让状态可检查可修改，也把有限模型容量集中到视觉合成上。为处理不同几何粒度的参考，作者用视觉编码器把它们映射到共享特征空间，再以这些特征条件化视频生成，减轻外观泄漏。为了让生成流式化，生成器被蒸馏成少步分块自回归模型，并部署在把模拟、编码、生成三级流水化的服务系统里，带一块前瞻。实验显示参考控制与画质都不错，且在单张 GPU 上以 720P 输出超过 24FPS。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：VAST·技术报告（English）

原文发布：2026-10-18

本期推送：2026-10-22

TECHNICAL REPORT EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering from Any Visual Reference Zehuan Huang1,*, Tian- Xing Xu1,*, Chunli Peng1,*, Cheng Zhang1,*, Zeyi Zheng1,†, Yifei Song1,†, Zekai Gu1,†, Zhipeng Yu1, Peng Wang1,‡, Y an-Pei Cao1,✉ 1VAST *Equal contribution †Intern at VAST ‡Project lead ✉ Corresponding author CORRESPONDENCE Yan-Pei Cao caoyanpei@gmail.com PROJECT https://vast-eden.ai/?p=edenlive CODE https://github.com/VAST-AI-Research/EdenLive WEIGHTS https://huggingface.co/VAST-AI/EdenLive DATE October 2026 Figure 1 Real-time generative rendering from diverse visual references. Each tile pairs a reference (left) with the generated frame at the same timestamp (right). Examples include game and 2D proxies, normal maps, scene previews, video restyling, and embodied scenes. All outputs use the EdenLive 5B model. EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 2 ABSTRACT We present EdenLive, a real-time generative video renderer for inter- active applications in the Project Eden series 1. EdenLive continuously renders enhanced and stylized video from reference videos of different geometric granularities that range from proxy videos, namely sim- plified renderings produced by a coding agent or a game engine, to directly recorded videos, with a target first frame and a text prompt as input to guide the appearance. This design conveys the world state to the model through the reference video and thereby decouples its interaction-induced evolution from visual rendering: the upstream code or engine maintains the game logic and world state explicitly and precisely , whereas EdenLive renders reference video into detailed visual output. This separation enables the world state to be inspected, modified, and tested directly , and interaction can extend to any quantity exposed by the upstream program. It also relieves the neural model from learning both state transitions and appearance, allowing the limited model capacity available for real-time deployment to concentrate on visual synthesis. To handle references for diverse rendering scenarios, we employ a vision encoder that maps them into a shared feature space despite their differences in geometric granularity and appearance, and condition the video generation model on these features, which mitigates leakage of the reference appearance into the generated video. To enable streaming generation, we distill the generator into a few-step chunk-wise autoregressive model and deploy it in a serving system that pipelines program simulation, reference encoding, and generation with a one-chunk lookahead, so that the system presents the generated video in real time and responds to user interaction. Experiments on short- and long-horizon generation show that EdenLive achieves good reference control and visual quality , while generating 720P videos in real time at over 24 FPS on a single GPU. 1 https://www.tripo3d.ai/research/project-eden EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 3 1 Introduction World models characterize how an environment evolves in response to actions and events [ 32, 34], a capability that underpins simulation for autonomous driving [ 10, 37], embodied intelligence [ 9, 100], and interactive games [18, 86]. Two properties are central in these settings: interactivity , since a player or an agent chooses its next action on the basis of its current observation, and low latency , since each observation must follow the corresponding action quickly enough to sustain closed-loop interaction. Video-based world models have recently advanced rapidly in both respects by leveraging the generative priors of large pretrained video models [ 71, 85, 103]: starting from latent-action and action-conditioned models [ 4, 13, 86], recent methods synthesize environments that users explore through keyboard, mouse, and camera inputs [ 36, 39, 48, 54, 79, 84, 92], alter through text-triggered events [ 23, 29, 74], and revisit with the help of meory mechanisms [ 75, 95, 99], while achieving increasingly photorealistic visual quality . These models, however , learn the evolution of the world state jointly with its visual appearance in a single generative network, which predicts each new observation from the generated history and the current input. The state of an interactive world is complex and heterogeneous, spanning entity positions and attributes, numerical quantities such as health and score, objects outside the current view , and the rules that determine how each action takes effect. Scaling model parameters and training data can improve how well such state is captured implicitly , but the same network must then devote its capacity to both dynamics and appearance, which is in tension with the computational budget permitted by real-time deployment. Moreover , the state is held only implicitly in the latent context and the generated frames, so it cannot be directly inspected, edited, or verified [ 42, 70], and control remains largely confined to actions, camera trajectories, and text prompts rather than extending to individual entities and their interaction rules. To address this limitation, in Project Eden [ 88] we proposed to decouple the evolution of the world state from its visual rendering. An evolving structured state persists over time, is updated by actions, and can be queried from different viewpoints. A state-to-observation interface converts this state into camera-conditioned constraints that expose its local semantics and geometry . And a generative renderer maps these state-derived constraints to high-fidelity visual output. In this work, we instan- tiate this principle with EdenLive. Upstream code or an engine maintains and advances the world state by executing the game logic and interaction mechanisms. The engine renders each updated state into a temporally aligned video stream. Then a reference-conditioned, real-time generative renderer , which is trained starting from pretrained video diffusion models [ 85], follows the scene layout, camera motion, and dynamics conveyed by this video stream while synthesizing detailed visual output. Compared with modeling state evolution and appearance jointly in pixels, this sepa- ration keeps the game logic, interaction mechanisms, and world state explicit and precise: they can be inspected, modified, and tested directly , and interaction can extend to any quantity exposed by the upstream program. It also relieves the neural model from learning both state transitions and appearance, allowing the limited model capacity available for real-time deployment to concentrate on visual synthesis. We refer to the conditioning video supplied to the renderer as a reference video , which is either a proxy video , namely a simplified rendering produced by a coding agent, a game engine, or a workbench that captures scene layout, camera motion and coarse dynamics, or a recorded video that is used directly as the reference. This formulation leads to a question: can a single renderer accept reference videos from diverse upstream sources, ranging from proxies of 2D and 3D games to recorded footage, and render them in real time? Answering this question requires the renderer to EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 4 recover layout and motion from references of widely varying geometry and appearance without copying unwanted reference appearance, learn despite the limited availability of paired reference– target videos, and generate causally and continuously within a real-time latency budget. To address these challenges, We present EdenLive, a real-time generative video renderer that con- ditions on a reference video, a target first frame, and a text prompt. To handle heterogeneous references, we condition the generator on dense features rather than on reference pixels, extracted by a vision encoder that we fine-tune on reference–target image pairs to map reference videos that differ in appearance and geometric granularity but share layout and motion into a shared feature space. Conditioning on this feature space eases the learning of the generator and mitigates the degradation of its output toward the appearance of the reference video. Furthermore, the same feature space allows unpaired videos to serve as self-paired training data, in which the generator is conditioned on features extracted from an appearance-perturbed copy of the target video itself. To enable streaming generation, we distill the generator into a few-step model that performs chunk- wise autoregressive inference over a bounded attention cache, so that each chunk depends only on the current reference frames and the retained history . Finally , our serving system overlaps upstream simulation and neural rendering, and streams the decoded frames to the user . Our contributions are threefold: – A vision encoder fine-tuning approach that aligns the representations of reference–target image pairs, enabling a generator trained on both self-paired and paired videos to be controlled by reference videos at inference. – A streaming generative renderer that combines few-step chunkwise generation, a bounded his- torical context, and pipelined serving to synthesize video continuously from evolving reference videos. – A complete real-time interactive system built on EdenLive, in which an upstream engine executes the game rules and maintains the world state while EdenLive renders the resulting proxy videos into the displayed stream; the system supports real-time previews of agent-built games with exact game state and appearance control through the target first frame, and extends to the offline re- rendering and stylization of recorded videos. We evaluate both the learned representation and the complete renderer through image and video encoder ablations, short- and long-horizon generation comparisons, and runtime measurements. Compared with the pretrained DINOv3 encoder , the fine-tuned encoder improves the transfer from proxy conditions to detailed outputs in image generation and reduces camera rotation error in video generation, and the generation comparisons show competitive reference adherence and appearance preservation. The optimized 5B renderer exceeds 24 FPS at 1280 × 704 on a single NVIDIA H100, measured from model-side condition processing to decoded frames in CPU memory . 2 Related Work

  1. 1 Controllable Video Generation

Large pretrained video diffusion models [ 52, 71, 85, 103] provide strong priors over appearance and motion, but precise structural control often requires additional conditioning. Beyond first-frame appearance editing [ 53, 72], a broad line of work introduces dense visual cues to guide scene structure, object motion, and camera motion, such as depth, edges, and segmentation [ 2, 3, 19, 49, 90], or through camera poses, trajectories, optical-flow-warped noise, and rendered 3D caches [ 14, EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 5 35, 77, 91]. These conditioning signals differ in both their representation and the level of structural detail they provide. These conditioning interfaces also vary in how much scene structure they require, ranging from dense rendering buffers to coarse proxies and sparse geometric primitives. Buffer-based methods [ 43, 58, 62, 78] receive dense rendering buffers to provide rich scene attributes for photorealistic image and video synthesis. Some works [ 15, 50] utilize coarse meshes and rendered proxies to reduce the required geometric detail while retaining control over layout and motion. ProxyUp [ 117] uses proxy videos with foreground masks to preserve selected dynamics while regenerating appearance and surroundings. Geometric conditions such as depth, 3D point tracks, and oriented bounding boxes also guide video generation [ 11, 31, 98]. These approaches rely on geometric representations or region-specific guidance that must be constructed or extracted from the source. Inspired by the feature-based conditioning of Coarse-to-Real [ 30], EdenLive learns a shared rep- resentation for references with varying appearance and geometric granularity . Whereas Coarse-to- Real uses a frozen DINOv3 encoder [81], we fine-tune the encoder on a large, independently curated set of reference–target image pairs to preserve shared structure while suppressing appearance dif- ferences. This alignment reduces reference appearance leakage and enables a generator trained on self-paired ordinary videos to generalize to proxy inputs. 2.2 Interactive World Models Interactive world models formulate environment simulation from generation history and user in- teraction. Genie [ 13] learns latent actions from unlabeled videos, while action-conditioned diffu- sion models demonstrate playable game simulation [4, 86]. Subsequent video world models extend action- and camera-conditioned generation across diverse environments [18, 36, 39, 54, 79, 84, 92, 111], with advances in real-time interaction and long-horizon generation [48, 112, 118]. Interaction also extends to text-driven events and scene editing [ 23, 29, 74] and object interactions [ 96], while Cosmos 3 [ 1] unifies multimodal understanding, visual generation, and action prediction. When world evolution is modeled through observation prediction, consistency with underlying rules is learned rather than enforced by an executable state-transition mechanism, and control depends on the inputs the model has learned to interpret. A recent trend in interactive world modeling is to decouple state evolution from visual rendering, using video models as renderers. The Project Eden research preview [ 88] outlines a shared-state architecture in which camera-conditioned semantic and geometric constraints connect the evolving world state to generative rendering. Related efforts make world state explicit: StatePlay [ 66] jointly predicts game-state variables and visual content, while Marionette [ 70] and MASS [ 16] advance an explicit world state through learned dynamics and render it into observations. Other systems dele- gate state evolution to executable logic. Code World Model [ 20], Programmable World Model [42], Oneira [102], and CoDeR [24] use coding agents to maintain and evolve explicit world states, which are translated into proxy videos or spatial conditions. AgentGarten [ 21] and Magpie [108] advance states through simulators and game engines, while GameDirector [ 65] introduces an agentic layer that tracks game state and enforces gameplay rules. Several renderers use specialized geometric interfaces, including oriented boxes, depth and surface normals, or articulated poses [ 21, 42, 70]. EdenLive learns a common reference-video interface across varying appearance and geometric gran- ularity , allowing diverse upstream programs to condition the same renderer on inputs ranging from agent-built proxies to recorded videos. EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 6 2.3 Acceleration, Distillation, and Streaming Few-step diffusion methods reduce generation cost by distilling iterative sampling into fewer model evaluations. Latent Consistency Models [ 69] learn consistency mappings for few-step latent-space synthesis, while Distribution Matching Distillation [104, 105] trains a one-step generator to match a diffusion teacher’s output distribution. Streaming video generation additionally requires causal pre- diction from generated histories. CausVid [106] distills a bidirectional teacher into a few-step causal generator , while Self Forcing [ 41] addresses the training-inference history mismatch through au- toregressive training on the model’s own predictions. Subsequent work extends generation to longer sequences [22, 101] and improves autoregressive distillation through student initialization, rollout perturbation, and gradient propagation through historical context [ 113, 115, 116, 119, 120]. Sus- tained streaming also requires bounded context and efficient execution. Attention sinks [ 94], com- bined with rolling windows, retain initial tokens and recent history while bounding the context size. Streaming pipelines use batched denoising and scheduling for continuous frame delivery [ 25, 51], while streaming video-to-video methods preserve temporal consistency through historical feature reuse or dedicated training objectives [ 57, 114]. EdenLive combines few-step chunkwise autore- gressive generation with a bounded cache containing an attention sink and a rolling window . Its serving system overlaps upstream simulation and reference encoding with generation, conditioning each chunk only on reference frames that have already arrived. 3 Problem Formulation and System Overview

  1. 1 Problem Formulation

We decouple the interaction-induced evolution of the world state from its visual presentation: an upstream program maintains the world state explicitly , whereas EdenLive acts as a reference- conditioned generative renderer that synthesizes only its appearance. Given an 𝑁-frame reference video 𝑟1∶𝑁 , a target first frame 𝑦, and a text condition 𝑝, EdenLive generates a refined or restyled video ̂𝑥1∶𝑁 = ℛ(𝑟1∶𝑁 , 𝑦, 𝑝), (1) in which the three inputs play complementary roles: the reference video conveys the evolving world state, namely the layout, camera motion, object trajectories, and event timing; the first frame, aligned with the opening reference view , anchors subject identity and appearance; and 𝑝 is ei- ther a single prompt held fixed over the sequence or a time-varying prompt schedule, which may include time-specific event descriptions in interactive applications. Achieving this in real time poses two challenges: a generator conditioned on reference videos that range from coarse proxies to recorded videos tends to degrade toward their appearance, and train- ing a model for real-time, minute-scale generation is difficult. We address them with a vision en- coder that maps reference videos into a shared feature space ( Sec. 4.2) and a distilled, chunkwise autoregressive generator (Secs. 4.3 and 4.4), respectively . 3.2 Real- Time Interactive System The real-time generation capability of EdenLive allows it to be integrated into an interactive system that responds to user input as it arrives. Fig. 2 illustrates the system we build upon EdenLive, which operates as a closed loop over successive chunks indexed by 𝑘. While viewing the most recently displayed chunk ̂𝑥(𝑘−1), the user issues keyboard and mouse actions 𝑎𝑡 at interaction steps 𝑡 ∈ ℐ𝑘, where ℐ𝑘 denotes the steps covered by chunk 𝑘. For concreteness, we take as a running example an EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 7 Code Agent code User observes & acts Keyboard & Mouse live input Engine rules, collisions & state Proxy Video Chunk successive engine observations graybox / simplified rendering EdenLive visual synthesis Displayed Video Chunk successive generated frames photorealistic display generated display informs the next user input Figure 2 Real-time interactive system built on EdenLive. User input drives an upstream engine that maintains the rules and state and emits proxy video chunks, from which EdenLive synthesizes the displayed video; the displayed video in turn informs the user’s next input. upstream game engine whose code is authored by a coding agent ( Sec. 6.1 ); the engine executes the rules, collisions, and state updates through a transition function 𝒯 , and an observation function 𝒪 renders each updated state as a graybox proxy frame: 𝑠𝑡 = 𝒯 (𝑠𝑡−1, 𝑎𝑡), 𝑟 𝑡 = 𝒪(𝑠𝑡), 𝑡 ∈ ℐ𝑘. (2) The proxy frames form the reference chunk 𝑟(𝑘) = {𝑟𝑡}𝑡∈ℐ𝑘 , and the engine may additionally emit a caption 𝑒(𝑘) describing salient events within the chunk, which we append to the static prompt 𝑝 to obtain the chunk-level text condition 𝑝(𝑘) = 𝑝 ⊕ 𝑒 (𝑘). EdenLive then synthesizes the next displayed chunk ̂𝑥(𝑘) = ℛstream⒧𝑟(𝑘), 𝑦, 𝑝(𝑘), ℋ𝑘⒭, (3) where ℋ𝑘 denotes the retained generation history , and ̂𝑥(𝑘) in turn informs the user’s next actions, closing the loop. With the state 𝑠𝑡 conveyed to EdenLive only through 𝑟(𝑘) and 𝑝(𝑘), the renderer can be paired with diverse upstream programs without application-specific interfaces. Under this division of responsibility , collisions, scores, health bars, and other discrete outcomes are computed by 𝒯 rather than inferred from generated pixels, and exact text and numerical indicators can be rendered directly from 𝑠𝑡 and composited over the generated video. In contrast to recent interactive video world models [ 29, 79, 84, 109, 110], which model dynamics and appearance jointly and therefore cannot guarantee that such outcomes remain consistent with the underlying rules, our design keeps rule execution in the engine and dedicates the model to visual synthesis. 3.3 Offline Re-rendering System For offline applications, EdenLive re-renders or restyles existing footage, taking as the reference video 𝑟1∶𝑁 a complete recorded video or animation whose frames are all available before generation. For a fixed-length clip, it generates ̂𝑥1∶𝑁 = ℛbi⒧𝑟1∶𝑁 , 𝑦, 𝑝⒭, (4) where ℛbi denotes bidirectional generation that jointly synthesizes all 𝑁 output frames conditioned on the entire clip 𝑟1∶𝑁 , 𝑦 is the target first frame that anchors the output appearance, 𝑝 is a text condition authored in advance as either a single prompt or a time-varying prompt schedule, and ̂𝑥1∶𝑁 is the re-rendered video. Longer videos are instead processed in successive chunks by the streaming renderer ℛstream of Eq. (3), with each reference chunk 𝑟(𝑘) taken directly from the recorded sequence. EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 8 This mode makes EdenLive applicable to visual content creation, such as film, animation, and game production, as well as to data synthesis for embodied intelligence. 4 Method

  1. 1 Data

Training EdenLive requires reference–target video pairs with reliable correspondence. We construct such pairs through fine-to-coarse transformations of real-world and game-rendered videos and through coarse-to-fine synthesis from agent-built 3D proxy videos [ 6], and we complement them with unpaired open-source videos to improve generalization. Neither source guarantees perfect su- pervision, and we therefore curate each separately: paired data curation (Sec. 4.1.1) screens for spa- tial and temporal alignment, geometric granularity , and temporal consistency , whereas unpaired data curation ( Sec. 4.1.2) screens for visual quality , motion intensity , and semantic suitability . 1 Paired videos Paired clips Fine-to-coarse Coarse-to-fine Spatial & temporal alignment MLLM · DINOv3 Geometric granularity MLLM Temporal consistency Frame diff · AMT-S TransNetV2 Curated paired videos

  • Captions

2 Unpaired videos Unpaired clips Standardized segments Visual quality DOVER · Exposure / Blur OCR · SAM3 Motion intensity GMFlow · VGGT-Omega Semantic suitability MLLM Curated video clips

  • Captions

Figure 3 Data curation pipeline. Paired reference–target videos and unpaired open-source videos are screened by separate pipelines, and the curated data from both sources are accompanied by captions.

  1. 1. 1Paired Data Curation

Spatial and temporal alignment. Reference and target frames at the same index must depict cor- responding scene states. We stack frames sampled at identical indices from both videos and use a multimodal large language model (MLLM) [ 7] to assess their scene layout, viewpoint, and object placement, as well as camera motion and object trajectories across the sequence. We additionally average the cosine similarity between DINOv3 [ 81] patch features at corresponding grid positions to obtain a per-frame alignment score. Geometric granularity. During pair construction, the generated video may degrade toward its in- put: a fine-to-coarse reference may retain the detailed geometry of its source video, and a coarse-to- fine target may inherit the simplified geometry of its proxy . We prompt the MLLM to score whether sampled frames of the generated video exhibit the intended level of geometric detail, and discard pairs whose scores fall below a threshold. EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 9 T emporal consistency. We measure the intensity variation of each reference video as the mean absolute difference between consecutive sampled frames, its motion smoothness as the interpolation error of AMT -S [56], and its shot transitions with TransNetV2 [ 82], and exclude references with excessive flicker , irregular motion, or abrupt discontinuities.

  1. 1.2 Unpaired Data Curation

Visual quality. We split each video into segments that do not cross editing boundaries using shot or transition detection, score each segment with DOVER [ 93], mean brightness, and Laplacian-based sharpness, and detect visible text with PaddleOCR [ 73] and watermarks, logos, and borders with SAM3 [ 17]. Based on these measurements, we remove clips that are degraded, poorly exposed, blurred, or visually obstructed. Motion intensity. We measure image motion as the average magnitude of GMFlow [ 97] optical flow between sampled neighboring frames, and camera motion as the mean angular speed during rotation and the peak angular speed derived from VGGT -Omega [ 89] camera poses, and exclude clips with sustained fast rotation or abrupt viewpoint changes. Semantic suitability. From sampled frames of each clip, the MLLM generates a descriptive caption and multi-label category annotations under a fixed taxonomy; we exclude clips with any label in a predefined exclusion set and retain the captions with the selected clips. 4.2 Vision Encoder 4.2. 1 Shared Feature Space EdenLive accepts reference videos ranging from graybox proxies to recorded footage. These refer- ences convey the desired layout and motion, but their appearance may differ from the intended output. We therefore fine-tune a vision encoder on a large, independently curated set of reference– target image pairs so that references and targets that share the same layout are mapped to a shared feature space that retains their common structure while suppressing their appearance differences, which reduces reference appearance leakage in the generated output. This shared space allows a generator trained on self-paired ordinary videos (conditioned on their own features) to generalize to proxy inputs at inference. Inspired by Coarse-to-Real [ 30], we initialize the vision encoder 𝐸𝜙 from pretrained DINOv3 ViT - L/16 [ 81]. Reference and target images share the same backbone and learned linear projection. For an input image 𝐼, we project each backbone patch token and apply L2 normalization, yielding unit-normalized features f𝑞(𝐼) at spatial position 𝑞 and the feature grid 𝐸𝜙(𝐼) = [ f𝑞(𝐼)] 𝑞 of spatial resolution ̄𝐻 × ̄𝑊. The parameter set 𝜙 collects the backbone and projection parameters. Both are updated during fine-tuning and frozen during downstream generator training. For video condition- ing, we apply this image encoder frame by frame and leave temporal modeling to the downstream video generator . We next describe how we fine-tune the encoder on reference–target image pairs to align corresponding content in this shared feature space. 4.2.2 Representation Learning To exploit both the dense correspondence within each reference–target pair and the contrast across samples, we fine-tune the encoder with a combination of supervised and contrastive learning, com- plemented by domain-adversarial learning. Let {(𝐼 ref 𝑖 , 𝐼tgt 𝑖 )}𝐵 𝑖=1 denote a batch of 𝐵 reference–target image pairs, where 𝐵 is the global batch size across training workers, and let fref 𝑖,𝑞 and ftgt 𝑖,𝑞 denote the normalized features of 𝐼 ref 𝑖 and 𝐼 tgt 𝑖 at patch 𝑞. EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 10 Supervised learning. Given that the reference and target images in each pair share the same layout, we directly supervise the encoder by aligning their features at corresponding grid positions: ℒalign = 1 𝐵 ̄𝐻 ̄𝑊 𝐵  𝑖=1  𝑞 ⒧1 − fref 𝑖,𝑞, ftgt 𝑖,𝑞⒭ , (5) where ⟨⋅, ⋅⟩ denotes the inner product, which equals the cosine similarity for the unit-normalized features. Patch-level contrastive learning. To preserve discrimination across samples, we apply a symmetric, multi-positive InfoNCE objective [87] between domains at matching spatial positions. The positive set 𝒫(𝑖) includes pair 𝑖 and pairs sharing its group identifier , such as multiple references of the same target image; all other pairs in the batch are negatives. We obtain ℒctr by averaging ℓ𝑈→𝑉 𝑖,𝑞 over all samples, spatial positions, and both reference-to-target and target-to-reference directions. Domain-adversarial learning. To suppress domain-specific cues, we train a transformer discrimina- tor 𝐷𝜓 on the complete projected feature grid F𝑈 𝑖 = [f𝑈 𝑖,𝑞]𝑞, 𝑈 ∈ { ref, tgt}, with target and reference grids labeled 1 and 0, respectively: ℒdom = − 1 2𝐵 𝐵  𝑖=1 log ⒧1 − 𝐷𝜓(Fref 𝑖 )⒭ + log 𝐷𝜓(Ftgt 𝑖 ) . (7) The discriminator minimizes ℒdom, while gradient reversal [28] sends a reversed and scaled gradient to the encoder , updating both in a single backward pass. Overall objective. To realize the rendering interface in Eq. (1), dense features extracted from the reference video by the frozen vision encoder 𝐸𝜙 (Sec. 4.2) serve as the condition through which the world state is conveyed to the generator , alongside the target first frame and the text prompt. EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 11 4.3. 1 Reference-Conditioned Video Generation Reference injection. The pretrained generators operate in the latent space of a video VAE, which compresses the input video by a temporal factor 𝜌𝑡. To align the reference with these latent time steps, we encode one reference frame out of every 𝜌𝑡 frames. Each encoded frame is a feature grid of 𝐶𝑟 channels at resolution ̄𝐻 × ̄𝑊 (Sec. 4.2); we resize it to the spatial size of a latent frame and concatenate the resulting features with the native DiT input along the channel dimension, widening the patch-embedding projection by 𝐶𝑟 zero-initialized input channels. With our encoder mapping references of different appearance into a shared feature space ( Sec. 4.2), this concatenation injects the reference while mitigating the degradation of the output toward the reference appearance. Com- pared with token concatenation or additional cross-attention layers, it also leaves the token length and the attention cost of the base model unchanged. Self-paired training. The shared feature space further allows us to construct self-paired examples from unpaired videos, in which the reference and the target are the same clip and only the reference branch receives appearance perturbations before encoding, so that the generator is discouraged from reproducing the target by copying the reference appearance. Self-paired examples thus turn abundant unpaired videos into self-supervised training data, and we combine them with paired reference–target examples, which share the underlying motion but differ in rendering and anchor the intended cross-domain behavior . We train the generator with flow matching [ 67], minimizing the squared error between its predicted velocity and the flow-matching target, on all latent frames except the conditioned first frame. 4.3.2 Autoregressive Video Generation To satisfy the chunk-causal streaming requirement in Sec. 3.2 , we convert the bidirectional model of Sec. 4.3.1 into a causal, few-step autoregressive generator , a transition that has been explored in prior work [ 22, 41, 106, 113, 119, 120]. Specifically , teacher-forcing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) first adapts the model to chunk-causal attention, and few-step distillation on the model’s own roll- outs then concludes training. T eacher-forcing SFT .To expose the model to the causal structure used at inference while retaining the efficiency of parallel training, we divide a latent sequence into chunks 𝒞𝑘 of 𝐿 latent frames and, within a single forward pass, process the two-copy sequence [ 𝑧clean 1∶𝑇 | 𝑧 noisy 1∶𝑇 ], in which the clean copy serves as the history and the noisy copy as the prediction target. The attention mask allows a noisy query in 𝒞𝑘 to attend to the clean history preceding 𝒞𝑘 and to the noisy tokens within 𝒞𝑘, but never to future chunks, whereas clean queries attend only to clean history . To match deployment, we further bound the context to 𝑀 latent frames, so that the mask reproduces the key/value visibility of the streaming cache within a single teacher-forcing forward pass. Few-step distillation. The model is trained on ground-truth history during teacher-forcing SFT, whereas at inference it conditions on its own previously generated chunks. We close this gap with few-step distillation on the model’s own rollouts, initialized from teacher-forcing SFT and following the on-policy design of Self Forcing [ 41] and the rollout–replay formulation of Self-Gradient Forc- ing [120]. We generate chunks autoregressively with a few-step denoising schedule and a bounded key/value cache of 𝑀 latent frames, whose first 𝑆 latent frames form a permanent prefix and whose remainder holds the most recent history , and commit each predicted clean chunk to the cache before proceeding to the next one. The rollout states are then detached and replayed in a differentiable teacher-forcing pass whose attention visibility and rotary positions match those of the inference EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 12 cache (Sec. 4.4.1), which allows gradients to reach the generator without backpropagating through the entire denoising rollout. For the generator update, a frozen real score model, namely the bidirectional model of Sec. 4.3.1 , and a learned fake score model evaluate noisy versions of the replayed samples, following the score- difference construction of distribution matching distillation [ 105]. The normalized difference be- tween their predictions of the clean latent, 𝑔 ∝ ̂𝑧fake 0 − ̂𝑧real 0 , supplies the update direction for the generated latent 𝑧gen, and the generator minimizes the stop-gradient objective ℒSGF = 1 2 𝑧gen − stopgrad(𝑧gen − 𝑔) 2 2 , (9) whose gradient with respect to 𝑧gen equals 𝑔, while the fake score model is trained on generated samples with the same flow-matching loss. Both updates exclude the conditioned first frame. 4.4 Real- Time Inference To support real-time interaction with programs such as the agent-built games, we build a serving system that comprises four stages—player interaction, program simulation, generative rendering, and video streaming—and requires no additional training. Sec. 4.4.1 describes the inference-time adaptations of the generator and the serving optimizations we adopt, and Sec. 4.4.2 presents the module pipeline that couples the four stages, as illustrated in Fig. 4. 4.4. 1 Autoregressive Streaming Generation At inference, EdenLive generates the latent stream in chunks of 𝐿 latent frames and, as in training, attends to a bounded cache of 𝑀 latent frames, of which the first 𝑆 form a permanent attention sink [ 94] and the rest a rolling window . Each chunk is sampled in four denoising steps without classifier-free guidance, so that only the conditional branch and a single key/value cache are re- quired. We make three inference-time adaptations to this procedure. RoPE repositioning. Under a 3D rotary embedding [ 83], attention logits depend on the temporal offset between query and key; since sink keys keep their original indices while queries advance with the stream, this offset soon exceeds the range seen in training. We instead index frames by cache slot: keys are cached without rotation, and queries and keys are rotated at attention time according to their current slots. Once the cache is full, the temporal indices of the cached frames, from oldest to newest, are fixed to  0, … , 𝑆−1 sink , 𝑆, … , 𝑀−𝐿−1 window history , 𝑀−𝐿, … , 𝑀−1 current chunk , (10) so that query–key offsets remain within the training range throughout the session. Lightweight decoding. To reduce per-chunk decoding latency , we replace the native VAE decoder with the lightweight LightT AE decoder of LightX2V [61], which shares the compression ratios of the corresponding backbone and can therefore decode the same latents. Event-driven text conditioning. In our game instantiation, the program emits a short sentence for each salient gameplay event, such as a landed hit, and the text condition of a chunk appends the recent event sentences to the static scene prompt. The updated embeddings replace only the cross-attention key/value cache, leaving the self-attention history intact. Following OmniDreams [ 10], we build the inference system upon Flash- Dreams [26], and compile the transformer and the decoder with torch.compile [5]. At the start of a session, the generator warms up until the key/value cache reaches its full 𝑀 frames; since the key/value tensors are pre-allocated at full size, the attended length and hence all tensor shapes remain fixed from then on, and we capture the transformer step once as a CUDA graph and replay it for every subsequent chunk. In the multi-GPU setting, we additionally shard the token sequence of the diffusion transformer with Ulysses-style sequence parallelism [ 45]. 4.4.2 Module Pipeline Real-time interaction requires the program, the encoders, and the generator to sustain a common frame rate, and a player action to appear in the displayed video as early as the causal generator permits. Rather than executing the stages sequentially , which adds the time of every stage to each chunk, we pipeline them with a one-chunk lookahead ( Fig. 4) that hides simulation and encoding behind generation and thus raises throughput. Player interaction and program simulation. The program owns the game logic and the world state and advances at a fixed simulation step that is independent of the generator . For visual encoding, we capture one proxy frame per latent frame, namely the last frame of each group of four , which matches the 4× temporal compression of the video VAE. Generative rendering and streaming. Before the generator starts chunk 𝑘−1, a dedicated worker begins simulating and rendering chunk 𝑘 concurrently with the denoising of chunk 𝑘−1, and the visual encoding of chunk 𝑘 is chained to that rendering on a separate GPU stream, so that its features are ready when chunk 𝑘 is denoised; only the opening chunk exposes rendering and encoding on the critical path. To keep simulation and generation on a common clock, we stretch the rendering time of chunk 𝑘 to 𝜏render 𝑘 = max⒧𝜏gen 𝑘−1, 𝑛 𝑘/𝑓pre⒭, where 𝜏gen 𝑘−1 is the wall time of the preceding generation, 𝑛𝑘 is the number of frames in the chunk, and 𝑓pre is the upper bound on the presentation rate, so that the program state never advances ahead of the generated video. The text condition of chunk EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 14 𝑘, in contrast, is complete only once its simulation has finished. Since text encoding and LightT AE decoding are inexpensive relative to denoising, we keep both on the critical path: the generator produces chunk 𝑘 from the 𝐿 encoded reference frames, the text cache, and the self-attention history , and the decoded frames are streamed to the client over WebRTC, which also carries keyboard and mouse events back. Response delay and chunk size. Under this schedule, an input that arrives during the generation of chunk 𝑘−1 enters the simulation of chunk 𝑘 and becomes visible only once chunk 𝑘 has been generated, decoded, and played back; in steady state, the input-to-display delay is therefore about two chunk durations plus transmission and scales with the chunk length 𝐿. A shorter chunk reduces this delay , but a rollout of fixed duration then involves more autoregressive steps and is more prone to drift, and each step denoises fewer tokens, which lowers GPU parallelism and the achievable frame rate. We use 𝐿 = 3 latent frames to trade off the response delay against these costs. 5 Experiments We evaluate EdenLive through short- and long-horizon video generation, runtime measurements, and encoder fine-tuning ablations.

  1. 1 Evaluation Setup

Evaluation dataset. Our evaluation set spans diverse scenes, subject motions, camera movements, and interactions, including video restyling scenarios. The short- and long-horizon evaluations tar- get five- and thirty-second videos, respectively . Each sample provides a reference video, a target first frame, and text conditions. The reference conveys scene layout, camera motion, and coarse dynamics, while the target first frame specifies the desired subject appearance and visual style. Baselines and generation settings. The short-horizon baselines are C2R [ 30], CWM [ 20], depth- conditioned Wan2.1-VACE-14B (VACE) [49, 85], LTX-2.5 22B with the Layout-to-Render IC-LoRA (LTX 2.5) [33, 40, 60], Seedance 2.0 [80], and MiniMax H3 [71]. We compare them with the bidirec- tional 5B and 14B configurations of EdenLive. The long-horizon comparison evaluates autoregres- sive methods, including AgentGarten [ 21], StreamCWM [ 59], and the 5B and 14B configurations of EdenLive. Each method uses its supported conditioning interface. For VACE, we provide depth estimated by DA3 [ 63] from the reference video, the target first frame as a reference image, and the text prompt. To adapt StreamCWM to our reference inputs, we use OneFormer [46] semantic predictions and ViPE–DA3 [ 38, 63] depth estimates, while keeping the generator weights unchanged. Short-horizon comparisons use a static prompt. For long-horizon generation, EdenLive combines a static prompt with dynamic prompts associated with temporal intervals, whereas AgentGarten and StreamCWM use a static prompt. Evaluation metrics. We evaluate reference control, first-frame consistency , text alignment, tempo- ral consistency , and visual quality using the metrics below . Reference control. Reference-DINO Patch averages cosine similarities between corresponding spa- tial tokens, using the same frozen, fine-tuned DINOv3-L/16 encoder [81] and projection for all meth- ods. We also independently estimate reference and generated camera trajectories with DA3 [ 63], expressing each relative to its initial pose. Camera Rotation Error is the mean angular difference EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 15 in degrees; Camera Translation Error is the mean positional distance after least-squares scale align- ment, in the reference reconstruction scale. Both feature and trajectory comparisons align clips at normalized temporal positions. First-frame consistency. I2V Subject and I2V Background measure preservation of the target first frame using VBench++ [ 44]. T ext alignment. VQAScore [64] measures video–text semantic alignment using the Qwen2.5-VL- 3B [8] video backend. T emporal consistency. For long videos, we use VBL Subject [ 44] with semantic scene splitting disabled, and Helios Aesthetic Drift [ 107], which compares aesthetic quality over the first and last 15% of frames. Visual quality. DOVER-Technical [93] measures technical quality , applying the official standard- ization and sigmoid mapping to 0–100 per video before averaging. We use VBL Aesthetic for long videos [44]. VLM-based pairwise evaluation. We additionally use Gemini-3.8-Flash to assess a 45-case subset of the long-horizon evaluation set. The judge receives the target first frame, text conditions, and reference and candidate frame sequences sampled synchronously at 2 fps. It independently eval- uates reference control, first-frame consistency , physical plausibility , visual quality , and reference- appearance leakage, following the core instructions in Fig. 5. We evaluate every model pair in both presentation orders, average the order-swapped preferences, and fit a Bradley–Terry model sepa- rately for each dimension to obtain Elo ratings. Higher ratings indicate stronger preference; for Leakage Avoidance, they indicate less reference-appearance leakage. COMMON INSTRUCTIONS Judge one dimension at a time. Compare anonymous candidates A and B using the same reference anchors and timestamps. The reference video specifies motion and events; the target first frame specifies appearance. Respect the intended style specified by the text. Inspect early, middle, and late frames using only supplied evidence; allow ties. Reference control Match camera motion, subject paths, interaction targets, event order, and timing to the reference, including late events. Do not reward appearance similarity or more motion. First-frame consistency Track visible identity, design, materials, and style from the target first frame throughout the video. Allow normal changes in viewpoint, pose, lighting, and temporary occlusion. Physical plausibility Check shape, motion, support, contact, occlusion, and cause and effect across nearby frames. Judge visible contradictions within the intended physical or fictional setting. Visual quality Compare clarity, detail, surface rendering, exposure, and texture stability throughout the video. Respect the intended style; do not score task completion or favor photorealism. Appearance leakage Identify visible source-like appearance that conflicts with the target first frame. Poor rendering alone is not leakage; limited visibility does not establish its absence. Figure 5 Core evaluation instructions.   1. 1 Real- Time Previews of Agent-Built Games

EdenLive delegates the evolution of the world state to an upstream program and only synthesizes the visuals, and playable graybox games provide a natural testbed for this design: their programs maintain explicit game state, while their coarse geometry allows coding agents to build them rapidly without detailed assets or rendering effects and still yields a reference stream suitable for condition- ing. We first introduce EdenGolem, an agent skill that equips a coding agent to convert natural- language gameplay descriptions into playable 3D graybox games, and then demonstrate real-time interactive rendering and appearance control through the target first frame. repair State + evidence store tool-produced results, review bound to evidence hashes Figure 11 Overview of EdenGolem. Four stages progressively turn a gameplay description into a standalone, playable graybox game. Each stage must pass tool checks and a bound review before the next begins, with failed checks triggering repair within that stage; all results are recorded in a shared evidence store. EdenGolem. EdenGolem guides a coding agent to turn a natural-language gameplay description into a standalone, playable 3D graybox game ( Fig. 11 ). It creates the upstream program that re- sponds to player input and supplies visual references to EdenLive. Using stage-specific instructions and reusable graybox assets, the coding agent progressively builds the same game through four stages: – Intake defines what the game should do: its mechanics, key parameters, win/loss conditions, and scene theme. – Static scene builds a viewable graybox scene containing the environment, characters, and inter- active objects. – Interactive behavior combines controls, collisions, progression, and win/loss logic into a playable game. – Interface and acceptance adds the player-facing interface and verifies complete playthroughs, win/loss outcomes, restarting, and standalone execution. Three design choices make EdenGolem reliable. First, to ensure that completion is demonstrated rather than asserted, each stage must pass checks appropriate to its output before the next begins: interactive behavior is checked by running the game with real input and observing the resulting state, and the final stage checks the complete game as a whole. Second, to avoid unbounded repair loops and silent simplification of the request, failed checks trigger repairs within a fixed budget, and missing assets are replaced with simple primitives while the requested gameplay is preserved. Third, to generalize beyond familiar genres, we compose behavior from reusable capabilities such as locomotion, aiming, and timing rather than from genre labels, so that different combinations of mechanics share the same components. Integration with EdenLive. Games built by EdenGolem have coarse visuals but complete game logic (Fig. 12 ): during play , the game program handles movement, collisions, and win/loss decisions. To connect a game to EdenLive, we supply its rendered graybox frames and short descriptions of gameplay events as the visual and text conditions of each chunk, from which, together with the target first frame, EdenLive generates the displayed video. Fig. 13 shows the workflow from game creation with EdenGolem and first-frame generation to live preview . EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 23 Figure 12 Games built by EdenGolem. Fig. 14 shows three interactive games built by Eden- Golem, namely a street fight, a Sokoban-style puzzle, and a city-destruction game. Since the game state is maintained by the program rather than inferred from pixels, interaction outcomes strictly EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 24 follow the game rules: in the street fight, a kick lowers the opponent’s health from 100 to 83 only once the program registers the hit; in the puzzle, each push moves the crate exactly one tile and advances the move and push counters; and in the city-destruction game, a building collapses under the fire breath, which advances the destruction counter from 0 to 1 out of 10. Interface elements such as health bars, move counters, and destruction counters are rendered directly from the game state and overlaid on the generated video, and therefore remain exact and legible. Top to bottom: a street fight, a Sokoban-style puzzle, and a city-destruction game. Appearance control via the target first frame. A single game can be rendered in different visual styles without changing its code ( Fig. 15 ). The target first frame defines the desired appearance while preserving the spatial layout of the initial reference frame. In summary , EdenLive renders games in real time, whether they are built by EdenGolem or taken from existing projects, and varies their appearance without modifying the game program. The fol- lowing subsections extend the same interface to applications beyond games. 6.2 Appearance Exploration for Scenes and Animations EdenLive supports exploration of different visual appearances for the same scene or animation. References can come from agent-built blockouts, artist-authored coarse animations, or normal-map videos rendered from detailed geometry (Fig. 16). These inputs provide scene structure and motion, while the target first frame and text prompt specify the desired appearance. Keeping the reference fixed allows users to explore materials, lighting, and color palettes without modifying the underlying scene or animation. EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 25 Figure 15 Games under different target appearances. Each row shows the initial reference frame (left) and generated frames at matching times under two appearance conditions (middle and right), using the same reference video. Game inputs in the second and third rows come from SUNBREAK by Imirushik and Fishslop by vasu-devs, respectively . 6.3 Video Re-rendering and Stylization EdenLive can re-render recorded videos or live camera streams without requiring a scene graph or corresponding 3D assets (Fig. 16). The target first frame and text prompt specify a new appearance, such as cartoon or pixel art, while the reference video supplies the underlying actions and camera motion. 6.4 Embodied Data Augmentation EdenLive supports visual data augmentation for embodied tasks by varying the appearance of an interaction while retaining its motion and scene layout ( Fig. 16). For human egocentric videos, the target first frame and text prompt can specify a robot gripper in place of the human hand [ 47], a different manipulated object, or changes to object color and material. These transformations provide visual variants of an existing demonstration without requiring the interaction to be recorded again. 7 Limitations and Future Work EdenLive leaves the mapping between reference objects and their intended identities implicit; ex- plicit object associations could improve control over which entity each proxy represents. Its bounded temporal cache also lacks a dedicated memory for fine appearance details, motivating retrieval of object- or scene-specific visual evidence after extended occlusion or scene revisiting. Finally , the encoder provides a single learned representation without explicit control over which levels of refer- ence detail to preserve. Learning multi-level coarse–fine features could allow users to adjust control strength and granularity , balancing reference fidelity with freedom for visual refinement. EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 27 8 Conclusion We have presented EdenLive, a real-time generative renderer that treats the reference video as the interface between an interactive program and neural visual synthesis: the upstream program ex- ecutes the rules and maintains the world state, whereas EdenLive renders the resulting reference video, guided by a target first frame and a text prompt, into detailed frames. A fine-tuned vision encoder that maps heterogeneous references into a shared feature space, together with a distilled chunkwise autoregressive generator served in a pipelined system, makes this division practical un- der real-time constraints. Through their visual references, diverse upstream sources, ranging from graybox game engines to camera recordings, can drive the same renderer , so that a single interface supports agent-built game previews, appearance exploration, video re-rendering, and embodied data augmentation without application-specific designs. We hope that this work encourages viewing the visual reference as a general interface to generative rendering, through which existing engines, tools, and recordings can be connected to neural renderers, and that decoupling state from render- ing offers a practical path toward interactive worlds whose logic remains exact and inspectable in code while their appearance is synthesized by generative models. 9 Authors

item.content:encoded:
一句话：VAST 开源的 5B 实时生成式渲染器，单张 5090 上 720P 超 24FPS，端到端延迟百毫秒级。

要点：

  • 输入是「代理视频」（引擎或编码智能体渲染的简化画面）加目标首帧与文本提示，模型按参考的布局与运镜实时重绘成写实或指定画风。
  • 用视觉编码器把几何粒度差异很大的参考（2D/3D 代理、法线图、实拍视频）映射到共享特征空间，抑制参考外观泄漏进生成画面。
  • 蒸馏成少步分块自回归模型，服务端把程序模拟、参考编码与生成排成带一块前瞻的流水线；权重、推理代码与技术报告全部开源。

为什么值得看：这是「状态由上游程序维护、视觉由生成模型负责」这条路线目前最完整的可跑实现：世界状态可检查、可修改、可测试，交互还能挂到程序暴露的任意量上。做 AI 原生引擎时，可以直接照它的接口拆状态层与渲染层。

中文摘要：VAST 的 Project Eden 推出 EdenLive，一个面向交互应用的实时生成式视频渲染器。它把世界状态与视觉渲染解耦：上游程序（游戏引擎或编码智能体生成的代理画面）显式维护游戏逻辑与世界状态，EdenLive 只负责把简化参考视频、目标首帧和提示词渲染成高质量画面。这既让状态可检查可修改，也把有限模型容量集中到视觉合成上。为处理不同几何粒度的参考，作者用视觉编码器把它们映射到共享特征空间，再以这些特征条件化视频生成，减轻外观泄漏。为了让生成流式化，生成器被蒸馏成少步分块自回归模型，并部署在把模拟、编码、生成三级流水化的服务系统里，带一块前瞻。实验显示参考控制与画质都不错，且在单张 GPU 上以 720P 输出超过 24FPS。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：VAST·技术报告（English）

原文发布：2026-10-18

本期推送：2026-10-22

TECHNICAL REPORT EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering from Any Visual Reference Zehuan Huang1,*, Tian- Xing Xu1,*, Chunli Peng1,*, Cheng Zhang1,*, Zeyi Zheng1,†, Yifei Song1,†, Zekai Gu1,†, Zhipeng Yu1, Peng Wang1,‡, Y an-Pei Cao1,✉ 1VAST *Equal contribution †Intern at VAST ‡Project lead ✉ Corresponding author CORRESPONDENCE Yan-Pei Cao caoyanpei@gmail.com PROJECT https://vast-eden.ai/?p=edenlive CODE https://github.com/VAST-AI-Research/EdenLive WEIGHTS https://huggingface.co/VAST-AI/EdenLive DATE October 2026 Figure 1 Real-time generative rendering from diverse visual references. Each tile pairs a reference (left) with the generated frame at the same timestamp (right). Examples include game and 2D proxies, normal maps, scene previews, video restyling, and embodied scenes. All outputs use the EdenLive 5B model. EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 2 ABSTRACT We present EdenLive, a real-time generative video renderer for inter- active applications in the Project Eden series 1. EdenLive continuously renders enhanced and stylized video from reference videos of different geometric granularities that range from proxy videos, namely sim- plified renderings produced by a coding agent or a game engine, to directly recorded videos, with a target first frame and a text prompt as input to guide the appearance. This design conveys the world state to the model through the reference video and thereby decouples its interaction-induced evolution from visual rendering: the upstream code or engine maintains the game logic and world state explicitly and precisely , whereas EdenLive renders reference video into detailed visual output. This separation enables the world state to be inspected, modified, and tested directly , and interaction can extend to any quantity exposed by the upstream program. It also relieves the neural model from learning both state transitions and appearance, allowing the limited model capacity available for real-time deployment to concentrate on visual synthesis. To handle references for diverse rendering scenarios, we employ a vision encoder that maps them into a shared feature space despite their differences in geometric granularity and appearance, and condition the video generation model on these features, which mitigates leakage of the reference appearance into the generated video. To enable streaming generation, we distill the generator into a few-step chunk-wise autoregressive model and deploy it in a serving system that pipelines program simulation, reference encoding, and generation with a one-chunk lookahead, so that the system presents the generated video in real time and responds to user interaction. Experiments on short- and long-horizon generation show that EdenLive achieves good reference control and visual quality , while generating 720P videos in real time at over 24 FPS on a single GPU. 1 https://www.tripo3d.ai/research/project-eden EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 3 1 Introduction World models characterize how an environment evolves in response to actions and events [ 32, 34], a capability that underpins simulation for autonomous driving [ 10, 37], embodied intelligence [ 9, 100], and interactive games [18, 86]. Two properties are central in these settings: interactivity , since a player or an agent chooses its next action on the basis of its current observation, and low latency , since each observation must follow the corresponding action quickly enough to sustain closed-loop interaction. Video-based world models have recently advanced rapidly in both respects by leveraging the generative priors of large pretrained video models [ 71, 85, 103]: starting from latent-action and action-conditioned models [ 4, 13, 86], recent methods synthesize environments that users explore through keyboard, mouse, and camera inputs [ 36, 39, 48, 54, 79, 84, 92], alter through text-triggered events [ 23, 29, 74], and revisit with the help of meory mechanisms [ 75, 95, 99], while achieving increasingly photorealistic visual quality . These models, however , learn the evolution of the world state jointly with its visual appearance in a single generative network, which predicts each new observation from the generated history and the current input. The state of an interactive world is complex and heterogeneous, spanning entity positions and attributes, numerical quantities such as health and score, objects outside the current view , and the rules that determine how each action takes effect. Scaling model parameters and training data can improve how well such state is captured implicitly , but the same network must then devote its capacity to both dynamics and appearance, which is in tension with the computational budget permitted by real-time deployment. Moreover , the state is held only implicitly in the latent context and the generated frames, so it cannot be directly inspected, edited, or verified [ 42, 70], and control remains largely confined to actions, camera trajectories, and text prompts rather than extending to individual entities and their interaction rules. To address this limitation, in Project Eden [ 88] we proposed to decouple the evolution of the world state from its visual rendering. An evolving structured state persists over time, is updated by actions, and can be queried from different viewpoints. A state-to-observation interface converts this state into camera-conditioned constraints that expose its local semantics and geometry . And a generative renderer maps these state-derived constraints to high-fidelity visual output. In this work, we instan- tiate this principle with EdenLive. Upstream code or an engine maintains and advances the world state by executing the game logic and interaction mechanisms. The engine renders each updated state into a temporally aligned video stream. Then a reference-conditioned, real-time generative renderer , which is trained starting from pretrained video diffusion models [ 85], follows the scene layout, camera motion, and dynamics conveyed by this video stream while synthesizing detailed visual output. Compared with modeling state evolution and appearance jointly in pixels, this sepa- ration keeps the game logic, interaction mechanisms, and world state explicit and precise: they can be inspected, modified, and tested directly , and interaction can extend to any quantity exposed by the upstream program. It also relieves the neural model from learning both state transitions and appearance, allowing the limited model capacity available for real-time deployment to concentrate on visual synthesis. We refer to the conditioning video supplied to the renderer as a reference video , which is either a proxy video , namely a simplified rendering produced by a coding agent, a game engine, or a workbench that captures scene layout, camera motion and coarse dynamics, or a recorded video that is used directly as the reference. This formulation leads to a question: can a single renderer accept reference videos from diverse upstream sources, ranging from proxies of 2D and 3D games to recorded footage, and render them in real time? Answering this question requires the renderer to EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 4 recover layout and motion from references of widely varying geometry and appearance without copying unwanted reference appearance, learn despite the limited availability of paired reference– target videos, and generate causally and continuously within a real-time latency budget. To address these challenges, We present EdenLive, a real-time generative video renderer that con- ditions on a reference video, a target first frame, and a text prompt. To handle heterogeneous references, we condition the generator on dense features rather than on reference pixels, extracted by a vision encoder that we fine-tune on reference–target image pairs to map reference videos that differ in appearance and geometric granularity but share layout and motion into a shared feature space. Conditioning on this feature space eases the learning of the generator and mitigates the degradation of its output toward the appearance of the reference video. Furthermore, the same feature space allows unpaired videos to serve as self-paired training data, in which the generator is conditioned on features extracted from an appearance-perturbed copy of the target video itself. To enable streaming generation, we distill the generator into a few-step model that performs chunk- wise autoregressive inference over a bounded attention cache, so that each chunk depends only on the current reference frames and the retained history . Finally , our serving system overlaps upstream simulation and neural rendering, and streams the decoded frames to the user . Our contributions are threefold: – A vision encoder fine-tuning approach that aligns the representations of reference–target image pairs, enabling a generator trained on both self-paired and paired videos to be controlled by reference videos at inference. – A streaming generative renderer that combines few-step chunkwise generation, a bounded his- torical context, and pipelined serving to synthesize video continuously from evolving reference videos. – A complete real-time interactive system built on EdenLive, in which an upstream engine executes the game rules and maintains the world state while EdenLive renders the resulting proxy videos into the displayed stream; the system supports real-time previews of agent-built games with exact game state and appearance control through the target first frame, and extends to the offline re- rendering and stylization of recorded videos. We evaluate both the learned representation and the complete renderer through image and video encoder ablations, short- and long-horizon generation comparisons, and runtime measurements. Compared with the pretrained DINOv3 encoder , the fine-tuned encoder improves the transfer from proxy conditions to detailed outputs in image generation and reduces camera rotation error in video generation, and the generation comparisons show competitive reference adherence and appearance preservation. The optimized 5B renderer exceeds 24 FPS at 1280 × 704 on a single NVIDIA H100, measured from model-side condition processing to decoded frames in CPU memory . 2 Related Work

  1. 1 Controllable Video Generation

Large pretrained video diffusion models [ 52, 71, 85, 103] provide strong priors over appearance and motion, but precise structural control often requires additional conditioning. Beyond first-frame appearance editing [ 53, 72], a broad line of work introduces dense visual cues to guide scene structure, object motion, and camera motion, such as depth, edges, and segmentation [ 2, 3, 19, 49, 90], or through camera poses, trajectories, optical-flow-warped noise, and rendered 3D caches [ 14, EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 5 35, 77, 91]. These conditioning signals differ in both their representation and the level of structural detail they provide. These conditioning interfaces also vary in how much scene structure they require, ranging from dense rendering buffers to coarse proxies and sparse geometric primitives. Buffer-based methods [ 43, 58, 62, 78] receive dense rendering buffers to provide rich scene attributes for photorealistic image and video synthesis. Some works [ 15, 50] utilize coarse meshes and rendered proxies to reduce the required geometric detail while retaining control over layout and motion. ProxyUp [ 117] uses proxy videos with foreground masks to preserve selected dynamics while regenerating appearance and surroundings. Geometric conditions such as depth, 3D point tracks, and oriented bounding boxes also guide video generation [ 11, 31, 98]. These approaches rely on geometric representations or region-specific guidance that must be constructed or extracted from the source. Inspired by the feature-based conditioning of Coarse-to-Real [ 30], EdenLive learns a shared rep- resentation for references with varying appearance and geometric granularity . Whereas Coarse-to- Real uses a frozen DINOv3 encoder [81], we fine-tune the encoder on a large, independently curated set of reference–target image pairs to preserve shared structure while suppressing appearance dif- ferences. This alignment reduces reference appearance leakage and enables a generator trained on self-paired ordinary videos to generalize to proxy inputs. 2.2 Interactive World Models Interactive world models formulate environment simulation from generation history and user in- teraction. Genie [ 13] learns latent actions from unlabeled videos, while action-conditioned diffu- sion models demonstrate playable game simulation [4, 86]. Subsequent video world models extend action- and camera-conditioned generation across diverse environments [18, 36, 39, 54, 79, 84, 92, 111], with advances in real-time interaction and long-horizon generation [48, 112, 118]. Interaction also extends to text-driven events and scene editing [ 23, 29, 74] and object interactions [ 96], while Cosmos 3 [ 1] unifies multimodal understanding, visual generation, and action prediction. When world evolution is modeled through observation prediction, consistency with underlying rules is learned rather than enforced by an executable state-transition mechanism, and control depends on the inputs the model has learned to interpret. A recent trend in interactive world modeling is to decouple state evolution from visual rendering, using video models as renderers. The Project Eden research preview [ 88] outlines a shared-state architecture in which camera-conditioned semantic and geometric constraints connect the evolving world state to generative rendering. Related efforts make world state explicit: StatePlay [ 66] jointly predicts game-state variables and visual content, while Marionette [ 70] and MASS [ 16] advance an explicit world state through learned dynamics and render it into observations. Other systems dele- gate state evolution to executable logic. Code World Model [ 20], Programmable World Model [42], Oneira [102], and CoDeR [24] use coding agents to maintain and evolve explicit world states, which are translated into proxy videos or spatial conditions. AgentGarten [ 21] and Magpie [108] advance states through simulators and game engines, while GameDirector [ 65] introduces an agentic layer that tracks game state and enforces gameplay rules. Several renderers use specialized geometric interfaces, including oriented boxes, depth and surface normals, or articulated poses [ 21, 42, 70]. EdenLive learns a common reference-video interface across varying appearance and geometric gran- ularity , allowing diverse upstream programs to condition the same renderer on inputs ranging from agent-built proxies to recorded videos. EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 6 2.3 Acceleration, Distillation, and Streaming Few-step diffusion methods reduce generation cost by distilling iterative sampling into fewer model evaluations. Latent Consistency Models [ 69] learn consistency mappings for few-step latent-space synthesis, while Distribution Matching Distillation [104, 105] trains a one-step generator to match a diffusion teacher’s output distribution. Streaming video generation additionally requires causal pre- diction from generated histories. CausVid [106] distills a bidirectional teacher into a few-step causal generator , while Self Forcing [ 41] addresses the training-inference history mismatch through au- toregressive training on the model’s own predictions. Subsequent work extends generation to longer sequences [22, 101] and improves autoregressive distillation through student initialization, rollout perturbation, and gradient propagation through historical context [ 113, 115, 116, 119, 120]. Sus- tained streaming also requires bounded context and efficient execution. Attention sinks [ 94], com- bined with rolling windows, retain initial tokens and recent history while bounding the context size. Streaming pipelines use batched denoising and scheduling for continuous frame delivery [ 25, 51], while streaming video-to-video methods preserve temporal consistency through historical feature reuse or dedicated training objectives [ 57, 114]. EdenLive combines few-step chunkwise autore- gressive generation with a bounded cache containing an attention sink and a rolling window . Its serving system overlaps upstream simulation and reference encoding with generation, conditioning each chunk only on reference frames that have already arrived. 3 Problem Formulation and System Overview

  1. 1 Problem Formulation

We decouple the interaction-induced evolution of the world state from its visual presentation: an upstream program maintains the world state explicitly , whereas EdenLive acts as a reference- conditioned generative renderer that synthesizes only its appearance. Given an 𝑁-frame reference video 𝑟1∶𝑁 , a target first frame 𝑦, and a text condition 𝑝, EdenLive generates a refined or restyled video ̂𝑥1∶𝑁 = ℛ(𝑟1∶𝑁 , 𝑦, 𝑝), (1) in which the three inputs play complementary roles: the reference video conveys the evolving world state, namely the layout, camera motion, object trajectories, and event timing; the first frame, aligned with the opening reference view , anchors subject identity and appearance; and 𝑝 is ei- ther a single prompt held fixed over the sequence or a time-varying prompt schedule, which may include time-specific event descriptions in interactive applications. Achieving this in real time poses two challenges: a generator conditioned on reference videos that range from coarse proxies to recorded videos tends to degrade toward their appearance, and train- ing a model for real-time, minute-scale generation is difficult. We address them with a vision en- coder that maps reference videos into a shared feature space ( Sec. 4.2) and a distilled, chunkwise autoregressive generator (Secs. 4.3 and 4.4), respectively . 3.2 Real- Time Interactive System The real-time generation capability of EdenLive allows it to be integrated into an interactive system that responds to user input as it arrives. Fig. 2 illustrates the system we build upon EdenLive, which operates as a closed loop over successive chunks indexed by 𝑘. While viewing the most recently displayed chunk ̂𝑥(𝑘−1), the user issues keyboard and mouse actions 𝑎𝑡 at interaction steps 𝑡 ∈ ℐ𝑘, where ℐ𝑘 denotes the steps covered by chunk 𝑘. With the state 𝑠𝑡 conveyed to EdenLive only through 𝑟(𝑘) and 𝑝(𝑘), the renderer can be paired with diverse upstream programs without application-specific interfaces. Under this division of responsibility , collisions, scores, health bars, and other discrete outcomes are computed by 𝒯 rather than inferred from generated pixels, and exact text and numerical indicators can be rendered directly from 𝑠𝑡 and composited over the generated video. In contrast to recent interactive video world models [ 29, 79, 84, 109, 110], which model dynamics and appearance jointly and therefore cannot guarantee that such outcomes remain consistent with the underlying rules, our design keeps rule execution in the engine and dedicates the model to visual synthesis. 3.3 Offline Re-rendering System For offline applications, EdenLive re-renders or restyles existing footage, taking as the reference video 𝑟1∶𝑁 a complete recorded video or animation whose frames are all available before generation. For a fixed-length clip, it generates ̂𝑥1∶𝑁 = ℛbi⒧𝑟1∶𝑁 , 𝑦, 𝑝⒭, (4) where ℛbi denotes bidirectional generation that jointly synthesizes all 𝑁 output frames conditioned on the entire clip 𝑟1∶𝑁 , 𝑦 is the target first frame that anchors the output appearance, 𝑝 is a text condition authored in advance as either a single prompt or a time-varying prompt schedule, and ̂𝑥1∶𝑁 is the re-rendered video. Longer videos are instead processed in successive chunks by the streaming renderer ℛstream of Eq. (3), with each reference chunk 𝑟(𝑘) taken directly from the recorded sequence. EdenLive: Real- Time Generative Rendering 8 This mode makes EdenLive applicable to visual content creation, such as film, animation, and game production, as well as to data synthesis for embodied intelligence. 4 Method

  1. 1 Data

Training EdenLive requires reference–target video pairs with reliable correspondence. We construct such pairs through fine-to-coarse transformations of real-world and game-rendered videos and through coarse-to-fine synthesis from agent-built 3D proxy videos [ 6], and we complement them with unpaired open-source videos to improve generalization. Neither source guarantees perfect su- pervision, and we therefore curate each separately: paired data curation (Sec. 4.1.1) screens for spa- tial and temporal alignment, geometric granularity , and temporal consistency , whereas unpaired data curation ( Sec. 4.1.2) screens for visual quality , motion intensity , and semantic suitability . 1 Paired videos Paired clips Fine-to-coarse Coarse-to-fine Spatial & temporal alignment MLLM · DINOv3 Geometric granularity MLLM Temporal consistency Frame diff · AMT-S TransNetV2 Curated paired videos
