Appendix A Implementation Details

A.1 Audiovisual Generator and Action Conditioning

We build on the LTX [(HaCohen et al., 2026)] audiovisual architecture, using the LTX-2.3 22B dev backbone [(Lightricks, 2026)]. Separate video and audio autoencoders produce latent sequences processed by coupled transformer streams. Each stream uses self-attention and text cross-attention, with cross-modal attention connecting video and audio. At 20 video frames per second, each generated chunk contains two video latent steps, corresponding to 16 new frames, and 20 audio latent steps, corresponding to 0.8 seconds. Generation is causal between chunks. Tokens within a chunk are denoised jointly.

The action interface provides four continuous movement/camera channels and supports fire, jump, and reload inputs. For each generated video latent step, the eight aligned raw-frame vectors are concatenated into a 32-dimensional continuous-action vector Jₜ and broadcast over spatial locations. After projection, per-layer networks produce feature scale and shift through FiLM [(Perez et al., 2018)]

h^′_ℓ,t=(1+γ_ℓ(Jₜ))⊙h_ℓ,t+β_ℓ(Jₜ).

(6)

Buttons remain at the raw-frame rate and enter through an additional cross-attention residual. Each generated video latent attends to its eight aligned action frames and earlier retained actions, with future actions masked. Temporal rotary embeddings [(Su et al., 2024)] align these queries and keys. Continuous scale/shift outputs and button-attention output projections are initialized to zero. The action branches act on the video stream, while cross-modal attention connects the resulting dynamics to audio.

Writing zⱼ for the audiovisual latents of generated chunk j, the causal model uses a compact context

[first-frame anchor|z_k-4:k-1|Tₖ|r].

(7)

Here r denotes the encoded character reference. At steady state, four previous chunks are clean context and only the target chunk Tₖ is denoised. Tokens in each generated chunk attend to tokens in that chunk and earlier chunks. Reference-image tokens attend only to one another and are readable directly by the target video chunk. Direct cross-modal attention excludes the reference. The anchor and reference receive no action or text updates. As the window advances, old history is removed and temporal positions are rebased locally. The same layout supports zero to three history chunks during startup. An optional cache reuses clean-context keys and values within a chunk’s denoising steps. It is rebuilt when the window advances.

A.2 Chunk-wise Prompt Routing and Guidance Construction

The generator’s prompt does not encode numerical health, hit counters, or internal generation identifiers. High-frequency player controls remain in the action tensors, while text specifies the actor behavior and consequences those controls should realize.

Each chunk has its own text condition cⱼ=(g,pⱼ). The global description covers the environment, weapon, and character appearance. Local guidance describes the current actor behavior, visibility, and observable interaction outcomes. Each chunk’s combined text condition is encoded independently, and the resulting context tokens are concatenated. The text attention mask routes both video and audio queries to the corresponding prompt, with padding excluded and anchor/reference queries receiving no text-attention update in the causal model. In bidirectional adaptation, the initial frame instead shares the first generated chunk’s prompt. Historical chunks use their corresponding prompts, while the target directly attends only to its current prompt. Historical context remains available through audiovisual attention, which is causal across chunks during autoregressive training and generation.

At inference, a deterministic text renderer converts the controller’s structured predictions and rule-updated state into local guidance.

A.3 Training Objectives and Distillation

Generator training optimizes the audiovisual backbone and action branches while freezing the text encoder and autoencoders. The Interaction Agent uses InternVL3-8B [(Zhu et al., 2025)] without task-specific fine-tuning, while the rule engine and prompt compiler are programmed. The loader aligns video, audio, player controls, reference images, and chunk text conditions at shared temporal boundaries.

Training hyperparameters.

We train on 16 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs with a global batch size of 16 and BF16 mixed precision. Table 1 lists the generator learning rates. Consistency distillation and distribution matching use AdamW with β=(0,0.999), weight decay 0.01, and 100 warmup steps. The learned score model uses a learning rate of 10⁻⁵. Both refiner stages use 8-bit AdamW with a learning rate of 10⁻⁵, β=(0.9,0.999), weight decay 0.01, and 100 warmup steps. The domain LoRA has rank 384 and scaling parameter α=384.

Action and prompt adaptation.

Basic Dynamics data teach control-conditioned local dynamics, while the Interaction data add chunk-local behavior and outcome guidance. Arena post-training starts from the Interaction-trained bidirectional model and adapts it to sustained combat before causal training and distillation. Bidirectional adaptation uses chunk-specific text conditions and a linear-path flow-matching objective [(Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023)]. For modality m∈{v,a}, a clean latent sequence zᵐ is perturbed as zᵐ_σ=(1-σ)zᵐ+σεᵐ, with Gaussian noise εᵐ. The model predicts the flow velocity εᵐ-zᵐ and is trained by minimizing

L_bi=∑_m∈{v,a}λₘ𝔼[∥v_θᵐ(z_σ,σ;u,c)-(εᵐ-zᵐ)∥_Ωₘ²],

(8)

where c denotes the sequence of chunk text conditions and the norm averages supervised tokens, excluding the conditioning video frame and ineligible audio samples. The text attention mask restricts each generated chunk to its own text condition, while audiovisual self- and cross-attention remain bidirectional at this stage.

Sliding-window autoregressive training.

We initialize the causal model from the adapted checkpoint and train the layout in Equation 7. The anchor, reference, and available history chunks remain clean. Noise is applied only to the next chunk. For clean target latents zₖ, Gaussian noise εₖ, and noise level σ∈[0,1], the noisy input and predicted clean estimate are

z_k,σ=(1-σ)zₖ+σεₖ,(9)
ẑₖ=z_k,σ-σv_θ(z_k,σ,σ|Hₖ,uₖ,cₖ).

Here v_θ predicts flow velocity, and Hₖ, uₖ, and cₖ follow Equation 5. Superscripts v and a denote video and audio. The target-chunk reconstruction objective is

L_AR=𝔼 [w(σ)(MSE(ẑₖᵛ,zₖᵛ)+λₐMSE(ẑₖᵃ,zₖᵃ))],

(10)

where w(σ)=\exp[-2(σ-0.5)²] weights the noise level and λₐ=0.16 weights the audio loss. Squared errors are averaged over target tokens only. This stage uses ground-truth history. Bidirectional and autoregressive adaptation share the chunk-wise prompt routing used at inference, but only autoregressive adaptation enforces temporal causality through audiovisual attention.

Consistency distillation and startup coverage.

For few-step generation, the implementation follows the teacher-forcing consistency initialization in Causal-rCM [(Zheng et al., 2026a)]. This recipe builds on Consistency Models [(Song et al., 2023)], sCM [(Lu & Song, 2025)], and rCM [(Zheng et al., 2026b)]. A frozen autoregressive teacher advances a noisy sample between nearby noise levels. At the advanced point, the current student produces a clean estimate without gradients, which serves as the consistency target for its prediction at the starting point. Video and audio both contribute to this loss. Checkpoint EMA is maintained separately.

Startup and continued generation use the same sliding-window context layout. The training recipe alternates an update with four history chunks and an update with zero, one, two, or three history chunks.

The final Arena recipe further distills text classifier-free guidance [(Ho & Salimans, 2022)] into the student. The teacher combines conditional and text-unconditional predictions while retaining player actions and visual context. The student uses a single conditional forward pass per denoising step.

Self-forcing distribution matching.

After consistency distillation, we apply self-forcing distribution matching [(Huang et al., 2025)] as the second stage of the Causal-rCM [(Zheng et al., 2026a)] recipe. The objective follows DMD [(Yin et al., 2024b)] and DMD2 [(Yin et al., 2024a)], with bidirectional-teacher supervision of an autoregressive student as in CausVid [(Yin et al., 2025)]. One student starts from the initial frame, generates four startup chunks, and continues for five additional chunks using the same reference, chunk-wise prompt routing, and sliding context. No ground-truth history is inserted into this rollout. Both the startup chunks and the later chunks receive distribution-matching supervision.

A frozen bidirectional score model and a learned score model for student samples evaluate the same perturbed rollout with aligned controls and semantic conditions. These score models receive no reference-image tokens, so their text conditions describe character appearance explicitly. The final Arena recipe applies text guidance to the frozen score model, while the learned score model and student remain conditional. Their normalized difference in denoised predictions defines a stop-gradient target. The generator then replays the recorded final denoising step of each chunk to optimize a masked video–audio regression loss against that target. Rollout generation runs without gradients, avoiding storage of its full computation graph.

Video refiner training.

We construct temporally aligned training pairs from the same arena clip. Its original VAE encoding serves as the target. To construct the degraded input, we spatially downsample the RGB frames, encode them, and apply a frozen LTX-2.3 2× spatial upscaler v1.1 [(Lightricks, 2026)] to restore the target spatial size. We train a domain LoRA [(Hu et al., 2022)] on the refiner with truncated flow matching [(Lipman et al., 2023)] between the original target and a noise-perturbed upsampled latent. The refiner is first trained bidirectionally. Causal adaptation starts from this checkpoint, conditions on the first frame, character reference, and up to four clean history chunks, and applies loss only to the current chunk. Training uses ground-truth history, while deployment uses previously refined outputs. Both stages optimize only the domain LoRA, keeping the upsampler and backbone frozen. The official LTX-2.3 distilled LoRA v1.1 [(Lightricks, 2026)] is disabled for this training loss and enabled for few-step refinement at inference.

Inference settings.

The distilled Arena generator uses four denoising steps with noise levels (1,0.9375,0.8333,0.625,0). Refinement uses two denoising steps with noise levels (0.725,0.421875,0), a classifier-free guidance scale of 1, and no spatiotemporal guidance.

A.4 State Updates and Visual Verification

Prediction and state commitment.

At a chunk boundary, the controller retains the corrected state and uses predicted events to compute provisional outcomes and local guidance. Generation does not commit those predictions to the persistent ledger. After decoding, verification produces the feedback used to obtain the next retained state in Equation 2. The implementation recomputes this state from the saved pre-generation state and observed events, preventing predicted and verified damage from being counted twice. The first chunk uses the initial frame and configured state without a preceding verification step. The retained gameplay state is stored independently of the generator’s sliding visual context. When earlier frames leave that context, their recorded interaction consequences remain available to subsequent rule updates and enter generation through the current guidance.

Observation selection and shot prediction.

The online Arena implementation uses decoded RGB frames directly, without an observation refiner. Within each chunk, it selects the first frame of each uninterrupted firing interval and every fourth frame thereafter (5 Hz at 20 FPS). Before generation, the latest available frame is the preceding chunk’s last frame, or the initial image at startup. For each selected firing time, a calibrated control-to-pixel mapping estimates the image displacement from the intervening controls. We translate the latest frame accordingly, take a 320×320 crop centered on the screen, and overlay a hollow green aiming ring. The Interaction Agent receives this projected crop and a separate enemy appearance reference, and predicts whether the enemy’s body overlaps the marked aiming region.

Visual verification.

After generation, we decode the corresponding actual firing frames, the chunk’s final frame, and the frame three positions before it. Together with the pre-generation frame, these form the sampled observations Iₖ₋₁. A firing-frame audit receives the selected firing frames in temporal order, with the same ring overlay, alongside the pre-generation and two late frames. Unlike prediction, verification uses full frames rather than center crops. The ring radius is 5% of the shorter image dimension and leaves its interior unobstructed. A separate state query places the final frame first and uses the pre-generation and earlier late frame only as temporal context. It classifies the enemy as alive, dead, or not visible in the final frame. Both queries receive an appearance reference for identity only. Full frames are padded to a 2:1 canvas and the reference to a square, without cropping their contents. Aim markers appear only in the VLM inputs. The requested outcome is the condition being checked, not visual evidence, and verification uses separate calls from prediction.

The rule engine specifies intended transitions, while committed visual outcomes ground the state used for subsequent interaction. When an observed outcome contradicts a prediction, the controller revises the affected state and derives subsequent guidance from that revision. Numerical attributes remain rule-maintained rather than directly estimated from images, and occlusion alone is not treated as death.

Action constraints and opponent behavior.

Ammunition gates the executed fire commands and is consumed when a shot is permitted, independently of whether it hits. Before an enemy can attack, the Interaction Agent checks visual preconditions, including whether the enemy is visible and facing the player. When these conditions hold, attacks are sampled at a configured rate, and each attack hits with a preset probability. Successful hits subtract a fixed per-shot damage from player health. Reaching zero health disables player controls and adds the corresponding terminal outcome to guidance. For opponent behavior, the agent assesses movement feasibility from the current scene. The behavior policy combines this assessment with retained state and the configured strategy to select a movement description. Attack rules and strategy-transition conditions can be edited in the rule layer. Numerical state remains in the controller, while the generator receives observable behavior and outcome descriptions. World-side events thus combine visual assessment of the current scene with executable game rules that update player state and constrain subsequent controls.

A.5 Design Rationale

Reciprocal interaction concerns the causal effects of player actions on the world and of world events on the player. It does not require every game mechanic to be learned. Executable rules make damage, ammunition, and termination conditions explicit and configurable, while scene-conditioned behavior reasoning determines how actors act under those conditions. Their combination connects world-side decisions to persistent consequences for the player during continuous interaction.

Realizing these interactions also requires a generator that can express their consequences. Explicit state specifies intended outcomes, and text guidance communicates them, but the generator must learn to realize them as visible behavior. We therefore develop interaction data, train the conditioned generator, and connect event reasoning, executable updates, and visual feedback in an online loop. The contribution is the reciprocal generative gameplay enabled by this coordinated system, including its data and training procedure. Reconciliation supplies feedback within this loop by grounding subsequent decisions in committed observations.

Appendix B Dataset Construction

All routes share the capture and alignment pipeline below. Counts refer to accepted source recordings, excluding candidate jobs, prompt variants, and overlapping training windows.

B.1 Shared Capture and Alignment

Execution and recording.

We specify the map, assets, initial conditions, actor policies, and player controls before capture. The engine records gameplay demos together with applied inputs, frame timing, state, and interaction events. Requested controls and realized events are retained separately, with damage labels taken from realized engine events. Offline replay renders the recorded trajectory and game audio under a fixed client configuration. Presentation settings, including HUD, crosshair, and effect suppression, are versioned per route. Renderer telemetry records camera position and orientation, transforms, and projection parameters, synchronized with simulation ticks.

Time and action interface.

The capture pipelines use a 64 Hz simulation/control clock. Warm-up is removed using the recorded capture boundary before aligning model time zero. The model-facing stream uses 20 video frames per second, with four continuous movement/camera channels and fire, jump, and reload inputs under the shared action contract. Camera and movement values follow the recorded applied controls. Button resampling preserves short active runs that might otherwise disappear between sampled frames. In the long Interaction release, the action profiles explicitly remove 64 warm-up ticks and align row zero with the first video frame.

Native media differ across routes. Basic Dynamics stores 320 frames at 64 fps and 1280×720 resolution. Short and long Interaction sequences store 81 and 1,201 frames at 20 fps and 1280×720. Arena stores 1,201 frames at 20 fps and 1664×960. Representative files in all four subsets contain 48 kHz stereo game audio. The model loader resizes video and resamples audio according to the training configuration. The generator training configuration uses 832×480 video and 16 kHz stereo audio. The 81-frame layout comprises an initial frame and five 16-frame chunks. The 1,201-frame layout similarly supports 75 chunks.

Semantic labels and packaging.

We use Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite [(Google DeepMind, 2026)] (gemini-3.1-flash-lite) to separately annotate map style, weapon appearance and operation, and player and enemy appearance. Interaction releases add chunk-local motion, visibility, damage, and death descriptions derived from telemetry. Prompts distinguish no damage, nonlethal damage, a new death event, and an already-dead actor. Off-screen intervals are described using visibility records rather than invented visible motion. Player controls remain in action tensors. Enemy movement and jumping belong to semantic conditions. Where reference images are used, the manifest binds them to the appropriate actor and time interval.

B.2 Basic Dynamics

Basic Dynamics contains 50,140 five-second clips across 28 maps and nine weapons, including 39,539 without an enemy and 10,601 with a non-damaging enemy distractor. Movement, camera changes, firing, and local collision responses provide the principal supervision. The supplement emphasizes pure idle, idle-to-action, action-to-idle, interrupted action, smooth routes, and wall impacts.

Route validation and camera filtering remove unsuitable trajectories.

B.3 Interaction

Short interactions.

The short Interaction subset contains 42,000 recordings across five maps, nine weapons, and 42 model–skin–color appearances. Capture varies distance, opponent movement, direction changes, stopping, jumping, visibility transitions, and firing. Firing times are sampled deterministically from the scenario seed. Weapon-specific schedules include isolated shots, repeated taps, and bounded bursts. Opponent motion and jump programs are specified separately from player controls.

Outcome labels follow the realized engine events, yielding 6,535 no-fire examples, 16,666 misses, 14,496 nonlethal-hit examples, and 4,303 kills. The visibility allocation is 37,800 continuously visible examples, 2,100 exit-and-hold examples, and 2,100 exit-and-return examples. The annotation identifies visibility transitions within each 0.8-second chunk. The underlying timestamped records also support constructing annotations over windows of arbitrary duration within each recording. This release describes view-frustum transitions, not geometric occlusion behind arbitrary cover. Crosshair and casing effects are disabled in its capture configuration.

Each recording has one 81-frame bidirectional view and one five-chunk autoregressive view.

Long interaction sequences.

Interaction-Long contains 1,791 accepted recordings with blood-hit effects disabled during capture. Each episode contains four actor slots, arranged either as distinct actors or a controlled-return sequence, and zero, one, or two scheduled kills. The accepted collection contains 900 controlled-return and 891 distinct-actor episodes.

The maps are Bromine, Courtfun, Geoplanetary, and Stormkeep. The weapons are MachineGun, Rifle, and Shotgun. Scripted trajectories undergo collision and ground-support checks. Camera schedules use frozen calibration traces, with scan and aiming phases, rather than live feedback that tracks the current enemy.

The reference bank contains 42 appearances with five clean views each. Bindings expose the current actor reference, retain the outgoing reference through its despawn transition, and mask intervals without an actor. Each source episode provides fifteen 81-frame bidirectional windows. The autoregressive view keeps each full sequence and its 75 chunk prompts.

B.4 Arena: Sustained Combat

Arena contains 1,800 one-minute bot-versus-bot recordings in a compact arena, using MachineGun combat and a fixed opponent appearance. Independent bot controls produce ongoing movement and exchanges instead of prescribing a short outcome sequence. The capture configuration bounds locomotion and camera motion and removes crosshair and pickup clutter.

The release constructs the action stream from authoritative gameplay records. Chunk descriptions summarize opponent motion, attacks, visibility, nonlethal damage, kills, and player death from telemetry aligned with the rendered camera. Fully off-screen chunks suppress visible-motion claims. The manifest provides 75 prompts per episode and a fixed opponent reference binding. Arena trains RIGen-Arena.

B.5 Quality Control and Test Set Construction

Capture validation checks route geometry, camera behavior, and consistency between scheduled interactions and recorded events. Manifest validation checks media metadata, finite and aligned controls, complete prompt schedules, and reference bindings.

Test set construction.

We reserve 100 Interaction recordings for quantitative evaluation. Their maps and enemy appearances are excluded from all task-specific training subsets, including Basic Dynamics, Interaction, Interaction-Long, and Arena, and are not used in subsequent adaptation or distillation.

Appendix C Evaluation Details

C.1 Evaluation Protocol

The 100 Xonotic scenarios comprise 50 survival targets and 50 death targets. All RIGen variants in Table  use the same Interaction-trained generator after sliding-window autoregressive training on Interaction-Long, without Arena post-training or distillation. SCOPE and LingBot-World 2.0 receive the prescribed combat outcomes directly as text guidance.

Enemy motion is supplied by source annotations in place of online behavior selection. The interaction agent handles hit, injury, and death reasoning and correction of predicted state. All variants use their own generated video history. Online interaction variants compute guidance from that history, while RIGen (w/ Reference guidance) uses frozen reference guidance.

Fixing enemy motion gives methods common behavior requirements and focuses the comparison on motion adherence and combat-outcome realization, separating behavior selection from its execution in generated video.

We combine controlled experiments, state-dependent branching examples, and continuous closed-loop gameplay. Controlled experiments compare the realization of specified interaction outcomes. Branch comparisons show how state and strategy affect generated behavior, while RIGen-Arena demonstrates the mutual effects of player actions and world events during continued play. Together, these complementary evaluations examine outcome realization, state dependence, and reciprocal interaction in the implemented system.

The external comparisons evaluate complete systems, including their data and training recipes. Learning to realize interaction outcomes is part of the proposed method. Specifying an outcome in text alone does not ensure that a generator can express it. We therefore assess the resulting system capability against external models and use fixed-generator ablations to examine the online interaction mechanisms separately.

Evaluating generated trajectories.

Once a generated trajectory diverges from its source recording, source-engine hit and visibility labels cannot automatically serve as ground truth for the generated scene. Rule execution can be checked against configured transitions, while judging whether a generated attack hits requires independent evidence from the generated video itself. Autonomous behavior also admits multiple valid choices under the same state, calling for task-based criteria that accommodate alternative behaviors. Our benchmark uses prescribed motion and outcome targets with video-based assessment. Event-level visual correctness and autonomous decision quality require annotations or task criteria for the generated trajectories, rather than direct reuse of source-engine labels.

C.2 Metrics

Qwen3.8-27B [(Qwen Team, 2026)] judges complete generated videos offline.

Enemy Behavior.

Enemy Behavior averages satisfaction of directional motion checks within predefined time windows, first within each video and then equally across the 100 scenarios. A check receives credit only when the judge reports it as satisfied and cites visual evidence within its time window. Lateral and depth motion are checked separately, relative to the environment rather than camera-induced image motion. For death-target cases, the prescribed lethal chunk and subsequent motion requirements are excluded for all methods using the same fixed windows.

Final-state Agreement.

Final-state Agreement compares the enemy’s visible state in the final 0.8 seconds with its preassigned survival or death target. The target is withheld from the judge. Unreadable outcomes and failures remain in the denominator and receive no agreement credit. Overall FSA uses all 100 cases. Survival-target and death-target success rates each use the corresponding 50 cases, so overall FSA is their mean. FSA tests whether the prescribed final combat outcome is actually realized. Locally plausible motion and high visual quality do not establish that an opponent survives or dies as required, making outcome agreement a distinct interaction criterion. EB measures motion adherence, while qualitative sequences illustrate intermediate combat responses.

Visual quality and dynamics.

The five visual metrics use the official dimension-specific VBench pipelines on complete generated videos. Each reported score is the mean per-video normalized score multiplied by 100. Dynamic Degree is the percentage of videos meeting the official motion threshold.

The system also generates audio jointly with video.

C.3 Ablations and Reference Comparison

The ablation rows in Table  compare inference-time variants using the same video checkpoint, initial conditions, player inputs, and sampling settings.

  • 1.

    Full RIGen. Predict interaction consequences before generation, apply executable rules, and guide the current chunk. Observe the generated chunk and reconcile predicted state with its visible outcome before the next decision.

  • 2.

    Motion guidance only. Retain player inputs, scene, appearance, and source motion annotations. Remove hit, injury, and death guidance and the online interaction VLM.

  • 3.

    Semantic prompting. The VLM maintains persistent textual state and selects the next chunk’s combat outcome. Rules are supplied as text, without an executable rule engine or an independent verification-and-correction module. This variant compares agent-managed state updates with executable rules and separate visual reconciliation.

  • 4.

    Post-hoc event updates. Generate first, observe events, apply rules, and pass consequence guidance to the following chunk. There is no pre-generation prediction of current-chunk consequences.

  • 5.

    Without reconciliation. Retain pre-generation prediction and executable state updates, but do not correct the planned state from post-generation verification. The next reasoning step still sees the newly generated frames.

  • 6.

    RIGen (w/ Reference guidance). Freeze reference event guidance in advance and remove online VLM calls. Death instructions are derived from source hit annotations combined with configured health and damage rules. They specify a counterfactual task answer, not ground-truth death in the source recording. The guidance is not revised from generated observations, but autoregressive video context uses this variant’s own outputs.

    • C.4 Runtime

    Runtime is measured on a single NVIDIA GB300 GPU. In Table 2, Replay disables online VLM calls and reuses the same guidance, while Online runs the interaction loop. Both include refinement and remain below the target playback rate of 20 FPS.

一句话：生成式玩法要有持久后果与自身规则：状态、规则、交互推理、动作条件生成四件套。

要点：

  • 三块拼起来：持久状态与可配置规则、上下文交互推理、动作条件化视听生成；生成内容由玩家动作的后果与角色自身行为共同决定。
  • 自建 Xonotic 对局数据集训练视听生成器，后训练出可交互 FPS 原型 RIGen-Arena。
  • 攻击有状态相关后果（血量、资源约束、重生规则），敌人会按自身血量与战况调整行为，战斗结果更可靠。

为什么值得看：现在多数生成式玩法只是「按键→画面」的即时响应。这篇把世界自身规则与角色决策补进来，正好是可以用来判断一个生成式引擎「能放视频」还是「能做玩法」的判据。

中文摘要：生成式玩法不只是对玩家动作做即时响应：动作应当留下持久后果，生成的世界也应当按自身状态与规则行动，反过来塑造玩家的处境与后续选择。视频生成擅长局部动力学，但有限的历史、部分可观测的游戏状态、以及需要上下文的行为决策，让单靠视听预测难以支撑这种交互。作者提出 RIGen（互惠交互生成）框架，组合持久状态与可配置规则、上下文交互推理、动作条件化的视听生成；三者一起让交互后果与角色行为共同决定生成内容，并保持游戏状态与可见结果一致。他们构造 Xonotic 玩法数据集训练视听生成器，再经后训练得到可交互的第一人称射击原型 RIGen-Arena。实验显示战斗结果更可靠，玩家与生成世界之间存在真正的双向互动。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·生成式玩法（English）

原文发布：2026-10-14

本期推送：2026-10-22

RIGen: Beyond Action Following with Reciprocal Interaction in Generative Gameplay

Abstract

Generative gameplay requires more than immediate responses to player actions. Actions should have persistent consequences, while the generated world should act according to its own state and rules, shaping the player’s situation and subsequent choices. Video generation captures local dynamics, but limited history, partially observed game state, and the need for contextual behavior decisions make such interactions difficult to sustain through audiovisual prediction alone. We introduce RIGen (Reciprocally Interactive Generation), a framework for reciprocal interaction in generative gameplay. RIGen combines persistent state and configurable rules, contextual interaction reasoning, and action-conditioned audiovisual generation. Together, these components make interaction consequences and actor behavior jointly determine generated content while maintaining consistency between game state and visible outcomes. We construct a Xonotic gameplay dataset to train an audiovisual generator for learning dynamics and interactions. Further post-training enables RIGen-Arena, an interactive generative first-person shooter (FPS) prototype. Experiments demonstrate more reliable combat outcomes and reciprocal interaction between the player and the generated world. Project page: https://murphylmf.github.io/RIGen/.

1 Introduction

Generative models offer a route to game experiences whose environments, characters, and events can be created during play [(Bruce et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025)]. Such experiences could be personalized to each player’s preferences and choices. Realizing this potential requires reciprocal interaction: players should be able to change the world through their actions, while the world follows its own operating logic. Its characters act according to their situation and goals, and its rules and events shape the player’s circumstances and subsequent choices.

Recent video-based world models have made progress toward this goal. DIAMOND [(Alonso et al., 2024)] and GameNGen [(Valevski et al., 2025)] demonstrate playable game simulation. LingBot-World [(Robbyant Team et al., 2026)] and SCOPE [(Tong et al., 2026)] provide responsive camera and movement control, while LingBot-World 2.0 [(Gao et al., 2026)] and Incantation [(Zhu et al., 2026b)] incorporate semantic guidance for character behavior and interaction events. Table  compares these systems across control, gameplay, and output capabilities. It highlights the remaining gap in combining reciprocal state changes with scene- and state-conditioned actor planning.

The prevailing approach builds on video models that capture rich local dynamics and generate continuous audiovisual feedback conditioned on player controls, making them a natural foundation for interactive games. However, sustaining reciprocal interaction through audiovisual prediction alone faces three challenges. (1) Coordinating reciprocal interaction. Responding to player actions does not by itself determine how the world should act upon the player. Actors must choose behavior based on current conditions and their own goals, and the consequences must update player state and constrain subsequent interactions. (2) Limited history. Events beyond the model’s context window can still have consequences for current interactions [(Xiao et al., 2025)]. (3) Partially observed state. Gameplay variables such as health and ammunition may not be recoverable from the visible scene, yet determine whether an action can be executed and what outcome it should have.

In sustained combat, for example, accumulated damage must determine whether the next hit is lethal, even when earlier attacks fall outside the video context. The opponent’s remaining health and goals should shape whether it attacks or retreats. Damage dealt by the opponent must likewise affect the player’s health and ability to continue fighting.

To address these challenges, we introduce RIGen, a framework for reciprocal interaction in generative gameplay (Figure ). The state and rules layer maintains persistent gameplay variables and configurable rules, including strategic goals and constraints. The interaction reasoning layer interprets the scene and player actions to infer events and plan actor behavior under these conditions. The audiovisual generation layer realizes the resulting guidance alongside player controls. Together, these layers let player actions change the state that governs subsequent interactions. The world also acts according to its own rules and goals, affecting the player’s state and available actions.

We instantiate RIGen in first-person shooter (FPS) environments. Our experiments assess combat outcomes, while qualitative demonstrations and RIGen-Arena illustrate state-dependent interactions and autonomous enemy behavior that affects the player (Figure 1).

Our contributions are threefold. (1) A system for reciprocal generative gameplay. We integrate interaction prediction, executable state updates, and audiovisual generation into a closed loop in which player actions change world state and world behavior affects the player. Model comparisons and controlled ablations demonstrate more reliable realization of state-dependent interaction outcomes. (2) FPS gameplay dataset. We construct a dataset covering basic dynamics, controlled interactions, and sustained combat, pairing audiovisual observations with player controls and interaction annotations, with a reproducible data creation pipeline. (3) Interactive gameplay prototype. We build RIGen-Arena, integrating few-step audiovisual generation with closed-loop interaction to support continued play under persistent game rules.

2 Related Work

Video generation and interactive worlds.

Video and audiovisual foundation models provide appearance and dynamics priors [(Kong et al., 2024; Wan Team et al., 2025; Ruan et al., 2023; Polyak et al., 2024; HaCohen et al., 2026; Su et al., 2026)]. Controllable visual simulation [(Kim et al., 2020; Menapace et al., 2021; Menapace et al., 2022)] has developed into generative game environments [(Bruce et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2025; Alonso et al., 2024; Kanervisto et al., 2025; Decart et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025)] and interactive content creation [(Che et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025)]. Recent work broadens scene coverage and streaming control [(He et al., 2025a; Tong et al., 2026; Robbyant Team et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026a; Huang et al., 2026a)], adds multiplayer or audiovisual interaction [(Hu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026)], and improves long-horizon consistency through memory [(Xiao et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b; AlayaWorld Team et al., 2026)]. We focus on persistent gameplay state and rule-governed interaction consequences.

Actor control and semantic interaction.

Reactive opponents and language-guided character control extend player-driven generation [(Agarwal et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a; Cao et al., 2026; Ouyang et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2025)]. LingBot-World 2.0 [(Gao et al., 2026)] uses pilot and director agents for character control and scene events. Incantation [(Zhu et al., 2026b)] tracks damage after generation, leaving hit/miss resolution to the video model and risking delayed death responses during fast-paced combat. RIGen couples behavior planning with executable gameplay rules, predicts interaction consequences before generation, and reconciles state with committed video.

Explicit state and generative rendering.

Prior systems combine structured state or game logic with generative rendering [(Li et al., 2025a; Cheng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026b; Cai et al., 2026)], while planning-based video methods organize content before synthesis [(Lin et al., 2024; Lian et al., 2024)]. Geometric rendering interfaces provide explicit spatial control [(Huang et al., 2026c; Lin et al., 2026a; Meng et al., 2026)]. Programmable World Model [(Huang et al., 2026b)] compiles state-augmented 3D bounding boxes into rendering controls, while Code World Model [(Chen et al., 2026)] compiles executable state into proxy videos. RIGen instead connects gameplay state to generation through player actions and local interaction guidance, without constructing explicit spatial trajectories. The PixVerse Game Engine technical blog [(PixVerse Research, 2026)] describes a separation of game mechanics, agent orchestration, and generative expression. We provide a concrete implementation for continuous player control, connecting interaction prediction, executable state updates, and video feedback, with corresponding generator training and controlled ablations.

3 Method

3.1 Overview

RIGen couples three layers to align player actions, persistent state, and generated audiovisual outcomes (Figure ). The State and Rule Engine maintains persistent state, applies transition rules, and specifies strategic constraints (Section 3.2). The Interaction Agent reasons about action consequences and plans actor behavior (Section 3.3). The Audiovisual Generator models local dynamics under player controls and generation guidance (Section 3.4).

At each chunk boundary, the agent uses recent video, player controls, and persistent state to predict interaction events and plan actor behavior. The rule engine evaluates these events, and the updated state and planned behavior jointly guide the next audiovisual chunk. After generation, the agent checks which events occurred, and the rule engine uses this evidence to determine the state for the next decision.

3.2 Persistent State and Rule-Based Updates

We represent gameplay as an event-driven state machine with numerical variables, following standard state-based game AI [(Millington & Funge, 2009)]. The engine maintains player and enemy health and life/death state, player ammunition, and opponent strategy modes, together with configurable rule parameters such as the player’s per-shot damage and transition conditions. Writing s for the complete game state and e for an interaction event record, the engine maps s to its successor s^′ through

s^′=Rules(s,e).

(1)

For example, firing requires a living player with available ammunition and consumes a round regardless of whether the shot hits. A hit reduces the target’s health by the configured damage, for either the player or an enemy. Reaching zero health triggers death. If an opponent survives with low health, a configured rule can switch its strategy from engagement to retreat. The updated strategy guides the Interaction Agent’s next decision, such as choosing a retreat direction suited to the current scene (Section 3.3).

3.3 Event Reasoning, Behavior Planning, and Visual Feedback

Before generating chunk oₖ, we perform reconciliation through verification and state correction. The agent verifies oₖ₋₁ using sampled verification frames Iₖ₋₁, player controls uₖ₋₁, and local guidance pₖ₋₁. The rule engine then corrects the planned state sₖᵖˡᵃⁿ using feedback fₖ₋₁:

fₖ₋₁=Verify(Iₖ₋₁,uₖ₋₁,pₖ₋₁),(2)
sₖ=Correct(sₖᵖˡᵃⁿ,fₖ₋₁).

Using this updated state, feedback, and current player controls uₖ, the agent proposes events eₖ and behavior bₖ:

(eₖ,bₖ)=Agent(oₖ₋₁,sₖ,uₖ,fₖ₋₁).

(3)

The rule engine computes a provisional successor sₖ₊₁ᵖˡᵃⁿ and local interaction guidance pₖ without overwriting sₖ:

sₖ₊₁ᵖˡᵃⁿ=Rules(sₖ,eₖ),(4)
pₖ=Prompt(sₖ₊₁ᵖˡᵃⁿ,eₖ,bₖ).

The generator realizes this guidance as the next audiovisual chunk oₖ (Section 3.4). At the next boundary, verification of oₖ reconciles sₖ₊₁ᵖˡᵃⁿ with committed visual outcomes to obtain sₖ₊₁. These observations take precedence over conflicting predictions, and the corrected state conditions the next decision. Implementation scope and verification details are given in the appendix.

3.4 Audiovisual Generation

The global prompt g describes the scene and character identity shared across chunks. Local guidance pₖ specifies the current chunk’s actor behavior and observable interaction outcomes, derived from the agent’s proposals and rule-based state updates (Section 3.3). Together, they form text condition cₖ. Given audiovisual context Hₖ and player controls uₖ, the generator produces the next chunk:

cₖ=(g,pₖ), oₖ∼G_θ(Hₖ,uₖ,cₖ).

(5)

The context Hₖ contains a first-frame anchor, a character reference, and recent generated chunks with their controls and text conditions. The generator denoises the target under these conditions, and the resulting oₖ provides observations for the next interaction decision.

We instantiate G_θ with the LTX-2.3 [(HaCohen et al., 2026; Lightricks, 2026)] audiovisual backbone, using coupled video and audio transformer streams (Figure ). Continuous movement/camera controls modulate video features through FiLM [(Perez et al., 2018)], while button inputs enter through causal cross-attention. Audiovisual attention connects the two streams and is causal across chunks and joint within each chunk. The anchor and reference provide visual context without text or action updates.

Chunk-wise prompt routing.

In both video and audio streams, each chunk attends only to the global prompt and its corresponding local guidance through text cross-attention (Figure ). Historical chunks retain their original text conditions, while the target receives the current guidance. The same routing is used in bidirectional and causal training.

Training and continued generation.

Following the bidirectional-to-autoregressive adaptation used in CausVid [(Yin et al., 2025)], we first train the model bidirectionally to follow player controls and chunk-level guidance, then adapt it to autoregressive next-chunk prediction conditioned on clean audiovisual history. Sliding-window training retains a window of recent chunks alongside the first-frame anchor and character reference, keeping Hₖ bounded during continued generation. Training objectives and implementation details are provided in the appendix.

4 Xonotic Interaction Dataset

We modify the open-source engine of Xonotic [(Xonotic Team, 2023)] to construct an audiovisual gameplay dataset with controlled capture and synchronized annotations. Three complementary routes target different aspects of gameplay. Basic Dynamics captures how player controls affect local visual dynamics. Interaction covers the relationships between player actions, opponent behavior, and combat outcomes in controlled encounters, including longer sequences of successive encounters. Arena captures sustained combat between independently controlled bots to support continued interactive play. The collection contains 95,731 source recordings and 176.8 hours of encoded video (Table ).

Each recording provides synchronized first-person video, game audio, player controls, and engine-grounded camera poses, together with scene and character descriptions. The interaction subsets pair chunk-level descriptions of opponent behavior, visibility, and combat outcomes with engine state and event annotations. Actor reference images are bound to the corresponding identities where used. Table  compares our dataset with existing gameplay datasets. Our collection jointly targets local dynamics, controlled combat outcomes, and sustained interaction. The appendix details the capture routes, alignment, filtering, and test set construction.

5 Post-training for RIGen-Arena

RIGen-Arena is an interactive one-on-one FPS prototype in which the player fights an opponent, with either side respawning after defeat to continue the match (Figure ).

We initialize post-training for RIGen-Arena from the bidirectional model trained on the Interaction subset. We first fine-tune it bidirectionally on the Arena subset to adapt to sustained combat. We then train the adapted model to generate chunks autoregressively using a sliding window of recent history together with the first-frame anchor and character reference (Section 3.4).

We adopt the two-stage distillation recipe of Causal-rCM [(Zheng et al., 2026a)]. Teacher-forcing consistency distillation first produces a few-step generator. Distribution matching then trains this generator on its own autoregressive rollouts.

We additionally train a video refiner to recover high-frequency details in dynamic gameplay. Training pairs spatially degraded latents with the original encodings of the same arena clips. We first train the refiner bidirectionally with paired flow matching [(Lipman et al., 2023)], then fine-tune it for causal, chunk-wise refinement with a bounded history window. At inference, it refines each generated chunk without access to future chunks. We integrate the generator and refiner with the state and rule engine and interaction agent to form RIGen-Arena. Training objectives, sampling schedules, and implementation details are provided in the appendix.

6 Experiments

This section evaluates motion adherence, combat outcomes, and visual quality through quantitative comparisons and ablations. RIGen-Arena (Figure ) and the qualitative results (Figures  and ) illustrate state-dependent interactions, continued gameplay, and the world’s effects on the player.

6.1 Quantitative Evaluation

Setup.

We compare RIGen’s checkpoint trained on Interaction-Long with sliding-window autoregressive training against SCOPE [(Tong et al., 2026)] and LingBot-World 2.0 [(Gao et al., 2026)] on 100 Xonotic combat scenarios. Test maps and enemy appearances are excluded from all task-specific training. Enemy motion follows source annotations. Both baselines receive prescribed combat outcomes as text guidance. InternVL3-8B [(Zhu et al., 2025)] is our Interaction Agent for event reasoning and visual state correction.

Ablation Variants.

Motion guidance only retains player inputs and source motion, without interaction guidance or an online agent. Semantic prompting provides state-update rules as text for the agent to interpret and iteratively update its textual state, without an executable rule engine or independent verification. Post-hoc event updates moves interaction reasoning and rule-based state updates from before generation to after it, so the resulting guidance conditions the next chunk rather than the current one. Without reconciliation disables visual correction of planned state. RIGen (w/ Reference guidance) freezes event guidance derived from source hit annotations and health/damage rules, without an online agent.

Metrics.

Qwen3.8-27B [(Qwen Team, 2026)] evaluates two interaction metrics offline. Enemy Behavior (EB) measures adherence to prescribed enemy motion within specified time windows. Final-state Agreement (FSA) measures agreement between the final visible enemy state and its survival/death target. FSA-S is the percentage of the 50 survival-target cases in which the enemy is visibly alive at the end. FSA-D is the percentage of the 50 death-target cases in which the enemy is visibly dead at the end. Overall FSA averages these two rates. Incorrect or unjudgeable outcomes count as failures, so FSA can fall below 50%. We also report Motion Smoothness (MS), Aesthetic Quality (AQ), Subject Consistency (SC), Background Consistency (BC), and Dynamic Degree (DD), following VBench [(Huang et al., 2024)]. Scores are on a 0–100 scale. Higher is better except for DD, which measures motion prevalence rather than quality.

Results.

Table  shows that RIGen achieves 81% FSA, compared with 29% for LingBot-World 2.0 and 4% for SCOPE, and higher EB than both baselines. With the generator fixed, FSA falls to 39% with motion-only guidance, 35% with semantic prompting, 64% with post-hoc updates, and 76% without reconciliation. These results support predicting interaction consequences before generation, executing state updates, and reconciling them with visual feedback. Visual metrics remain nearly unchanged across ablations. Lower AQ than LingBot-World 2.0 may reflect our smaller training dataset. The appendix provides further details and analysis.

6.2 Qualitative Evaluation

Combat responses.

Figure  compares visible combat responses from the same initial image and attack requests. In this example, RIGen produces a hit reaction followed by a fall and a sustained downed state, while the baseline opponents remain active under repeated fire despite receiving text guidance specifying the correct combat outcomes.

State-dependent interactions.

Figure  varies initial enemy health, player ammunition, and state-dependent opponent strategy from a shared starting scene under the same player input requests. The low-health opponent falls, depleted ammunition suppresses the third shot, and an injured opponent switches from hold to retreat, moving left and crouching at cover. These examples illustrate how explicit state and strategy affect visible gameplay.

7 Conclusion

We presented RIGen, a framework for reciprocal interaction in generative gameplay. Player actions change persistent world state, while world rules and actor decisions affect the player. Quantitative comparisons demonstrate more reliable combat outcomes, and qualitative results illustrate state-dependent interactions and autonomous enemy behavior.

Limitations and future work.

RIGen is not yet real-time, supports only single-opponent FPS gameplay, and relies on VLM perception and reasoning for interaction decisions and state verification. Future work will optimize generation and agent inference, extend to multiple opponents and broader action spaces and game genres, and improve visual grounding and reasoning reliability.

AI use statement

We used generative AI tools to assist with drafting and polishing the manuscript and with research execution, specifically code implementation, debugging, experiment scripting, and development of the dataset construction pipelines. The authors reviewed and revised the AI-assisted text and checked the AI-assisted code and experimental outputs for correctness. The authors take full responsibility for the final content of this work.

Ethics statement

We construct our dataset through scripted and bot-controlled gameplay in Xonotic, without collecting human-player data or conducting human-subject experiments. The official Xonotic distribution is licensed under GPL-3.0-or-later, with its DarkPlaces engine under GPL-2.0-or-later.111https://github.com/xonotic/xonotic/blob/master/COPYING Code and assets remain subject to their applicable upstream licenses. Our release will document the licenses for the dataset and accompanying code and preserve required attribution and notices. We follow the applicable usage terms of pretrained models. The proposed method is intended for research purposes. Deployment should account for potential misuse of generated content, including misleading or deceptive media.

Reproducibility statement

The main text describes the proposed method and experimental setup. Additional implementation details, hyperparameter settings, and evaluation protocols are provided in the appendix to support reproducibility. The datasets and baseline methods used in our experiments are identified and referenced in the paper.

Acknowledgments

This research was supported by the Theme-based Research Scheme (T45-205/21-N) from the Hong Kong Research Grants Council (RGC), and by the Generative AI Research and Development Centre from InnoHK. We also thank Vivix for providing computational resources and research support during the internship. The work by Mengfei Li, Xingtong Ge, Lunjie Zhu, and Fangyu Lin was completed during their internships at Vivix Group Limited.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A Implementation Details

A.1 Audiovisual Generator and Action Conditioning

We build on the LTX [(HaCohen et al., 2026)] audiovisual architecture, using the LTX-2.3 22B dev backbone [(Lightricks, 2026)]. Separate video and audio autoencoders produce latent sequences processed by coupled transformer streams. Each stream uses self-attention and text cross-attention, with cross-modal attention connecting video and audio. At 20 video frames per second, each generated chunk contains two video latent steps, corresponding to 16 new frames, and 20 audio latent steps, corresponding to 0.8 seconds. Generation is causal between chunks. Tokens within a chunk are denoised jointly.

The action interface provides four continuous movement/camera channels and supports fire, jump, and reload inputs. For each generated video latent step, the eight aligned raw-frame vectors are concatenated into a 32-dimensional continuous-action vector Jₜ and broadcast over spatial locations. After projection, per-layer networks produce feature scale and shift through FiLM [(Perez et al., 2018)]

h^′_ℓ,t=(1+γ_ℓ(Jₜ))⊙h_ℓ,t+β_ℓ(Jₜ).

(6)

Buttons remain at the raw-frame rate and enter through an additional cross-attention residual. Each generated video latent attends to its eight aligned action frames and earlier retained actions, with future actions masked. Temporal rotary embeddings [(Su et al., 2024)] align these queries and keys. Continuous scale/shift outputs and button-attention output projections are initialized to zero. The action branches act on the video stream, while cross-modal attention connects the resulting dynamics to audio.

Writing zⱼ for the audiovisual latents of generated chunk j, the causal model uses a compact context

[first-frame anchor|z_k-4:k-1|Tₖ|r].

(7)

Here r denotes the encoded character reference. At steady state, four previous chunks are clean context and only the target chunk Tₖ is denoised. Tokens in each generated chunk attend to tokens in that chunk and earlier chunks. Reference-image tokens attend only to one another and are readable directly by the target video chunk. Direct cross-modal attention excludes the reference. The anchor and reference receive no action or text updates. As the window advances, old history is removed and temporal positions are rebased locally. The same layout supports zero to three history chunks during startup. An optional cache reuses clean-context keys and values within a chunk’s denoising steps. It is rebuilt when the window advances.

A.2 Chunk-wise Prompt Routing and Guidance Construction

The generator’s prompt does not encode numerical health, hit counters, or internal generation identifiers. High-frequency player controls remain in the action tensors, while text specifies the actor behavior and consequences those controls should realize.

Each chunk has its own text condition cⱼ=(g,pⱼ). The global description covers the environment, weapon, and character appearance. Local guidance describes the current actor behavior, visibility, and observable interaction outcomes. Each chunk’s combined text condition is encoded independently, and the resulting context tokens are concatenated. The text attention mask routes both video and audio queries to the corresponding prompt, with padding excluded and anchor/reference queries receiving no text-attention update in the causal model. In bidirectional adaptation, the initial frame instead shares the first generated chunk’s prompt. Historical chunks use their corresponding prompts, while the target directly attends only to its current prompt. Historical context remains available through audiovisual attention, which is causal across chunks during autoregressive training and generation.

At inference, a deterministic text renderer converts the controller’s structured predictions and rule-updated state into local guidance.

A.3 Training Objectives and Distillation

Generator training optimizes the audiovisual backbone and action branches while freezing the text encoder and autoencoders. The Interaction Agent uses InternVL3-8B [(Zhu et al., 2025)] without task-specific fine-tuning, while the rule engine and prompt compiler are programmed. The loader aligns video, audio, player controls, reference images, and chunk text conditions at shared temporal boundaries.

Training hyperparameters.

We train on 16 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs with a global batch size of 16 and BF16 mixed precision. Table 1 lists the generator learning rates. Consistency distillation and distribution matching use AdamW with β=(0,0.999), weight decay 0.01, and 100 warmup steps. The learned score model uses a learning rate of 10⁻⁵. Both refiner stages use 8-bit AdamW with a learning rate of 10⁻⁵, β=(0.9,0.999), weight decay 0.01, and 100 warmup steps. The domain LoRA has rank 384 and scaling parameter α=384.

Action and prompt adaptation.

Basic Dynamics data teach control-conditioned local dynamics, while the Interaction data add chunk-local behavior and outcome guidance. Arena post-training starts from the Interaction-trained bidirectional model and adapts it to sustained combat before causal training and distillation. Bidirectional adaptation uses chunk-specific text conditions and a linear-path flow-matching objective [(Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023)]. For modality m∈{v,a}, a clean latent sequence zᵐ is perturbed as zᵐ_σ=(1-σ)zᵐ+σεᵐ, with Gaussian noise εᵐ. The model predicts the flow velocity εᵐ-zᵐ and is trained by minimizing

L_bi=∑_m∈{v,a}λₘ𝔼[∥v_θᵐ(z_σ,σ;u,c)-(εᵐ-zᵐ)∥_Ωₘ²],

(8)

where c denotes the sequence of chunk text conditions and the norm averages supervised tokens, excluding the conditioning video frame and ineligible audio samples. The text attention mask restricts each generated chunk to its own text condition, while audiovisual self- and cross-attention remain bidirectional at this stage.

Sliding-window autoregressive training.

We initialize the causal model from the adapted checkpoint and train the layout in Equation 7. The anchor, reference, and available history chunks remain clean. Noise is applied only to the next chunk. For clean target latents zₖ, Gaussian noise εₖ, and noise level σ∈[0,1], the noisy input and predicted clean estimate are

z_k,σ=(1-σ)zₖ+σεₖ,(9)
ẑₖ=z_k,σ-σv_θ(z_k,σ,σ|Hₖ,uₖ,cₖ).

Here v_θ predicts flow velocity, and Hₖ, uₖ, and cₖ follow Equation 5. Superscripts v and a denote video and audio. The target-chunk reconstruction objective is

L_AR=𝔼 [w(σ)(MSE(ẑₖᵛ,zₖᵛ)+λₐMSE(ẑₖᵃ,zₖᵃ))],

(10)

where w(σ)=\exp[-2(σ-0.5)²] weights the noise level and λₐ=0.16 weights the audio loss. Squared errors are averaged over target tokens only. This stage uses ground-truth history. Bidirectional and autoregressive adaptation share the chunk-wise prompt routing used at inference, but only autoregressive adaptation enforces temporal causality through audiovisual attention.

Consistency distillation and startup coverage.

For few-step generation, the implementation follows the teacher-forcing consistency initialization in Causal-rCM [(Zheng et al., 2026a)]. This recipe builds on Consistency Models [(Song et al., 2023)], sCM [(Lu & Song, 2025)], and rCM [(Zheng et al., 2026b)]. A frozen autoregressive teacher advances a noisy sample between nearby noise levels. At the advanced point, the current student produces a clean estimate without gradients, which serves as the consistency target for its prediction at the starting point. Video and audio both contribute to this loss. Checkpoint EMA is maintained separately.

Startup and continued generation use the same sliding-window context layout. The training recipe alternates an update with four history chunks and an update with zero, one, two, or three history chunks.

The final Arena recipe further distills text classifier-free guidance [(Ho & Salimans, 2022)] into the student. The teacher combines conditional and text-unconditional predictions while retaining player actions and visual context. The student uses a single conditional forward pass per denoising step.

Self-forcing distribution matching.

After consistency distillation, we apply self-forcing distribution matching [(Huang et al., 2025)] as the second stage of the Causal-rCM [(Zheng et al., 2026a)] recipe. The objective follows DMD [(Yin et al., 2024b)] and DMD2 [(Yin et al., 2024a)], with bidirectional-teacher supervision of an autoregressive student as in CausVid [(Yin et al., 2025)]. One student starts from the initial frame, generates four startup chunks, and continues for five additional chunks using the same reference, chunk-wise prompt routing, and sliding context. No ground-truth history is inserted into this rollout. Both the startup chunks and the later chunks receive distribution-matching supervision.

A frozen bidirectional score model and a learned score model for student samples evaluate the same perturbed rollout with aligned controls and semantic conditions. These score models receive no reference-image tokens, so their text conditions describe character appearance explicitly. The final Arena recipe applies text guidance to the frozen score model, while the learned score model and student remain conditional. Their normalized difference in denoised predictions defines a stop-gradient target. The generator then replays the recorded final denoising step of each chunk to optimize a masked video–audio regression loss against that target. Rollout generation runs without gradients, avoiding storage of its full computation graph.

Video refiner training.

We construct temporally aligned training pairs from the same arena clip. Its original VAE encoding serves as the target. To construct the degraded input, we spatially downsample the RGB frames, encode them, and apply a frozen LTX-2.3 2× spatial upscaler v1.1 [(Lightricks, 2026)] to restore the target spatial size. We train a domain LoRA [(Hu et al., 2022)] on the refiner with truncated flow matching [(Lipman et al., 2023)] between the original target and a noise-perturbed upsampled latent. The refiner is first trained bidirectionally. Causal adaptation starts from this checkpoint, conditions on the first frame, character reference, and up to four clean history chunks, and applies loss only to the current chunk. Training uses ground-truth history, while deployment uses previously refined outputs. Both stages optimize only the domain LoRA, keeping the upsampler and backbone frozen. The official LTX-2.3 distilled LoRA v1.1 [(Lightricks, 2026)] is disabled for this training loss and enabled for few-step refinement at inference.

Inference settings.

The distilled Arena generator uses four denoising steps with noise levels (1,0.9375,0.8333,0.625,0). Refinement uses two denoising steps with noise levels (0.725,0.421875,0), a classifier-free guidance scale of 1, and no spatiotemporal guidance.

A.4 State Updates and Visual Verification

Prediction and state commitment.

At a chunk boundary, the controller retains the corrected state and uses predicted events to compute provisional outcomes and local guidance. Generation does not commit those predictions to the persistent ledger. After decoding, verification produces the feedback used to obtain the next retained state in Equation 2. The implementation recomputes this state from the saved pre-generation state and observed events, preventing predicted and verified damage from being counted twice. The first chunk uses the initial frame and configured state without a preceding verification step. The retained gameplay state is stored independently of the generator’s sliding visual context. When earlier frames leave that context, their recorded interaction consequences remain available to subsequent rule updates and enter generation through the current guidance.

Observation selection and shot prediction.

The online Arena implementation uses decoded RGB frames directly, without an observation refiner. Within each chunk, it selects the first frame of each uninterrupted firing interval and every fourth frame thereafter (5 Hz at 20 FPS). Before generation, the latest available frame is the preceding chunk’s last frame, or the initial image at startup. For each selected firing time, a calibrated control-to-pixel mapping estimates the image displacement from the intervening controls. We translate the latest frame accordingly, take a 320×320 crop centered on the screen, and overlay a hollow green aiming ring. The Interaction Agent receives this projected crop and a separate enemy appearance reference, and predicts whether the enemy’s body overlaps the marked aiming region.

Visual verification.

After generation, we decode the corresponding actual firing frames, the chunk’s final frame, and the frame three positions before it. Together with the pre-generation frame, these form the sampled observations Iₖ₋₁. A firing-frame audit receives the selected firing frames in temporal order, with the same ring overlay, alongside the pre-generation and two late frames. Unlike prediction, verification uses full frames rather than center crops. The ring radius is 5% of the shorter image dimension and leaves its interior unobstructed. A separate state query places the final frame first and uses the pre-generation and earlier late frame only as temporal context. It classifies the enemy as alive, dead, or not visible in the final frame. Both queries receive an appearance reference for identity only. Full frames are padded to a 2:1 canvas and the reference to a square, without cropping their contents. Aim markers appear only in the VLM inputs. The requested outcome is the condition being checked, not visual evidence, and verification uses separate calls from prediction.

The rule engine specifies intended transitions, while committed visual outcomes ground the state used for subsequent interaction. When an observed outcome contradicts a prediction, the controller revises the affected state and derives subsequent guidance from that revision. Numerical attributes remain rule-maintained rather than directly estimated from images, and occlusion alone is not treated as death.

Action constraints and opponent behavior.

Ammunition gates the executed fire commands and is consumed when a shot is permitted, independently of whether it hits. Before an enemy can attack, the Interaction Agent checks visual preconditions, including whether the enemy is visible and facing the player. When these conditions hold, attacks are sampled at a configured rate, and each attack hits with a preset probability. Successful hits subtract a fixed per-shot damage from player health. Reaching zero health disables player controls and adds the corresponding terminal outcome to guidance. For opponent behavior, the agent assesses movement feasibility from the current scene. The behavior policy combines this assessment with retained state and the configured strategy to select a movement description. Attack rules and strategy-transition conditions can be edited in the rule layer. Numerical state remains in the controller, while the generator receives observable behavior and outcome descriptions. World-side events thus combine visual assessment of the current scene with executable game rules that update player state and constrain subsequent controls.

A.5 Design Rationale

Reciprocal interaction concerns the causal effects of player actions on the world and of world events on the player. It does not require every game mechanic to be learned. Executable rules make damage, ammunition, and termination conditions explicit and configurable, while scene-conditioned behavior reasoning determines how actors act under those conditions. Their combination connects world-side decisions to persistent consequences for the player during continuous interaction.

Realizing these interactions also requires a generator that can express their consequences. Explicit state specifies intended outcomes, and text guidance communicates them, but the generator must learn to realize them as visible behavior. We therefore develop interaction data, train the conditioned generator, and connect event reasoning, executable updates, and visual feedback in an online loop. The contribution is the reciprocal generative gameplay enabled by this coordinated system, including its data and training procedure. Reconciliation supplies feedback within this loop by grounding subsequent decisions in committed observations.

Appendix B Dataset Construction

All routes share the capture and alignment pipeline below. Counts refer to accepted source recordings, excluding candidate jobs, prompt variants, and overlapping training windows.

B.1 Shared Capture and Alignment

Execution and recording.

We specify the map, assets, initial conditions, actor policies, and player controls before capture. The engine records gameplay demos together with applied inputs, frame timing, state, and interaction events. Requested controls and realized events are retained separately, with damage labels taken from realized engine events. Offline replay renders the recorded trajectory and game audio under a fixed client configuration. Presentation settings, including HUD, crosshair, and effect suppression, are versioned per route. Renderer telemetry records camera position and orientation, transforms, and projection parameters, synchronized with simulation ticks.

Time and action interface.

The capture pipelines use a 64 Hz simulation/control clock. Warm-up is removed using the recorded capture boundary before aligning model time zero. The model-facing stream uses 20 video frames per second, with four continuous movement/camera channels and fire, jump, and reload inputs under the shared action contract. Camera and movement values follow the recorded applied controls. Button resampling preserves short active runs that might otherwise disappear between sampled frames. In the long Interaction release, the action profiles explicitly remove 64 warm-up ticks and align row zero with the first video frame.

Native media differ across routes. Basic Dynamics stores 320 frames at 64 fps and 1280×720 resolution. Short and long Interaction sequences store 81 and 1,201 frames at 20 fps and 1280×720. Arena stores 1,201 frames at 20 fps and 1664×960. Representative files in all four subsets contain 48 kHz stereo game audio. The model loader resizes video and resamples audio according to the training configuration. The generator training configuration uses 832×480 video and 16 kHz stereo audio. The 81-frame layout comprises an initial frame and five 16-frame chunks. The 1,201-frame layout similarly supports 75 chunks.

Semantic labels and packaging.

We use Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite [(Google DeepMind, 2026)] (gemini-3.1-flash-lite) to separately annotate map style, weapon appearance and operation, and player and enemy appearance. Interaction releases add chunk-local motion, visibility, damage, and death descriptions derived from telemetry. Prompts distinguish no damage, nonlethal damage, a new death event, and an already-dead actor. Off-screen intervals are described using visibility records rather than invented visible motion. Player controls remain in action tensors. Enemy movement and jumping belong to semantic conditions. Where reference images are used, the manifest binds them to the appropriate actor and time interval.

B.2 Basic Dynamics

Basic Dynamics contains 50,140 five-second clips across 28 maps and nine weapons, including 39,539 without an enemy and 10,601 with a non-damaging enemy distractor. Movement, camera changes, firing, and local collision responses provide the principal supervision. The supplement emphasizes pure idle, idle-to-action, action-to-idle, interrupted action, smooth routes, and wall impacts.

Route validation and camera filtering remove unsuitable trajectories.

B.3 Interaction

Short interactions.

The short Interaction subset contains 42,000 recordings across five maps, nine weapons, and 42 model–skin–color appearances. Capture varies distance, opponent movement, direction changes, stopping, jumping, visibility transitions, and firing. Firing times are sampled deterministically from the scenario seed. Weapon-specific schedules include isolated shots, repeated taps, and bounded bursts. Opponent motion and jump programs are specified separately from player controls.

Outcome labels follow the realized engine events, yielding 6,535 no-fire examples, 16,666 misses, 14,496 nonlethal-hit examples, and 4,303 kills. The visibility allocation is 37,800 continuously visible examples, 2,100 exit-and-hold examples, and 2,100 exit-and-return examples. The annotation identifies visibility transitions within each 0.8-second chunk. The underlying timestamped records also support constructing annotations over windows of arbitrary duration within each recording. This release describes view-frustum transitions, not geometric occlusion behind arbitrary cover. Crosshair and casing effects are disabled in its capture configuration.

Each recording has one 81-frame bidirectional view and one five-chunk autoregressive view.

Long interaction sequences.

Interaction-Long contains 1,791 accepted recordings with blood-hit effects disabled during capture. Each episode contains four actor slots, arranged either as distinct actors or a controlled-return sequence, and zero, one, or two scheduled kills. The accepted collection contains 900 controlled-return and 891 distinct-actor episodes.

The maps are Bromine, Courtfun, Geoplanetary, and Stormkeep. The weapons are MachineGun, Rifle, and Shotgun. Scripted trajectories undergo collision and ground-support checks. Camera schedules use frozen calibration traces, with scan and aiming phases, rather than live feedback that tracks the current enemy.

The reference bank contains 42 appearances with five clean views each. Bindings expose the current actor reference, retain the outgoing reference through its despawn transition, and mask intervals without an actor. Each source episode provides fifteen 81-frame bidirectional windows. The autoregressive view keeps each full sequence and its 75 chunk prompts.

B.4 Arena: Sustained Combat

Arena contains 1,800 one-minute bot-versus-bot recordings in a compact arena, using MachineGun combat and a fixed opponent appearance. Independent bot controls produce ongoing movement and exchanges instead of prescribing a short outcome sequence. The capture configuration bounds locomotion and camera motion and removes crosshair and pickup clutter.

The release constructs the action stream from authoritative gameplay records. Chunk descriptions summarize opponent motion, attacks, visibility, nonlethal damage, kills, and player death from telemetry aligned with the rendered camera. Fully off-screen chunks suppress visible-motion claims. The manifest provides 75 prompts per episode and a fixed opponent reference binding. Arena trains RIGen-Arena.

B.5 Quality Control and Test Set Construction

Capture validation checks route geometry, camera behavior, and consistency between scheduled interactions and recorded events. Manifest validation checks media metadata, finite and aligned controls, complete prompt schedules, and reference bindings.

Test set construction.

We reserve 100 Interaction recordings for quantitative evaluation. Their maps and enemy appearances are excluded from all task-specific training subsets, including Basic Dynamics, Interaction, Interaction-Long, and Arena, and are not used in subsequent adaptation or distillation.

Appendix C Evaluation Details

C.1 Evaluation Protocol

The 100 Xonotic scenarios comprise 50 survival targets and 50 death targets. All RIGen variants in Table  use the same Interaction-trained generator after sliding-window autoregressive training on Interaction-Long, without Arena post-training or distillation. SCOPE and LingBot-World 2.0 receive the prescribed combat outcomes directly as text guidance.

Enemy motion is supplied by source annotations in place of online behavior selection. The interaction agent handles hit, injury, and death reasoning and correction of predicted state. All variants use their own generated video history. Online interaction variants compute guidance from that history, while RIGen (w/ Reference guidance) uses frozen reference guidance.

Fixing enemy motion gives methods common behavior requirements and focuses the comparison on motion adherence and combat-outcome realization, separating behavior selection from its execution in generated video.

We combine controlled experiments, state-dependent branching examples, and continuous closed-loop gameplay. Controlled experiments compare the realization of specified interaction outcomes. Branch comparisons show how state and strategy affect generated behavior, while RIGen-Arena demonstrates the mutual effects of player actions and world events during continued play. Together, these complementary evaluations examine outcome realization, state dependence, and reciprocal interaction in the implemented system.

The external comparisons evaluate complete systems, including their data and training recipes. Learning to realize interaction outcomes is part of the proposed method. Specifying an outcome in text alone does not ensure that a generator can express it. We therefore assess the resulting system capability against external models and use fixed-generator ablations to examine the online interaction mechanisms separately.

Evaluating generated trajectories.
