Right: We feed the result to a neural network. Abstract We propose a novel input encoding method of 3D positions for neural networks used in ray tracing algorithms. Our encoding technique utilizes the bounding volume hierarchy (BVH), which serves both as an acceleration data structure for ray tracing and as a spatial data struc- ture for indexing learnable latent feature vectors. Our method naturally adapts to scene ge- ometry, supports general geometric primitives, and maintains a bounded memory footprint independent of scene complexity. We demonstrate an application of our technique in the context of neural radiance cache (NRC).

  1. Introduction

Despite the capabilities of modern graphics hardware, multi-bounce path tracing in the game industry remains elusive. A simple neural network, such as a multilayer 49 ISSN 2331-7418 Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques BVH Encoding for Neural-Assisted Ray Tracing V ol. 15, No. 2, 2026 http://jcgt.org perceptron (MLP), has been proven to credibly learn quantities such as visibility [Bokˇsansk´y and Meister 2025] or radiance [M¨uller et al. 2021], which are commonly used in ray tracing-based algorithms. Thanks to its compact representation, an MLP can be efficiently implemented on the GPU, allowing for online training at real-time frame rates. Such a neural network can serve as a cache for these quantities, sig- nificantly reducing the ray tracing workload at the cost of a small error (bias). The crucial component that allows an MLP to learn high frequencies of a signal is the input encoding. In this article, we present a novel encoding method tailored for ray tracing. All modern ray tracing APIs rely on the bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) [Meister et al. 2021] as an acceleration data structure. We demonstrate that the same data structure can be used for indexing learnable feature vectors that are used for encoding 3D positions in virtual scenes. Specifically, we find a cut of a fixed size in the BVH, wherein feature vectors are stored in the corners of the cut nodes’ bounding boxes. In this manner, each geometric primitive belongs to a single cut node such that its bounding box can be used for interpolating the corresponding feature vectors [M¨uller et al. 2022]. The benefits of our approach include the following: (1) naturally adapting to geometry, (2) a bounded memory footprint, and (3) a support for general geometric primitives.

  1. Related Work

Spectral bias is a phenomenon when a neural network struggles to learn high fre- quencies of a low-dimensional input signal [Rahaman et al. 2019]. To address this problem, various encoding methods have been proposed, mapping the input data to a higher-dimensional space prior to being fed to the neural network. Frequency en- coding [Mildenhall et al. 2021] transforms each input value by a series of sines and cosines with different angular frequencies. Parametric encoding introduces latent fea- ture vectors that are trained together with weights of the neural network using back- propagation, where an input point is encoded by interpolating feature vectors in the proximity of the input point. The feature vectors are indexed by a spatial data struc- ture to efficiently identify the feature vectors in the proximity of the encoded point. Hadadan et al. [2021] proposed to use multi-resolution grid encoding, which stores feature vectors in a set of uniform grids of different resolutions, where the input is encoded by concatenating feature vectors from each grid. M ¨uller et al. [2022] pro- posed to store the uniform grids in a hashed form, considerably reducing memory requirements. Fujieda et al. [2023] combined the hash-grid encoding with frequency encoding. Weier et al. [2026] proposed spatio-directional encoding that hierarchi- cally encodes a position and direction using a 5D hashed multi-resolution grid. The position is encoded in a similar manner as hash-grid encoding does. The method 50 Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques BVH Encoding for Neural-Assisted Ray Tracing V ol. 15, No. 2, 2026 http://jcgt.org distributes the feature vectors on a triangulated unit sphere, using barycentric interpo- lation to encode the direction. Yoshimura et al. [2026] proposed an unbounded hash grid, allowing unnormalized inputs by modifying the hash function. Takikawa et al. [2021] proposed storing feature vectors in an octree. Bok ˇsansk´y et al. [2025] and Su et al. [2025] proposed storing and interpolating feature vectors directly on the trian- gles. This approach naturally adapts to the geometry distribution, but it is limited to triangles only and the number of feature vectors grows with the scene complexity in contrast to uniform grids or octrees. Alber et al. [2025] proposed to store Markov chain states in a multi-resolution hash grid that selects the level based on the distance from the camera, to ensure roughly constant projected area on the screen. Weier et al. [2024] proposed to ap- proximate subtrees in the bottom levels of a BVH by a neural network. The subtrees are found by refining the cut in the BVH, iteratively splitting the nodes with the high- est training error. Our method stores feature vectors in the bounding volume hierarchy, combining the advantages of the approaches discussed above. Compared to octrees or uniform grids, our method naturally adapts to the scene geometry, efficiently handling the teapot-in-a-stadium problem. Unlike triangle-based encoding, our method supports general geometric primitives and maintains a bounded memory footprint independent of the scene complexity (see Table 1).   1. BVH Encoding

In this section, we describe the details of our BVH encoding. We first define the BVH cut and how it can be used to index feature vectors. Then, we show how to encode an input point using the cut and how to optimize the feature vectors by backpropagation. 3.1. BVH Cut We define a cut in the BVH as a set of nodes that separates the leaves and the root (both inclusively). The root and the leaves are trivial cuts. An important property of the cut is that each leaf node is included in a single cut node. An example of the BVH cut is illustrated in Figure 2. We form the cut iteratively by opening nodes with the 51 Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques BVH Encoding for Neural-Assisted Ray Tracing V ol. 15, No. 2, 2026 http://jcgt.org 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 0 9 10 1 2 3 BVH cut Feature vectors of cut node 8 0 1 2 3 Feature vector buffer Figure 2. An example of the BVH cut (blue nodes) and its memory layout. The sequential index of a cut node (the bottom-left numbers) determines, where the corresponding eight feature vectors are stored in the feature vector buffer. largest surface area starting from the root using a priority queue (in the same manner as Hendrich et al. [2017]). We keep opening the nodes until we fill a given maximum cut size. Besides the cut nodes, we also compute a mapping from each geometric primitive to the corresponding cut node index and the sequential index of the node within the cut that we later use for the encoding itself. In the case of a two-level BVH, we propose a simple heuristic that redistributes the cut size budget among individual bottom-level BVHs based on the surface area of the bottom-level BVH (in world space). Note that this is only a heuristic that does not take into account other factors such as the distance to the camera, visibility, and material properties. The cut is an inherent part of the bottom-level BVH rather than of an individual instance. All instances of a bottom-level BVH therefore share a single cut, whose budget is determined by the largest world-space surface area among those instances. Note that in many cases the instances are of the same size. The BVH cut can be generalized to multiple levels such that we start with an initial coarser cut that we further refine to get a finer cut. In this way, we can find multiple cuts, corresponding to multiple feature vectors that can be concatenated in the same way as multi-resolution grid encoding does. Since we form cuts only in the bottom-level BVHs, we do not care much about the construction times; as in real-time scenarios, only the top-level BVH is being rebuilt in each frame. 3.2. Encoding We assume that the input points are the hit points provided as results of ray tracing. Note that the input point could be spatially in multiple cut nodes since the bound- 52 Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques BVH Encoding for Neural-Assisted Ray Tracing V ol. 15, No. 2, 2026 http://jcgt.org ing boxes may overlap, but the determining factor is the BVH cut node where the corresponding intersected geometric primitive belongs. Feature vectors are stored on the application side outside the ray tracing frame- work. Each cut node has eight feature vectors corresponding to the corners of its bounding box. The feature vectors are stored using the sequential index that is re- turned in the hit structure (see Figure 2). The encoding procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1. We fetch the bounding box using the cut node index and the correspond- ing feature vectors using the sequential index. Then, we normalize the hit point (in the object space in the case of a two-level BVH) using the bounding box and tri-linearly interpolate the corresponding feature vectors. Since the shape of the bounding boxes is arbitrary in contrast to the grid cells, special care must be taken for flat bounding boxes (e.g., of an axis-aligned triangle) to avoid division by zero (see lines 16–20). In the case of a two-level BVH, we precompute offsets to the feature vector buffer for each object/instance (i.e., a prefix sum of the number of cut nodes in each object/in- stance). Note that each instance has its own set of feature vectors but uses the same BVH cut. 3.3. Training The feature vectors are optimized in two passes (in a similar manner as the grid en- coding). We first compute gradients with respect to a loss function L: ∂L ∂zk = ∂L ∂z ∂z ∂zk = wk ∂L ∂z , where z is the tri-linearly interpolated feature vector fed to the neural network, zk is a feature vector of the k-th corner, and wk is the corresponding interpolation weight. The gradients are accumulated over the whole training batch. Then, we compute the average gradient, which we use to update the feature values using an optimizer such as the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) or Adam.

  1. Implementation Details

To demonstrate that our method is compatible with modern ray tracing engines, we extend HIPRT [Meister et al. 2024], an open-source ray tracing framework in HIP. We need only three minor modifications of its API: (1) a build parameter specifying the maximum number of cut nodes in a bottom-level BVH, (2) an extension of the hit structure to return the cut node and sequential indices (see Algorithm 1), and (3) a function for normalizing the point given the instance and cut node indices. Alternatively, we could provide a function returning a bounding box, and normal- ize the point on the application side. However, the internal hardware format supports oriented bounding boxes, where we need to (inversely) transform the point into the space of the oriented bounding box prior to the interpolation. Exposing the rotation 53 Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques BVH Encoding for Neural-Assisted Ray Tracing V ol. 15, No. 2, 2026 http://jcgt.org Algorithm 1. The internal hardware BVH formats store child bounding boxes inside a parent internal node, and thus, there is no easy way to get the bounding box of the leaf node 54 Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques BVH Encoding for Neural-Assisted Ray Tracing V ol. 15, No. 2, 2026 http://jcgt.org directly from the leaf itself. In order to use leaf nodes as cut nodes, we represent the cut node index as an index of the parent node and an index of the child slot within the parent (packed in a single 32-bit integer). We define the minimal size of each cut as the branching factor (4 or 8) of the internal node format. Thereby, we avoid a singular case in which the root node is selected as a cut node (the root does not have a parent node). This also allows us to treat the parent and the child as a two-level cut with simple indexing in contrast to general cuts.

  1. Neural Radiance Cache

Our method is tailored for ray tracing, and thus, we evaluate our BVH encoding in the context of global illumination. We select the neural radiance cache (NRC) [M¨uller et al. 2021] as an application to evaluate the proposed method. NRC stores radiance at a given point outgoing in a given direction. We use the normal, albedo, and surface roughness as additional guiding inputs. In our implementation, NRC is trained and evaluated on the first secondary hit (i.e., after one bounce), and we use 10% of pixels as a budget for training samples. A caveat of our BVH encoding is that the training samples are unevenly dis- tributed among the cut nodes if we sample data uniformly (in contrast to the uniform grid). Thus, large nodes will have more samples, while smaller nodes might be com- pletely missed. This has a negative impact on performance due to uneven atomic pressure during the gradient accumulation. To address this problem, we propose a simple heuristic that redistributes the training samples uniformly across the cut nodes, introducing only a minimal overhead. When we trace the short paths terminating on the first secondary hit, we track the number of hits by atomically incrementing the corresponding counter for each cut node. We consider nodes with nonzero hits as vis- ible ones. Note that this is only a rough estimation since some of the nodes might be missed. We compute a desired number of training samples per visible cut node as the total training sample budget (e.g., 10% of the pixels) divided by the number of visible cut nodes. Then, we compute a ratio of the desired number and the actual count. We do not round the numbers and keep them as real numbers. Then, we stochastically discard or reuse multiple times some of the samples to match the desired count. The whole part of the ratio indicates how many times each sample is reused, and the frac- tional part is an acceptance ratio for the sample. For example, if there are four training samples in a cut node, but the desired count is ten, then the ratio is 10 4 = 2.5. In such a case, each sample is reused twice, and to match the remainder, we additionally use each sample with a probability of 50%. To reuse the training sample, we use the same position and the view direction but, each time, a different suffix of the light path. Dif- ferent suffixes provide different radiance estimates, which are subsequently averaged resulting in more precise gradient estimates. This approach reduces the atomic pres- 55 Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques BVH Encoding for Neural-Assisted Ray Tracing V ol. 15, No. 2, 2026 http://jcgt.org sure. However, since it is only a heuristic, it may actually increase the approximation error of the radiance field. For instance, the heuristic does not take the distance into account. Thus, a distant small cut node may get samples that could be used for more important larger cut nodes closer to the primary hits otherwise. Therefore, we use a defensive approach, generating r of samples by the redistribution heuristic (described above) and 1 − r of samples uniformly (in the screen space), where r is a parameter.

  1. Results

We use our in-house MLP framework and renderer implemented in HIP, built on top of the modified version of HIPRT-v3 [Meister et al. 2024]. We use an MLP with three hidden layers, each containing 64 neurons, using leaky rectified linear unit (ReLU) as an activation function. To encode a position, we use either our method or the multi- resolution hash-grid encoding [M¨uller et al. 2022]. The hash-grid encoding uses four levels with the initial resolution of 32 × 32 × 32 (doubling the resolution at each level), and our method uses 643 as a threshold for the base cut (using parents of the base cut nodes as the second level) unless stated otherwise. With such setting the MLP uses eight inputs for the encoded position in both cases. We modified the H-PLOC algorithm [Benthin et al. 2024] in HIPRT such that, as a post-process, it finds the base cut. We use the base cut nodes and their parents for encoding (see Section 4). The MLP weights and feature vectors are stored in the 16-bit floating-point (FP16) data type and updated by the Adam optimizer. All experiments were executed on a PC with the AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 GPU and Ubuntu 24.04 OS using ROCm 7.1. 6.1. Qualitative and Quantitative Comparison We train the neural network using 1024 iterations, where each iteration is distributed into 8 batches. Once the training is finished, we use 1024 samples per pixel to render the final result. Thereby, we ensure that the neural network is trained enough, avoid- ing errors from possible initial outliers and Monte Carlo integration. We observed additional variance in the results due to parallel processing on the GPU. Threads with the same seeds may process different training samples in different runs due to non- deterministic atomic operations. Therefore, we average the results over 16 test runs. In Figure 3, we compare indirect lighting provided by NRC using the hash-grid en- coding and our method. We use light sampler–based spherical Gaussians [Tokuyoshi et al. 2024] and r = 0 .9 unless stated otherwise. To emphasize the differences, we show only indirect lighting, without multiplying by the bidirectional scattering dis- tribution function (BSDF) and the cosine term. The results show that our method is competitive with the hash-grid encoding. Limitations Our approach adapts to scene geometry, which is a double-edged sword as it adapts to the geometry but cannot go below the leaf level. One could wonder: why not use spatial splits to enclose large triangles by multiple smaller bounding boxes in order to achieve a finer cut? The problem is that in such a case, the hit point might lie outside the corresponding cut node, leading to incorrect tri-linear interpolation. One could argue that we could pre-tessellate the scene to have triangles of roughly the same size. However, this would not help our method, since the cut is static. Imagine a teapot-in-a-stadium scene, where there are multiple teapots, but only one 59 Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques BVH Encoding for Neural-Assisted Ray Tracing V ol. 15, No. 2, 2026 http://jcgt.org HashGrid FLIP 0.388 BVHCode 323 (ours) FLIP 0.395 BVHCode 253 (ours) FLIP 0.373 Figure 6. Reducing the budget from 323 to 253 lowers the error below the hash-grid encoding, showing that the budget has to be matched to the scene rather than maximized. Total time per frame: 61.6 ms (HashGrid), 46.1 ms (323), and 49.1 ms (253). is visible from the camera. The strategy—how we currently build the cut—distributes the cut budget between all the teapots, which is not optimal in such a case. Another limitation is that the feature vectors indexed by the BVH belong only to a single bounding box compared to the uniform grid, where feature vectors are shared among neighboring cells. This results in fewer training samples per feature vector, making training more difficult. This is also why it is difficult to compete with the hash grid in the Cave scene. Lastly, we assume that the encoded positions are inside the cut nodes, which is not the case, for example, in volumetric rendering.

  1. Conclusion and Future Work

We presented a novel encoding method using BVH as a spatial data structure to index feature vectors. We demonstrated its application in the context of path tracing with neural radiance caching. The results indicate that the method could be a viable alter- 60 Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques BVH Encoding for Neural-Assisted Ray Tracing V ol. 15, No. 2, 2026 http://jcgt.org native to widely used grid encoding, especially for large scenes, where the resolution of the uniform grid is insufficient. One promising direction for future work is a combination with triangle-based encoding to achieve finer clusters even for large triangles. We proposed a heuristic for redistributing the training samples into clusters. This heuristic solves the issue with the atomic pressure, but it is not optimal in terms of quality. A better heuristic that takes into account the actual light transport is another possible direction for future work. It would also be interesting to investigate the possibility of the dynamic cut in combination with virtualized geometry and hierarchical level of detail [Benthin and Peters 2023]; however, it might be challenging to recover the per-frame overhead induced by the dynamic cut formation. item.title: 3DGS 致密化别数「看见几次」，要数「真贡献几次」 ｜ Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting
item.description:
一句话：遮挡感知过滤 + 贡献归一化：遮挡密集场景 LPIPS 最多低 6%，高斯数不到原来一半。

要点：

  • 指出自适应密度控制（ADC）的统计用了视锥可见性过滤：完全被遮挡的高斯仍被算作被观测，稀释平均梯度，让遮挡区反而不长点。
  • 改成遮挡感知过滤（只统计该高斯真正贡献的视角），并把原始的视角计数归一化换成平均贡献归一化。
  • 集成到 StopThePop 框架：遮挡密集场景所有画质指标都更好（LPIPS 最多低 6%），高斯数量不到视角计数方案的一半，长调度下数量有界不发散。

为什么值得看：大场景 3DGS 最容易在遮挡区糊掉、在高斯数量上失控。这处改动很小但直击根因，属于能直接打进现有 3DGS 训练管线的补丁。

中文摘要：3DGS 通过自适应密度控制（ADC）从稀疏初始化长出稠密场景，而 ADC 的决策依赖渲染时统计的逐高斯基量。作者发现这些统计经过视锥可见性过滤，对遮挡完全无知：完全被遮挡的高斯仍被计为被观测，从而稀释平均梯度信号，恰好在几何被遮挡的位置抑制致密化。他们用遮挡感知过滤修正——只把统计限制在该高斯真正有贡献的视角上，并把判据里原始的视角计数归一化换成平均贡献归一化。两者集成进 StopThePop 框架后，在遮挡密集场景上所有画质指标都优于遮挡盲基线（LPIPS 最多降低 6%），且高斯数量不到视角计数归一化方案的一半；在大型场景需要的更长调度下，数量保持有界，而多数判据会发散；在较小基准上以远低于竞争方法的数量保持竞争力。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-22

Counting Contributions, Not Views:
Occlusion-Aware Densification
for 3D Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting grows a dense scene from a sparse initialization through adaptive density control (ADC), driven by per-Gaussian statistics gathered during rendering. These statistics pass a frustum-based visibility filter blind to occlusion: fully occluded Gaussians still count as observed, diluting the averaged gradient signal and suppressing densification precisely where geometry is occluded. We correct this with an occlusion-aware filter that restricts densification statistics to views in which a Gaussian actually contributes, and replace the criterion’s raw view-count normalizer with an average-contribution one. Integrated into a StopThePop-based framework, the two together improve every image-quality metric over the occlusion-blind baseline on occlusion-heavy scenes (up to 6% lower LPIPS), at less than half the Gaussians a view-count normalizer requires. Under the longer schedules these large scenes require, the count stays bounded where most criteria diverge, and on smaller benchmarks our method stays competitive at a fraction of the competitors’ count.

Keywords:

Gaussian Splatting Adaptive Density Control Densification 3D Reconstruction Large-Scale Scenes Novel View Synthesis

1 Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [13] represents a milestone in 3D scene reconstruction and novel-view synthesis. It introduced a large multi-component system, with a tile-based rasterizer and adaptive density control (ADC) purpose-built for the new representation. Follow-up works improve these components largely in isolation, many focusing on ADC, which is essential for growing a dense reconstruction from the sparse initialization. However, we find that the accumulation of the densification statistics at the root of all ADC decisions has a fundamental flaw: the frustum-based visibility filter that gathers them tests only whether a Gaussian could appear in a view, not whether it actually contributes to the rendered image. A fully occluded Gaussian yields zero gradients, yet the filter still counts its view in the criterion’s denominator, dragging the average down and stalling densification wherever geometry is occluded. The resulting under-densification grows with the degree of occlusion and degrades quality most where high detail and occlusion co-occur. Large, occlusion-heavy scenes such as multi-room apartments are affected most severely (Counting Contributions, Not Views:
Occlusion-Aware Densification
for 3D Gaussian Splatting). We correct this with an occlusion-aware visibility filter that updates a Gaussian’s statistics only from views in which it is actually rendered; densification then reaches occluded regions whenever their level of detail requires it.

We further find that normalizing the accumulated gradient by a raw view count does not match the contribution-weighted nature of the tracked gradients. We derive a more natural normalizer that accumulates a Gaussian’s average contribution to each rendered view. To validate our occlusion-aware densification, we build a framework around StopThePop [20] that consolidates established densification improvements from separate prior methods into a strong baseline. We evaluate both changes on this baseline and directly on StopThePop. On the occlusion-heavy Zip-NeRF [2] scenes, the resulting method outperforms StopThePop on all image-quality metrics, reducing LPIPS by up to 12%. Its Gaussian count also stays bounded under the longer schedules these large scenes require, where most competing criteria diverge. On smaller benchmarks, it performs comparably to the state of the art with up to 63% fewer Gaussians. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to replace the visibility filter itself: the frustum-based test that underlies all densification statistics. Our occlusion-aware filter updates a Gaussian’s statistics only from views in which it is actually rendered, independent of the criterion built on top.

  • •

    We introduce a contribution-based densification criterion that is more closely related to the gradient signal used by ADC, leading to better densification decisions, demonstrated on small- and large-scale scenes.

  • •

    We combine both contributions with established densification improvements and other refinements into a strong framework that does not require per-scene tuning and has fewer hyperparameters (e.g. eliminating the unstable scene extent). We will make the code available to the research community.

    • 2 Background and Related Work

    2.1 Adaptive Density Control

    3D Gaussian Splatting [13] represents a scene as a set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by a 3D mean position, a 3D covariance matrix (parameterized by a rotation and per-axis scale), an opacity o, and a view-dependent color c derived from spherical harmonics [7]. For rendering, each Gaussian is projected onto the image as a 2D footprint with a screen-space mean and radius. Starting from a sparse point cloud, 3DGS grows and prunes its set of Gaussians via adaptive density control (ADC), executed every 100 iterations after a 500-iteration warm-up and disabled after the first half of training. A scene extent E, computed from the training cameras, provides the reference scale for several ADC decisions.

    Criterion.

    During rendering, a frustum-based visibility filter accumulates per-Gaussian statistics: the 2D screen-space positional gradient g_i,v of Gaussian i in view v, the screen-space radius, and a view count M. At each ADC event, a Gaussian is marked for densification if its accumulated gradient magnitude, averaged over the view count, exceeds a predefined threshold (0.0002 by default).

    Densification.

    To resolve the problem of an insufficient number of Gaussians capturing a region’s textural or structural detail (from here on described as under-densification), a marked Gaussian is densified in one of two modes: if it is large relative to the scene extent, it is split into two downscaled children sampled from the parent’s distribution, otherwise it is cloned, i.e. duplicated, in place.

    Pruning.

    Redundant or noisy Gaussians are removed using pruning mechanisms. An opacity prune removes every Gaussian whose opacity oᵢ falls below a predefined threshold (0.005). A size-based prune removes Gaussians whose screen-space radius or world-space scale exceeds a fixed threshold. To clear floater artifacts, 3DGS additionally resets all opacities to near zero (0.01) every 3000 iterations; important Gaussians recover quickly, floaters stay dim and fall to the opacity prune. StopThePop [20] offers a gradual opacity decay as an alternative to the drastic reset. We evaluate both as the (Reset) and (Decay) variants.

    2.2 Adaptive Density Control Improvements

    All of the following ADC improvements inherit the frustum-based visibility filter described above, which counts every in-frustum Gaussian, occluded or not. We make this filter occlusion-aware (Sec.3.1).

    Densification Criterion.

    AbsGS [28] and GOF [29] counter gradient cancellation in the accumulation, which otherwise causes under-densification of high-detail regions. PixelGS [31] instead questions the normalization by the observation count and proposes a pixel-count-weighted mean. Grubert et al.[9] adopt the PixelGS strategy with an ascending threshold that shifts densification earlier. Taming3DGS [18] replaces the threshold with a per-Gaussian multi-term score under a fixed densification budget. However, budget-controlled methods require a target count as input, a value that is not known and that a good densification criterion should find. We propose to normalize a Gaussian’s accumulated gradient by the accumulated average contributions of its rendered views (Sec.3.2), rather than the observation count of 3DGS or the visible-pixel count of PixelGS. We also adopt GOF’s absolute-gradient signal against cancellation.

    Densification Step (Split & Clone).

    GOF observes that clones remain clustered and instead samples the child’s position from the parent’s distribution, while Bulò et al.[22] show that the clone operation introduces an opacity bias. EFA-GS [23] and Deng et al.[4] drop the clone entirely, and Deng et al. additionally propose a geometrically more meaningful split procedure. Grubert et al. address inconsistencies in the scene-extent computation that governs some ADC decisions by also accounting for the input point cloud. Other works replace the densification step more radically [15, 3, 6, 24]. Our experiments also support dropping the clone: we notice large floater clusters due to excessive cloning on scenes where the scene extent is not well matched to the size of detail (Tab.4). We therefore follow the split-only approach of EFA-GS and Deng et al., including the latter’s split procedure. This removes one dependence on the scene extent.

    Pruning.

    Grubert et al. restrict the opacity prune to Gaussians that also contribute little; EAGLES [8] and OC2DGS [21] prune low- or non-contributing Gaussians at intervals long enough to observe every training view; ReLaGS [26] and RadSplat [19] prune by maximum contribution over a full pass, at isolated points of the optimization. We prune by maximum contribution, as in ReLaGS and RadSplat, but throughout the optimization, as in EAGLES and OC2DGS.

    2.3 Large-Scale Scenes

    Large-scale scenes harbor a range of problems for Gaussian Splatting: Kerbl et al.[14] partition them into chunks optimized individually after a coarse full-scene pass. They note problems with the regular densification regime and adopt the maximum 2D screen-space gradient as the criterion. OccluGaussian [17] makes the partitioning occlusion-aware, clustering by what each camera sees so that no chunk contains heavy occlusions, and optimizes chunks individually before merging them. RadSplat observes that lighting variations in the Zip-NeRF dataset [2] cause 3DGS to struggle and produce overly smooth results even with an exposure-handling module. SMERF [5] performs extensive densification-related hyperparameter tuning on Zip-NeRF yet reports low Gaussian counts, indicating under-densification. Lowering the gradient threshold raises the count only at the cost of more floaters. Neither work identifies the root cause. We argue it is occlusion-blind densification (a cause that exposure correction and hyperparameter tuning leave unaddressed) and provide supporting evidence in Sec.4.3. Unlike OccluGaussian, we do not avoid this problem by optimizing occluded regions as individual small scenes, but instead make the densification occlusion-aware, enabling a single full-scene optimization.

    3 Method

    We build on StopThePop [20], a state-of-the-art Gaussian Splatting renderer whose exact per-pixel depth ordering removes popping artifacts and keeps occlusion boundaries intact. Hybrid transparency [10], in contrast, sorts only the front-most Gaussians and composites all remaining ones without enforcing occlusion ordering. Leaving even fully occluded Gaussians with a nonzero contribution stands in opposition to our motivation of occlusion-aware densification. However, our method is not dependent on the per-pixel sorting of StopThePop: it relies only on the per-pixel blending weights that virtually every Gaussian Splatting rasterizer already computes. Our contributions can therefore transfer to other bases (evaluated on 2DGS [12] and 3DGS [13] in Sec. A.2 of the supplementary material).

    Differentiable rasterization.

    Projected onto the image plane, a Gaussian i forms a 2D footprint G_i,p∈(0,1] over pixels p[32], yielding the per-pixel opacity α_i,p=oᵢG_i,p. 3DGS renders with a tile-based differentiable rasterizer: a preprocessing step culls Gaussians against the camera view frustum, maps the remaining ones to the image tiles they overlap, and sorts them by view-space depth. Each pixel p is rendered by front-to-back alpha compositing of the depth-sorted Gaussians that overlap it, yielding its color Cₚ:

    Cₚ=∑ᵢcᵢ α_i,p T_i,p+c_bg T_final,p, T_i,p=∏_j

    		(1)

    where the transmittance T_i,p is the fraction of light that reaches Gaussian i at pixel p past the Gaussians in front of it. Rendering terminates early once T_i,p saturates (falls below 10⁻⁴), so Gaussians behind that point are never rendered. The remaining transmittance T_final,p is filled with a constant background color c_bg. The product w_i,p=α_i,p T_i,p is the blending weight with which Gaussian i contributes to pixel p: its per-pixel opacity α_i,p weighted by its visibility T_i,p.

    The complete integrated framework, which assembles established densification improvements around them, is described in Sec.4.2.

    3.1 Occlusion-Awareness

    As discussed in Sec.2.1, densification-related statistics are gathered via a visibility filter based on a view-frustum test. This reflects potential, not actual, observations of a Gaussian. From here on, we refer to Gaussians that are not rendered at all as occluded: transmittance saturates before reaching them at every pixel they cover. With a frustum-based filter, occluded Gaussians thus enter the accumulated densification statistics despite not participating in the rendered image. Although their gradients are zero, every occluded view still increases the criterion’s observation count and updates the maximum-radius tracking. Increasing the observation count results in a downward pressure on the densification criterion of any Gaussian that lies within the frustum while being obstructed. The consequence is under-densification in occlusion-heavy scenes such as the multi-room apartments of Zip-NeRF [2], as also observed by prior work [5, 19].

    We propose an occlusion-aware visibility filter that restricts the influence of rendering statistics to those Gaussians that actually participate in rendering the image. For the filter itself, a binary signal suffices: a Gaussian counts as observed in a view only if it contributes to at least one pixel. We obtain this signal from the total contribution the Gaussian accumulates during rendering: the sum of its blending weights w_i,p over all pixels of the view. This quantity is reused by our criterion in Sec.3.2. If the total contribution is zero, the Gaussian did not participate in the rendering and is therefore occluded (Fig.2). Replacing the original frustum-based visibility filter with our occlusion-aware filter thus ensures occlusion-aware densification statistics.

    The occlusion signal could equally come from a Boolean rendered flag as computed in OC2DGS [21] or a rendered-pixel count as in PixelGS [31]. However, it is essential that the filter gating the densification statistics is derived from such a rendering signal rather than remaining based on the view frustum.

    3.2 Average Contribution Criterion

    3DGS decides densification from a Gaussian’s positional gradients in screen space, averaged in magnitude across its observed views. For a Gaussian i observed in M views, let g_i,v=∂L/∂μᵢ denote the gradient of the training loss L with respect to the Gaussian’s projected screen-space mean μᵢ in view v. A Gaussian is densified (i.e. split or cloned) when

    γᵢ^3DGS=1/M∑ᵥ∥g_i,v∥

    		(2)

    exceeds a threshold. The denominator M weights every view equally: a view in which the Gaussian is barely visible counts the same as a fully visible one. As discussed in Sec.3.1, fully occluded views inflate M while contributing nothing to the gradient sum, biasing the average downward.

    To identify a more faithful measure of observation, we examine how the gradient is formed. The per-view gradient g_i,v=(g_i,v,x,g_i,v,y) is accumulated over pixels to which Gaussian i contributes (w_i,p>0), and the contribution of each pixel p is gated by the Gaussian’s blending weight w_i,p. Per pixel, the gradient factorizes into the scalar w_i,p and a weight-independent vector s_i,p:

    g_i,v=∑ₚw_i,ps_i,p,\hskip20.075ptw_i,p=α_i,p T_i,p,

    		(3)

    where the per-pixel vector s_i,p combines the photometric residual, the geometric steering direction, and the local contrast of the Gaussian’s color against what lies behind it, all independent of the Gaussian’s visibility (detailed derivation in Sec. A.1). The blending weight w_i,p is thus simultaneously the quantity with which the rasterizer composites the Gaussian’s color and the factor that scales every term of its positional gradient. A pixel where the Gaussian is mostly occluded (T_i,p→0) or barely present (α_i,p→0) contributes almost nothing to g_i,v, irrespective of that pixel’s error. The gradient is thus already visibility-weighted at the pixel level, which motivates measuring a Gaussian’s observation by its blending weights w_i,p rather than by a binary view count.

    We summarize a Gaussian’s participation in view v by its mean blending weight w̄_i,v over the N_i,v pixels in which it contributes as

    w̄_i,v=(1)/(N_i,v)∑ₚw_i,p∈[0,1)

    		(4)

    and replace the view count in Eq.2 with the accumulated w̄_i,v:

    γᵢ^Ours=(1)/(1+∑ᵥw̄_i,v)∑ᵥ∥g_i,v∥.

    		(5)

    We normalize by the mean per-view contribution w̄_i,v rather than the total W_i,v=∑ₚw_i,p=N_i,vw̄_i,v. Any denominator that scales with the pixel count N_i,v ties densification to screen-space footprint area and suppresses exactly the large Gaussians that are most likely to require it. In contrast, the mean measures how visible the Gaussian is where it is rendered, independently of coverage. Moreover, because w̄_i,v contains the transmittance T_i,p, the criterion is occlusion-aware without an explicit visibility test: a view in which the Gaussian is only faintly visible cannot dilute the average, unlike a view-count normalizer. Whether such a view pushes toward densification is then decided by its gradient alone: a faint view with a large residual contributes its full signal with minimal normalization cost, whereas a faint view with little error simply fades out.

    This incidental occlusion-awareness is shared by the pixel-count normalizer of PixelGS [31]: a fully occluded view renders no pixels and drops out of its denominator as well. Beyond that, however, a visible-pixel count entangles view visibility with screen-space footprint, over-densifying near-camera Gaussians. PixelGS counteracts this with a separate distance scaling term based on the scene extent E. Our per-view mean w̄_i,v avoids this entanglement entirely. Additionally, through the transmittance T_i,p, it attenuates partial occlusion, grazing observations, and low-opacity views that leave a pixel count unchanged.

    The constant in the denominator of Eq.5 is a fixed floor: without it, rarely observed Gaussians (∑ᵥw̄_i,v→0) would receive unbounded scores where evidence is weakest. The floor ensures that scores increase smoothly and monotonically with accumulated evidence, placing rarely and frequently observed Gaussians on a common scale. A sweep in Sec. F.2 of the supplementary material confirms this: without the floor training diverges, while other floor values mainly re-scale the threshold. The updated criterion operates on a new scale and therefore requires a one-time recalibration of the densification threshold. A threshold sweep on a subset of the Mip-NeRF360 dataset shows 0.002 to be the operating point. We keep this value fixed across all experiments.

    Finally, the normalization in Eq.5 depends only on the per-pixel blending weights w_i,p, not on how the 2D gradients are reduced to a scalar value. Therefore, it applies unchanged to the absolute-gradient formulations of AbsGS [28] and GOF [29]. We apply the same criterion computation to all gradient terms.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Datasets and Metrics

    We evaluate on the common Gaussian Splatting scenes: Mip-NeRF360 [1] (9 scenes), Tanks & Temples [16] (2 scenes), and Deep Blending [11] (2 scenes). Additionally, we evaluate on Zip-NeRF [2], whose 4 large apartment scenes (alameda, berlin, london, nyc) exhibit heavy occlusions between rooms, with an occlusion rate of 0.63 against 0.15–0.48 on the other datasets (definition and per-scene values in Sec. D). Zip-NeRF is the established stress test for this regime: prior work reports 3DGS under-densification and over-smoothing on these scenes despite extensive tuning [5, 19]. For Zip-NeRF, we use images at half their original resolution, mirroring common 3DGS target resolutions, and hold out every 8th image as the validation set, following the standard protocol [13]. We report peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity (SSIM) [25], learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS; VGG backbone) [30], the final number of Gaussians, and the training time. Large-scale scenes are prone to over-smoothing due to under-densification [19, 5]. We therefore also report the gradient magnitude similarity deviation (GMSD) [27], a metric specifically sensitive to blur. We read these metrics jointly: perceptual ones such as LPIPS credit reconstructed detail that e.g. PSNR penalizes when not pixel-aligned. Likewise, a lower Gaussian count is only better at comparable quality: a starved model is not more efficient.

    4.2 Implementation

    We embed our contributions in the integrated framework: the publicly available StopThePop [20], extended with the following improvements proposed by related work, which we do not claim as contributions. Unless stated otherwise, all runs use the opacity decay variant from StopThePop, and reported numbers are averaged over three training runs. All experiments run on an Nvidia A40 GPU.

    Absolute gradient.

    We include the absolute-gradient condition of GOF [29], which improves high-frequency detail at an increased Gaussian count (Tab.4).

    Gaussian densification.

    We follow a split-only strategy, as also adopted by EFA-GS [23] and Deng et al.[4]. In our setting this removes a dependence on the scene extent E and avoids the excessive cloning that leads to pronounced floaters or total failure (Tab.4). We also adopt Deng et al.’s geometrically meaningful long-axis split, which slightly reduces the count at competitive quality.

    Pruning.

    Following the recommendation of Grubert et al.[9], we disable size-based pruning, which we find has no significant impact on quality or Gaussian count (Tab.4). Disabling it also removes another dependence on the scene extent E. We additionally prune Gaussians whose maximum blending contribution wₘₐₓ stays below a fixed threshold (0.005), as discussed by ReLaGS [26] and RadSplat [19]. We track wₘₐₓ on the fly and prune throughout training [21, 8] on an automatic, hyperparameter-free schedule synchronized with the training queue. A single cheap pass over all training views at the end guarantees that the final model contains no fully occluded Gaussians (scheduling details in Sec. E.1, occluded-Gaussian counts per method in Sec. E.2).

    Densification statistics.

    Original 3DGS accumulates densification statistics already during warm-up, where the largely transparent scene does not yet reflect its geometry. We exclude the warm-up period, which affects only the first densification event and is confirmed safe (Tab.4).

    Competitor comparison.

    We replicate PixelGS [31] and Grubert et al.[9] on the same StopThePop renderer in two settings: their full methods on vanilla StopThePop for the state-of-the-art comparison (Tab.3), and their criterion alone inside the integrated framework, for the criterion comparison (Tab.1).

    4.3 Impact of Occlusion-Awareness

    Integrating the adopted densification components into StopThePop already yields a strong but still occlusion-blind baseline. It surpasses StopThePop on all image-quality metrics on both datasets (Zip-NeRF: LPIPS by 6%, PSNR by 0.57 dB; StopThePop comparison in Sec. B). On top of this baseline, we isolate the occlusion-aware visibility filter (Sec.3.1), leaving every other component unchanged. The top two rows of Tab.1 compare the occlusion-blind baseline against its occlusion-aware counterpart. Making the filter occlusion-aware improves all image-quality metrics while enabling the densification that occlusion-blindness suppresses (LPIPS improves by a further 9%; the count rises from 0.56M to 2.57M). Merely lowering the occlusion-blind threshold is no equivalent control: it densifies indiscriminately rather than where occlusion suppressed it, and SMERF [5] reports that this produces floaters on these scenes. Occlusion-blind densification is thus a primary cause of under-densification on large, occlusion-heavy scenes. On Mip-NeRF360, where occlusions are far lighter, the same pairing confirms the corrected filter does no harm: LPIPS improves by 4% at a moderately higher count (Sec. F.3).

    4.4 Impact of the Average Contribution Criterion

    We now compare densification criteria directly, holding the occlusion-aware filter and all other components fixed and varying only the criterion. We examine four criteria: the occlusion-aware observation count, the PixelGS [31] pixel-count-weighted mean without and with distance scaling (PixelGS, PixelGS + DS), and the average contribution (Ours). All criteria run at a single fixed threshold across every scene and dataset: the competitors at their published defaults, ours calibrated once on the Mip-NeRF360 sweep subset (Sec. F.1) and left unchanged elsewhere. Table1 reports the four criteria on the occlusion-heavy Zip-NeRF scenes (Mip-NeRF360 counterpart in Tab. S12). On the smaller Mip-NeRF360 scenes the criterion barely affects quality (across the four criteria, PSNR spans 0.13 dB and LPIPS 3%), so compactness is decisive: our average-contribution criterion produces the fewest Gaussians (roughly 55–75% of the other criteria’s counts) at matched quality. The criteria differ sharply on the large Zip-NeRF scenes. The raw pixel-count criterion is poorly behaved on its own: it over-densifies to 6.6M Gaussians, by far the largest count, yet reaches the worst PSNR. Under a long training schedule it diverges catastrophically (Sec.4.5). PixelGS therefore couples the criterion with distance scaling as a guard rail against runaway densification. This bounds the count, but on these large multi-room scenes the guard suppresses densification that is actually needed: quality degrades to the worst SSIM, LPIPS, and GMSD of the four. We attribute this to the reliance of distance scaling on the scene extent. We find the scene extent to be unreliable in general but especially on large scenes (Sec.4.2). Our method is instead fully independent of it. Our average-contribution criterion needs no guard rail: it is intrinsically self-limiting, giving the fewest Gaussians of the four at competitive quality. The occlusion-aware count is 0.5%, 3%, and 3% better on SSIM, LPIPS, and GMSD and 0.06 dB worse on PSNR, at 2.3× our count. This demand is structural: given more densification opportunity, it keeps growing until training diverges, whereas ours stays bounded (Sec.4.5).

    4.5 Scalability under a Matched Training Budget

    The large Zip-NeRF scenes are unevenly observed: training cameras cluster in interior hotspots and cover peripheral regions far more sparsely (camera map for the alameda example in Fig. S3). They also hold about seven times as many training images as Mip-NeRF360, so the default 30k schedule grants each image only 22 optimization steps against Mip-NeRF360’s 159, and lets it contribute to only 11 densification events against 77. Sparsely covered regions therefore receive few densification opportunities, and blur there can signal missing opportunity rather than poor densification decisions. Longer schedules restore this opportunity and reveal whether a criterion resolves the remaining detail or leaves these regions under-densified, and whether its growth stays bounded while doing so. We therefore additionally train the large Zip-NeRF scenes under a matched schedule of 210k iterations, which restores both quantities (157 steps and 76 densification events per image), and sample around it at 100k and 300k. Every other result keeps the standard 30k protocol for comparability. Table2 shows the results up to the matched schedule; the 300k table and schedule details are in Sec. G.2.

    Under these schedules the naive pixel-count criterion (PixelGS without distance scaling) is not merely inefficient but unstable: on every Zip-NeRF scene it over-densifies past the ∼16.8M trainable-count limit until training crashes (count-versus-iteration plot in Fig. S4). That limit lies nearly an order of magnitude beyond ours. The full PixelGS baseline, which includes the distance-scaling guard rail, does not diverge at its default threshold; the instability is a property of the pixel-count criterion in isolation. Our average-contribution criterion stays bounded throughout (2.75M even at 300k) and continues to improve in LPIPS and GMSD, whereas the guarded PixelGS remains behind on every image-quality metric while using 62% more Gaussians. Section G.4 traces this remaining gap to the guard itself: the distance term systematically suppresses near-object detail. At 210k, even the occlusion-aware count over-densifies past the same limit on the two occlusion-heaviest scenes. These divergences are mechanistic, not single-run artifacts: the Gaussian count grows steadily into the trainable limit. We therefore also report the 100k schedule, the longest that the remaining count-based criteria complete, to quantify their high-count behavior. There, the extra Gaussians buy no quality advantage, repeating the Mip-NeRF360 pattern: ours leads PSNR, SSIM, and GMSD outright and stays within about 1% LPIPS of the occlusion-aware count, at 39–67% of the competing counts. Two supplementary analyses corroborate this. A threshold sweep (Sec. F.5) confirms that the self-limiting behavior is not specific to the chosen threshold: at half the default, the count-based criteria reach roughly three times our count. A per-view analysis (Sec. G.5) shows that our per-view quality stays as tight as the guarded PixelGS’s, while the unguarded occlusion-aware count develops a growing low-quality tail.

    4.6 Comparison to State-of-the-Art

    Table3 compares our method against StopThePop [20], our shared-base re-implementations of PixelGS and Grubert et al., and published reference results. Across all four datasets our method reaches competitive or better image quality while using far fewer Gaussians than the strongest competitors, improving reconstruction efficiency rather than trading count for quality. On the occlusion-heavy Zip-NeRF scenes, both our variants lead every image-quality metric among the methods trained on the shared base, with up to 12% lower LPIPS than StopThePop and 8% (decay) to 11% (reset) better LPIPS than the best competitor. The decay variant achieves this at the same Gaussian count as Grubert et al., the strongest competitor. Figure3 shows this qualitatively: in heavily occluded interior regions, the occlusion-blind methods remain visibly blurry, while our method resolves the fine geometry. Even the RadSplat upper-bound reference trails both our variants in LPIPS, by 9–12%. On Deep Blending it matches the best quality (within 0.02 dB PSNR, tied SSIM with Grubert et al.) at less than half the Gaussians. On Mip-NeRF360 it achieves better LPIPS than every StopThePop, PixelGS, and Grubert variant with its other metrics within about 2% of the best. The decay variant uses 35–60% of the PixelGS and Grubert counts. On Tanks & Temples the competitors’ paper-reported PSNR advantage shrinks substantially on the shared base (Grubert et al. remain 0.56 dB ahead). Ours still holds the best LPIPS and stays within roughly 1% on SSIM, the pattern expected when detail is reconstructed but not perfectly pixel-aligned. Across scenes, the occlusion rate predicts where our contributions help: it correlates with our LPIPS gain over the occlusion-blind variant (Spearman +0.83). Ours also allocates its Gaussians more efficiently: even without the contribution prune, our models contain the smallest share of fully occluded Gaussians (7.2% on Zip-NeRF, against 10.5–22.7% for the occlusion-blind methods; occluded-Gaussian counts per method in Tab. S8). This is no artifact of lower counts: at a nearly matched count, our unpruned variant contains 43% fewer occluded Gaussians than Grubert et al.’s.

    4.7 Ablation Study

    We ablate our full model on the Zip-NeRF scenes by removing or reverting one component at a time (Tab.4). The isolation of our two contributions on vanilla StopThePop, and the clone failure it exposes, are analyzed in Sec. C.2 (Tab. S5) of the supplementary material. By far the most consequential component is split-only densification: restoring the original clone operation (+ clone) collapses reconstruction quality (nearly 5 dB PSNR and 31% LPIPS worse). Cloning depends on the unreliable scene extent that these large scenes expose. The GOF absolute-gradient signal (- GOF Grad) is the largest quality contributor among the remaining components (6% better LPIPS at a moderately higher count). Long-axis split reduces the count by 31% at a marginal 3% LPIPS trade, contribution pruning by 9% at unchanged quality, while the statistics warm-up and size prune are negligible. Reverting opacity decay to reset gives marginally better quality at 76% more Gaussians (both variants in Tab.3), confirming decay as the more efficient default.

    5 Conclusion & Limitations

    We expose the occlusion-blindness of the adaptive density control in standard 3DGS and propose a modular solution, transferable to existing Gaussian Splatting methods, that ensures occlusion-aware densification statistics. We further present a novel densification criterion that normalizes a Gaussian’s accumulated screen-space gradients by the accumulated average contributions of its rendered views. This avoids the view- and pixel-count biases of previous criteria under occlusion, large footprints, and varying distance. This leads to perceptually better reconstructions at fewer Gaussians on large, occlusion-heavy scenes. We additionally integrate established densification improvements into a framework that reduces the dependence on unreliable heuristics such as the scene extent.

    Large-scale reconstruction nevertheless does not yet reach small-scene quality. Beyond occlusion, the imbalanced camera coverage of the Zip-NeRF [2] scenes limits what densification can recover (Sec.4.5). Longer schedules restore the missing densification opportunity, but a fairer distribution of observations would address the imbalance at its source. Several works group cameras by scene sections to pursue divide-and-conquer strategies [14, 17]. Combining occlusion-aware densification with a balanced training strategy should enable higher-quality large-scale reconstructions via single joint optimizations. Our code will be made available at https://github.com/MarcelRogge/occlusion-aware-3dgs.

    Acknowledgements

    This work was partially funded by the European Union under the grant number 101298864, project Victor-XR.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Supplementary Material

    Counting Contributions, Not Views:
    Occlusion-Aware Densification
    for 3D Gaussian Splatting
    — Supplementary Material —

    Marcel Rogge René Schuster Didier Stricker

    This document supplements the main paper. References to the main paper’s figures, tables, and equations are written out explicitly, while all other references resolve within this document. As in the main paper, all runs use the (Decay) opacity schedule unless stated otherwise, and evaluation follows the protocol of the main paper’s experiments section.

    Overview.

    Appendix0.A derives the densification gradient behind our average-contribution criterion and transfers both contributions to 2DGS [12] and 3DGS [13]. Appendix0.B quantifies the integrated baseline against vanilla StopThePop. Appendix0.C analyzes the clone failure mode behind our split-only decision, including the scene-extent override and an ablation study. Appendix0.D quantifies how occluded each benchmark is and shows that the per-scene occlusion rate predicts where our contributions help. Appendix0.E details the contribution-prune schedule and takes a census of fully occluded Gaussians across methods. Appendix0.F compares densification criteria on Mip-NeRF360, maps where each allocates Gaussians, and examines the denominator floor, robustness to the threshold and the evaluation resolution, a hybrid of PixelGS and our criterion, and two alternative normalizers. Appendix0.G covers extended training schedules, count growth over iterations, the distance-scaling guard rail, and per-view statistics. Appendix0.H closes with full-frame qualitative results and error maps.

    Appendix 0.A Method Details

    In this section, we derive our average-contribution criterion from the per-pixel blending weights (Sec.0.A.1) and test how far our two contributions generalize beyond StopThePop [20] by porting them to 2DGS [12] and 3DGS [13] (Sec.0.A.2).

    0.A.1 Criterion Derivation

    We recall the projected footprint of Gaussian i at pixel p,

    G_i,p=\exp (-\tfrac12 (p-μᵢ)ᵀ Σᵢ^′⁻¹ (p-μᵢ)),

    		(S1)

    with the projected screen-space mean μᵢ and the projected 2D covariance Σᵢ^′. As in the main text, the densification gradient differentiates with respect to this projected mean, so all position derivatives below are two-dimensional.

    The 2D screen-space gradient g_i,v=(g_i,v,x,g_i,v,y) is used to determine how much a Gaussian i wants to move based on the loss computed in view v. The same holds independently for every Gaussian. Kerbl et al.[13] argue that a Gaussian that tries to fill many places at once requires densification. Therefore, the magnitude ∥g_i,v∥ is used for the criterion to determine densification. For a single fixed view v, we drop the view index and write gᵢ≡g_i,v. Additionally, we consider only the derivation of g_i,x, since g_i,y follows analogously.

    g_i,x=(∂L)/(∂μ_i,x)=∑ₚ(∂Lₚ)/(∂μ_i,x)=∑ₚ(∂Lₚ)/(∂α_i,p)·(∂α_i,p)/(∂μ_i,x)=∑ₚ(∂Lₚ)/(∂Cₚ)·(∂Cₚ)/(∂α_i,p)·(∂α_i,p)/(∂μ_i,x),

    		(S2)

    where ∑ₚ runs over the Nᵢ pixels to which Gaussian i contributes in view v. Using the chain rule, we express the gradient’s per-pixel term as a product of three derivatives: ∂Lₚ/∂Cₚ represents the photometric error, ∂Cₚ/∂α_i,p represents the blending sensitivity, and ∂α_i,p/∂μ_i,x represents the positional sensitivity.

    (∂Cₚ)/(∂α_i,p)=(cᵢ·T_i,p-A_i,pᵍˢ·T_i,p-c_bg·T_i,pᵗᵃⁱˡ·T_i,p)=(cᵢ-A_i,p)·T_i,p,

    		(S3)

    where A_i,pᵍˢ represents the color composited from all Gaussians behind Gaussian i, c_bg is the background fill color, A_i,p expresses the entire color composite behind Gaussian i, T_i,p is the transmittance reaching Gaussian i, and T_i,pᵗᵃⁱˡ represents the transmittance behind Gaussian i. Note that T_i,p·(1-α_i,p)·T_i,pᵗᵃⁱˡ=T_final,p, where T_final,p represents the leftover transmittance after blending all Gaussians overlapping pixel p. We can see that the blending sensitivity consists of the transmittance T_i,p at Gaussian i and a contrast term between the color cᵢ of Gaussian i and the composite color A_i,p behind it.

    (∂α_i,p)/(∂μ_i,x)=oᵢ·(∂G_i,p)/(∂μ_i,x)=oᵢ·G_i,p·(∂\ln(G_i,p))/(∂μ_i,x)=α_i,p·(∂\ln(G_i,p))/(∂μ_i,x),

    		(S4)

    where oᵢ is the peak opacity of Gaussian i (at its center) and α_i,p=oᵢG_i,p is its opacity at pixel p, attenuated by the Gaussian’s footprint G_i,p∈(0,1] on pixel p. The positional sensitivity term consists of a geometric steering term ∂\ln(G_i,p)/∂μ_i,x modulated by the Gaussian’s opacity at pixel p.

    Inserting Eq.S3 and Eq.S4 into Eq.S2 yields:

    \beginsplitg_i,x&=∑ₚ(∂Lₚ)/(∂Cₚ)·(cᵢ-A_i,p)·T_i,p·α_i,p·(∂\ln(G_i,p))/(∂μ_i,x) &=∑ₚ(∂Lₚ)/(∂Cₚ)·(cᵢ-A_i,p)·w_i,p·(∂\ln(G_i,p))/(∂μ_i,x),\endsplit

    		(S5)

    where w_i,p=α_i,pT_i,p is the Gaussian’s weight with which its color is blended into pixel p, i.e. its contribution. EquationS5 shows that g_i,x consists of a photometric error, a geometric steering, and a contrast term, which are all scaled according to its contribution w_i,p. These three weight-independent factors form the per-pixel vector s_i,p of Eq. (3) in the main paper. This shows that the gradient is intrinsically contribution-weighted, which motivates our normalization using the mean contribution w̄ᵢ=(1/Nᵢ)∑ₚw_i,p rather than a raw view count. The full criterion accumulates these per-view means over all views and adds the +1 floor (Eq. (5) of the main paper), which bounds the score of a Gaussian that has accumulated little contribution (more details on the floor in Sec.0.F.2). A contribution-based denominator is therefore the matched choice, though not every contribution-based denominator will do: the per-view total∑ₚw_i,p grows with the on-screen footprint and would reintroduce the very pixel-count dependence we argue against (Sec. 3.2 of the main paper), whereas the per-view mean w̄ᵢ is footprint-free.

    0.A.2 Generalizability (2DGS & 3DGS)

    Our contributions rely only on the per-pixel blending weights, so they should transfer to most other Gaussian Splatting renderers. To test this, we port both contributions to 2DGS [12], whose surfel-based rasterizer and regularization differ substantially from StopThePop [20]. We additionally port them to 3DGS [13], which shares StopThePop’s splatting formulation but none of its per-pixel sorting. We do not include any of the other adopted components to isolate the generality of our proposed contributions. We report results on each vanilla base, the occlusion-aware filter alone (+ filter), and the filter with criterion (+ filter + criterion).

    Mip-NeRF360.

    We calibrate each port with a small threshold sweep on the subset of the Mip-NeRF360 [1] dataset used for our own calibration (Sec.0.F.1), reported in Tab.S1. Both ports behave the same way. At our original threshold of 0.002, the criterion improves every quality metric over both the baseline and the filter-only variant, and on both ports it does so at a markedly increased Gaussian count (1.8× on 2DGS, 2.4× on 3DGS). Raising the threshold to 0.003 returns the count closer to the baseline’s level on both ports while retaining much of the gain. Raising it further under-densifies, with every metric falling below the baseline on both 2DGS and 3DGS. The port’s missing contribution prune does not explain the inflated count at our default threshold of 0.002: disabling it in our StopThePop framework raises the Mip-NeRF360 count by only 4% (Tab.S8). Later in this section, we will discuss a possible explanation in the clone operation.

    Zip-NeRF.

    TableS2 reports both ports on the occlusion-heavy Zip-NeRF [2] scenes. For 2DGS we find that 0.003 does not allow much more densification than the base, so we report the results for a threshold of 0.002. For 3DGS we report with the recalibrated threshold of 0.003. In both cases, we avoid the clone’s catastrophic failure through a manual override of the scene extent (Sec.0.C.1) so that the original densification strategy can be retained. Both baselines are starved here, at 0.57M and 1.10M Gaussians against the 1.8–2.8M they use on the smaller Mip-NeRF360 scenes, which is the same under-densification our contributions correct on StopThePop. The filter alone lifts the count sharply on both, to 3.03M and 2.90M, and the criterion then spends that budget more selectively, settling at 1.48M and 1.68M. On 2DGS the full port improves every metric over the baseline on three of the four scenes (+0.38 to +0.58 dB, 5–8% better LPIPS). On 3DGS it attains the best PSNR on all four scenes, while conceding a little SSIM and LPIPS to the filter-only variant. For 2DGS there is an exception on alameda, where it degrades: the vanilla 2DGS already exhibits large floater artifacts that we attribute to this scene’s strong exposure and lighting changes, which the surfel geometry consolidates into large floater blobs. Due to densification no longer getting suppressed, these floater clusters are amplified. Our criterion reduces the number of floaters and recovers most of the lost quality, while the 3DGS port does not show this degradation as it does not form the floaters into solid clusters.
