Overall, our learned sampler preserves the characteristic blue-noise spectral structure, with modest differences in its frequency response.

    Comparison with Fixed-Target Base Model

    The optimal-transport diffusion model of [Doignies et al. [12]] (i.e., base model) can generate non-uniform point distributions when trained on examples from a fixed target density. In Figure 6, we qualitatively compare the base model with our conditioned model and verify that the conditioning branch preserves its ability to generate multiple samples from the same target distribution.

    In the top experiment, the target density is ρ(x,y)=0.2e^-20(x²+y²)+0.2\sin²(πx)\sin²(πy)[5]. This density is challenging due to its sharp localized wells, requiring both accurate global mass allocation and strong local point repulsion. We generate a 1024-point distribution by importance sampling from this density and use the resulting point set to generate GBN exemplars for training.

    When trained on the same GBN exemplars as the base model, our model captures the main density structure while maintaining regular point spacing. Multiple generated samples exhibit consistent density structure and point spacing, demonstrating that the conditioning branch preserves the stochastic generation capability of the underlying diffusion model.

    The bottom example extends this experiment to a natural image, again using GBN exemplars generated from the image to train the base model. Our generated point sets follow the image structure while maintaining a well-distributed pattern. Together, these results show that the conditioning branch preserves the base model’s ability to reproduce the prescribed exemplar distribution.

    Metrics

    We evaluate each point set using seven metrics grouped by the property they assess: relaxation (CVT, HOT), capacity (capacity deviation, centroid displacement), global agreement with the target density (EMD, Sinkhorn), and local spacing (spatial measure).

  • •

    CVT energy[13]. Measures point relaxation by integrating, over each point’s Voronoi cell, the density-weighted squared distance from every location in the cell to that point. It is minimized when each point coincides with the density-weighted centroid of its cell, as in Lloyd-based stippling [36]:

    E_CVT=∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ∫_Vᵢρ(x) ∥x-sᵢ∥² dx,

    where sᵢ is the i-th point, Vᵢ its Voronoi cell, and ρ the target density.

  • •

    HOT energy[25]. The analogous energy over power cells, whose weights are chosen so that all cells have equal mass [4]. This is the ⋆₀-HOT2,2 energy minimized by BNOT [10]:

    E_HOT=∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ∫_Vʷᵢρ(x) ∥x-sᵢ∥² dx,

    where Vʷᵢ is the power cell of sᵢ.

  • •

    Capacity deviation δ_c[5]. Measures how uniformly the target mass is distributed across Voronoi cells. It is zero when every cell contains the same mass:

    δ_c=1/n∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ((mᵢ)/(m̄)-1)²,

    where mᵢ=∫_Vᵢρ(x) dx and m̄ is the mean cell mass.

  • •

    Centroid displacement D. Measures the distance between each point and the density-weighted centroid of its power cell. It is zero when the BNOT centroidal optimality condition is satisfied [10]:

    D=1/n∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ∥sᵢ-bᵢ∥, bᵢ=(∫_Vʷᵢx ρ(x) dx)/(∫_Vʷᵢρ(x) dx).

  • •

    EMD and Sinkhorn. Measure global agreement with the target density by transporting the point distribution to the target distribution. EMD is the 2-Wasserstein distance [43]; Sinkhorn is its entropy-regularized approximation [9]. Both measure global density agreement without directly assessing local point arrangement.

  • •

    Spatial measure ρₛ[18]. Measures local point spacing after rescaling distances by the local density [45]. Higher values indicate more uniform nearest-neighbor spacing relative to the local density:

    ρₛ=1/n∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ(rᵢ√n ρ(sᵢ)/ρ̄)/(r_\max),

    where rᵢ is the nearest-neighbor distance of sᵢ, ρ̄ is the mean target density at the points, and r_\max=(2/√3)^1/2 is the reference spacing for hexagonal packing at unit density.

    • Quantitative Comparison

    In Table 1, we compare our model with the optimization-based samplers WVS and GBN on all four datasets: the 1K-image Icons-50 and 500-image CelebA test splits at 1024 points, and the 400-image ShapeNet2D and 263-image Anime Chibi test splits at 1600 points (subtables). Our model is trained separately on WVS and GBN exemplars, and both variants are reported. Bold and underlined values denote the best and second-best results, respectively.

    Compared with its own exemplar sampler, each learned variant improves HOT energy, centroid displacement and EMD on all four datasets (on Icons-50, the HOT energy is 4.059 for Ours-GBN against 5.204 for GBN), and falls short in CVT energy and spatial measure. The Sinkhorn values of all methods lie within 0.002 of each other on every dataset. Capacity deviation stays close to the exemplar sampler on the two square 1024-point datasets, but the gap grows on the two non-square 1600-point datasets (Ours-GBN 0.038 against 0.013 for GBN on ShapeNet2D, and 0.107 against 0.030 on Anime Chibi). These two datasets differ from the first two in point budget, aspect ratio and training-set size at once, and our experiments do not separate these factors.

    The learned variants inherit the ranking of their exemplar samplers. In 27 of the 28 dataset–metric pairs, the variant trained on the better of WVS and GBN is also the better of our two variants, and the remaining pair (Sinkhorn on Anime Chibi) is a tie for both. Within the table, our variants rank best or second-best on all but three pairs (CVT on ShapeNet2D and Anime Chibi, and capacity deviation on Anime Chibi), while requiring no optimization at inference. WVS minimizes the CVT energy directly and therefore has the best CVT energy, and with it the best spatial measure. GBN’s Gaussian-kernel objective promotes capacity preservation and gives the best capacity deviation.

    Relation to BNOT

    BNOT optimizes the HOT energy directly and sets the reference on the transport metrics. On HOT energy, centroid displacement and EMD, each learned variant lies between its exemplar sampler and BNOT on all four datasets. Ours-WVS has a better spatial measure than BNOT on all four datasets, and a lower CVT energy on the two 1024-point datasets. BNOT reaches its optimum by per-target Newton iterations whose cost grows by more than two orders of magnitude across our budget range (Figure 7). Our variants instead run at a cost that grows little with the budget, generalize to unseen images and budgets, and are differentiable. BNOT appears as an unranked reference in the figures and in Table 4 (Appendix E).

    Running-time Evaluation

    We report runtime measurements in Figure 7 across multiple point budgets. Ours-WVS and Ours-GBN share the same architecture and therefore have identical inference costs. For each method and point count, we report the mean time to generate one stipple pattern.

    The optimization-based samplers use their published default stopping criteria: 50 Lloyd iterations for WVS, up to 25 Newton iterations for BNOT, and 1000 optimization steps for GBN. Our runtime is determined by a fixed number of denoising steps, independent of the target.

    Our cost grows little with point count. It is slower than WVS at smaller budgets but becomes the fastest method from about 1024 points onward. It is faster than BNOT and GBN at every evaluated budget, with the gap to BNOT widening as BNOT becomes increasingly expensive. Hardware details and CPU/GPU profiling are provided in Appendix B.

    Ablation Study

    For the architectural ablations, we disable all inference-time modifications and use standard diffusion sampling from pure noise. We compare our full model with four simplified variants: Vanilla, a standard ControlNet applied to the frozen base model of [Doignies et al. [12]]; Unfrozen, which jointly trains the randomly initialized base U-Net and control branch; GECCO, which augments the frozen Vanilla model with continuous GECCO feature extraction; and Gated, which replaces zero-convolutions with transform-gated 1×1 projections. The Full model combines joint training with both GECCO and Gated augmentations.

    The architectural ablation results are summarized in Table 2, with qualitative comparisons shown in Figure 8. Full lowers capacity deviation from 0.0626 (Vanilla) to 0.0259 and also improves HOT energy, EMD and centroid displacement. Gating alone brings little over Vanilla; the gains come from joint training and the per-point features, and are largest when the two are combined. Figure 8 shows the same ordering: Vanilla and Gated leave uneven point density inside the contours, while Full is close to the final SDEdit sampler.

    We next evaluate the inference-time sampling strategy using the Full model. Following SDEdit [24], we replace pure-noise initialization with a density-weighted rejection-sampled prior and denoise only the final 50% of the diffusion schedule.

    As shown in Table 2, inference time decreases from 11.08 s to 5.65 s at comparable quality. Capacity deviation is essentially unchanged (0.0255 against 0.0259), centroid displacement and EMD improve slightly, and HOT energy is slightly worse. Qualitatively, SDEdit and Full produce similar results (Figure 8), and both look clearly better than Vanilla.

    Differentiable Tone Correction

    Because our sampler is a neural network, it defines a differentiable mapping S from a density map ρ to a point set. Thus, any differentiable objective on the generated stipple can be optimized with respect to the requested density by back-propagating through S. In contrast, the iterative optimization samplers provide no direct gradient; differentiating through WVS, BNOT, or GBN would require back-propagation through their respective Lloyd, Newton, or gradient-based iterations, or implicit differentiation at their fixed point, which we do not attempt here.

    We evaluate this capability on dot gain, where finite-sized stipple dots cause the rendered tone to differ from the requested density: isolated dots can appear too dark, while overlapping dots in dark regions saturate (Figure 9, left). We therefore optimize the requested density ρ so that the rendered stipple better matches the target darkness.

    The renderer R places each point as a Gaussian dot with standard deviation 2 pixels on a 256×256 canvas and converts accumulated ink a to darkness using Beer–Lambert saturation, 1-e^-κa. We calibrate the ink gain κ once on six images so that uncorrected stipples match their mean target darkness, and then keep it fixed. Given target image I, the target darkness, which is also its target density, is ρ₀=1-I. We parameterize the corrected density as ρ=sigmoid (logit(ρ₀)+φ), where φ is a 64×64 correction field bilinearly upsampled to the image resolution. We optimize

    φ^⋆=\arg\min_φ \lVertR(S(ρ))-ρ₀\rVert₂²+λ₂\lVertφ\rVert₂²+λₜᵥTV(φ),

    with λ₂=10⁻³ and λₜᵥ=10⁻². Adam is used with a learning rate of 0.05 for 300 steps. Only ρ is optimized; the network weights, remaining conditioning, initial points, and noise are fixed, making the objective deterministic.

    We validate the gradients using central finite differences with step 0.02 at 24 randomly selected entries of φ. The analytic and numerical gradients achieve a cosine similarity of 0.995, agree in sign at all 24 locations, and have a magnitude slope of 0.98.

    We compare four strategies on 24 held-out Icons-50 targets at 1024 points. uncorrected directly uses ρ₀. tone curve replaces φ with a global 17-knot transfer curve and is optimized using the same objective. random search optimizes the full 64×64 field using gradient-free (1+1) random search with the 1/5 success rule and 600 sampler evaluations, matching the computational cost of 300 forward-and-backward steps. ours performs the gradient-based optimization described above. We evaluate the rendered stipples using PSNR, SSIM, and mean absolute error (MAE).

    For efficiency, we compute gradients through the closed-form x̂₀ estimate after a single denoising step at t=120, which is already differentiated through during training. Full back-propagation through the reverse process is also possible, with memory proportional to the number of denoising steps. Although the dot-gain model is a simplified printer proxy, the results consistently show improvement across all targets and over gradient-free optimization at equal cost.

    Our correction improves all 24 targets, with an average PSNR gain of +0.83 dB, compared with +0.22 dB for random search at equal cost and +0.17 dB for the tone curve (Table 3, Figure 10). Gradients outperform random search on 23 of 24 images. The optimized density reduces point crowding (Figure 9, right), lowering RMS error from 0.0913 to 0.0700. Across a 16× range of ink gains, the PSNR improvement remains between +0.31 and +1.44 dB and consistently exceeds the tone curve (Appendix A).

    5. Conclusions and Limitations

    We present a learned stippling algorithm that learns the stippling process itself rather than a single point distribution. A single checkpoint per dataset and exemplar sampler generates high-quality stipple patterns for unseen images and a range of point budgets, with an inference cost that grows little with output size and a fully differentiable mapping from density to stipples. This shifts stippling from a per-target optimization problem to a reusable, image-conditioned generative process. It enables fast generation, capacity generalization, and downstream optimization through the sampler.

    Visual quality remains the main limitation. Gaussian Blue Noise produces smoother density transitions and preserves fine details and sharp edges more faithfully, while our spectra retain the blue-noise structure but suppress low frequencies less effectively than optimization-based methods. Our method is also slower than deterministic low-discrepancy samplers, and its OT-grid representation relies on regular grids and convolutions that do not readily extend beyond 2D, motivating non-grid alternatives. Nevertheless, differentiability enables capabilities unavailable to these optimizers, as demonstrated by our tone-correction experiment. Future work can optimize through the full reverse process, support richer objectives such as stylization, and use generated stipples in downstream learned models.

    Appendix A Differentiability: Sensitivity to the Ink Gain

    Figure 11 sweeps the ink gain of the renderer in the dot-gain experiment of Figure 9, to show that the advantage of optimizing through the sampler is not an artifact of the calibrated value.
