一句话：可微的条件点扩散：推理成本由去噪步数决定，几乎不随点预算增长。

要点：

  • 在最优传输网格上做条件点扩散，加一个与主分支联合训练的条件分支输入逐点图像特征；推理时先用密度感知初始化，再做截断去噪。
  • 以加权 Voronoi 点画与高斯蓝噪声为范例采样器训练：在 HOT 能量、质心位移、EMD 上优于范例，在 CVT 能量与空间度量上不如。
  • 采样器可微，可反过来优化目标密度以补偿渲染点增益；生成的每个变体都能复现对应范例采样器的特性优势。

为什么值得看：点画与蓝噪声点集是植被散布、抖动、程序化贴图的底层工具。可微且成本不随点预算涨，意味着它能放进渲染循环里做在线优化。

中文摘要：点画图案是局部密度跟随目标图像的点集，传统做法用逐密度迭代优化，速度慢、不可微，且每换一个目标就要重跑。学到的点扩散方法则只能无条件生成：训练它复现某一种密度，却没有输入、无法适应新目标。作者提出一个条件点扩散采样器，接收目标图像并生成带有训练范例采样器风格的点画图案。模型运行在最优传输网格上，加入一个联合训练、带逐点图像特征的条件分支；推理时先用密度感知的初始化，再做截断去噪。他们在四个数据集上以加权 Voronoi 点画与高斯蓝噪声为范例采样器评估，每个学习变体都复现了对应范例的特性优势，在 HOT 能量、质心位移与 EMD 上优于范例，在 CVT 能量与空间度量上不如。推理成本由固定步数决定，几乎不随点预算增长；由于采样器可微，还能反过来优化所需密度以修正渲染点画的点增益。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-22

StippleDiffusion: Capacity-Constrained Stippling using Controlled Diffusion

Ofir Gilad1 Aleksander Plocharski2 Przemyslaw Musialski3 Andrei Sharf1

1Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Israel  2Warsaw University of Technology, Poland  3New Jersey Institute of Technology, USA

Abstract

Stipple patterns are point sets whose local density follows a target image. They are traditionally generated by iterative optimization, which must be re-run for every target and provides no gradients. Learned point-diffusion methods, in contrast, generate points unconditionally. A model can be trained to reproduce one density, but it takes no input and cannot adapt to a new one. We present a conditional point-diffusion sampler that takes a target image and generates a stipple pattern in the style of the sampler that produced its training exemplars. The model operates on an optimal-transport grid and adds a jointly trained conditioning branch with per-point image features. At inference, a density-aware initialization is refined by truncated denoising. We evaluate it on four datasets, with Weighted Voronoi Stippling and Gaussian Blue Noise as exemplar samplers. Each learned variant reproduces the characteristic strengths of its exemplar sampler across the metrics. It improves on that sampler in HOT energy, centroid displacement and EMD, and falls short of it in CVT energy and spatial measure. Its inference cost is set by a fixed number of denoising steps and grows little with the point budget. Our sampler is differentiable, enabling downstream optimization of the requested density to correct dot gain in rendered stipples.

Keywords: stippling, blue noise, diffusion, optimal transport, capacity constrained

1. Introduction

Generating high-quality 2D point sets with prescribed spatial properties is a fundamental problem in computer graphics, with applications including rendering, object placement, and image stippling. Classical approaches typically rely on iterative optimization or specialized sampling strategies to produce structured distributions such as blue noise. While effective, these methods can be computationally expensive and difficult to adapt to multiple constraints. In particular, a new target density generally requires a separate optimization process, limiting their scalability and suitability for interactive or large-scale generation.

Recently, denoising diffusion probabilistic models have emerged as a powerful framework for learning complex geometric distributions directly from data [12]. However, applying diffusion models to scattered point sets remains challenging because standard convolutional architectures are designed for grid-structured data rather than unordered points. To address this issue, [Doignies et al. [12]], building on the linear optimal-transport assignment of [Bonneel et al. [6]], represent point sets on an OT grid by assigning each point to a grid cell and encoding its position as a local offset. This representation enables efficient convolutional processing, but its grid-based formulation can make it challenging to capture fine-scale spatial relationships and structured point distributions.

Conditioning diffusion models on spatially varying targets introduces an additional challenge. Although standard conditioning mechanisms such as ControlNet [50] can be applied to OT-grid representations, enforcing fine-grained density and geometric constraints during generation remains difficult. The model must maintain globally well-distributed points while simultaneously capturing high-frequency variations in target density and shape. Poorly balanced conditioning can lead to outliers, uneven densities, residual clustering, and loss of fine geometric structure.

In this paper, we learn the stippling process of a chosen sampler. Given exemplars from Weighted Voronoi Stippling (WVS) or Gaussian Blue Noise (GBN), our model stipples unseen images in that sampler’s style, for different point budgets. It starts from a density-weighted initialization and refines it by truncated denoising, inspired by SDEdit [24] (Figure 1).

Our work makes the following contributions:

  • •

    We propose a conditional, example-based stippler. For each dataset and exemplar sampler, we train one network on images paired with their exemplar stipples at a single, fixed point budget. At inference, it generates stipples for unseen images, including at point budgets other than the training one, without per-target optimization. The learned variants reproduce the characteristic strengths of their exemplar samplers across the metrics.

  • •

    We combine an optimal-transport grid with a jointly trained conditioning branch (per-point image features, gated injection). In the ablation, this lowers capacity deviation from 0.063 to 0.026 compared with a standard ControlNet on the frozen base model. A density-aware initialization with truncated denoising halves the inference time at comparable quality.

  • •

    Our sampler is differentiable from the generated stipple back to the requested density, enabling downstream optimization. We demonstrate this for dot-gain correction by back-propagating through a single denoising step.

    • 2. Related Work

    Blue Noise Sampling. Blue-noise distributions are characterized by a power spectrum with suppressed low frequencies and energy concentrated in an isotropic high-frequency annulus. They arise in biologically optimized arrangements such as the retinal cone mosaic [49], and are widely used in digital halftoning [42], image stippling [11], and Monte Carlo integration [39, 31]. Existing construction methods include kernel-based formulations [14], pair-correlation matching [29], optimal transport [10, 32, 30], fast approximations [26], and Gaussian variants [3]. Tile-based methods instead precompute reusable patches, trading computation for memory [28, 17, 27, 44, 1].

    These methods use different mechanisms to enforce point separation, including Lloyd iterations [23, 11, 36, 5, 20, 46, 8], electrostatic forces [35], farthest-point optimization [34], and sampling on regular lattices [2]. While these approaches produce high-quality distributions, many require iterative computation whose cost increases with the number of points. We refer to [Yan et al. [48]] and [Singh et al. [37]] for broader surveys of blue-noise sampling and sample correlations.

    Blue-noise sampling produces well-distributed points at approximately uniform density, while stippling extends this idea to spatially varying densities by modulating point density according to an input image. This concept has also been extended to color stippling by formulating it as a multi-class blue-noise sampling problem [22].

    Image-Conditioned Diffusion Models for Stippling. Few works have addressed stippling with neural networks. The closest is the feed-forward stippling network of [Xue et al. [47]], which predicts color stipple positions at a fixed output size using a spectrum-based loss. In contrast, our method takes only the target image as input, supports different point budgets through the size of its OT grid, and preserves the prescribed point mass per region. We therefore consider this work related but not directly comparable to ours.

    Learned point samplers with fast inference and point-count generalization have also been explored. Deep Point Correlation Design [19] optimizes a composition of distance-based filters under a user-specified correlation loss and generalizes across point counts. However, its conditioning is based on spatial or spectral statistics rather than an image-defined density field, and it does not address capacity-constrained stippling.

    Diffusion models have recently enabled powerful conditional generation. SDEdit [24] uses a structural prior and a truncated reverse process for image-to-image refinement, while ControlNet [50] introduces spatial conditioning through parallel encoding branches. Although developed for image grids, these ideas provide useful principles for conditional geometric generation.

    Applying diffusion to scattered point sets presents an architectural challenge. [Doignies et al. [12]] address this by matching points to a regular grid through optimal transport, enabling standard convolutional architectures for point diffusion. While effective for unconditional point generation, extending this representation to high-frequency, spatial conditioning remains challenging, as strong spatial guidance can disrupt the underlying point distribution.

    GECCO [41] instead uses coordinate-based features for geometrically conditioned point diffusion, while gated architectures such as highway networks [38] provide a mechanism for integrating auxiliary features while preserving the underlying representation.

    Our method builds on these ideas to enable high-frequency spatial conditioning for image stippling.

    3. Method

    Architecture

    Our method builds upon diffusion models for 2D point-set generation, which progressively transform noisy point representations into structured distributions through iterative denoising. We use the optimal-transport (OT) point-set diffusion model of [Doignies et al. [12]], which represents unordered point sets on a grid to enable convolutional processing (see Figure 2).

    The denoising process consists of a sequence of steps indexed by t. At each step, a denoising network ε_θ predicts the noise in the noisy grid x̃ₜ, conditioned on the embedded timestep t. The network is a U-Net [33], with two convolutional residual blocks at each level and factor-of-two downsampling between consecutive levels.

    To enable spatial conditioning, our architecture introduces a conditioning branch in parallel with the base U-Net, inspired by ControlNet [50]. Unlike the original ControlNet paradigm, which keeps the pretrained base model frozen, we randomly initialize both the base U-Net and the conditioning branch and train them jointly from scratch.

    Rather than using standard Zero Convolutions to inject conditioning features, we replace them with Gated Zero Convolutions [38]. The motivation is to prevent strong spatial conditioning from disrupting the geometric regularity of the point distribution, particularly during early denoising. At the middle and decoding layers of the U-Net, a sigmoid-gated 1×1 projection controls the strength of the injected features, allowing the network to gradually and selectively incorporate spatial guidance while preserving the underlying point-distribution structure.

    The conditioning input c is rebuilt at every denoising step from the current noisy offsets (Figure 2). Following GECCO [41], a lightweight CNN processes the full-resolution input image into a dense feature map, and 16 feature channels are read from this map at the continuous positions of the current noisy points by bilinear interpolation. These are concatenated with the noisy offsets themselves (2 channels) and the downsampled density map (1 channel), giving a 19-channel condition on the N×N grid. A convolutional Conditioning Encoder with SiLU activations and no downsampling lifts it from 19 to 32, 64, and 128 channels, with dilation rates up to 4 to capture broader spatial context while preserving spatial resolution.

    The combined network learns a time-dependent noise model ε_θ(x̃ₜ,t,c), where x̃ₜ is obtained by adding noise εₜ to the offset grid x₀ of an exemplar point set:

    x̃ₜ=√ᾱₜ x₀+√1-ᾱₜ εₜ,

    at each time step t, conditioned on our spatial features c. Here εₜ∼ℕ(0,I) is Gaussian noise, and ᾱₜ=∏_τ=1ᵗ(1-β_τ) is the cumulative product of a linear noise schedule whose β_τ rise from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² over T=1000 steps. It sets how much of the clean offsets remains in x̃ₜ, falling from nearly 1 at t=0 to nearly 0 at t=T, where x̃ₜ is almost pure noise.

    At inference, we initialize the reverse process from a partially noised, rejection-sampled point set using a truncated SDEdit schedule (see Inference below) to reduce runtime. Training always uses the full diffusion schedule, and the same model can also sample from pure noise.

    Optimal-transport grid representation

    Our network operates on a regular 2D grid rather than directly on the raw point set, following the representation of [Doignies et al. [12]]. For a budget of n points, we partition the unit square [0,1]² into an N×N grid with N=√n (e.g., N=32 for 1024 points), with cell centers g_u,v. Each cell is assigned exactly one point s_u,v through a one-to-one linear optimal-transport matching [6] that minimizes the total squared distance between cell centers and assigned points. We store the continuous offset

    o_u,v=s_u,v-g_u,v

    in each cell, yielding a two-channel N×N representation x₀. Standard 2D convolutions can then process the point set as an image, with neighboring cells providing an approximate local neighborhood of nearby samples. Importantly, the representation does not quantize the points: offsets remain continuous, samples retain their coordinates in [0,1]², and generated points are never snapped to grid locations.

    The grid depends only on the point budget, not on the input image. The grayscale image defines the target density, with darker regions corresponding to higher density, and is mapped to the same unit square regardless of its resolution or aspect ratio. Each axis is normalized independently, allowing non-square images to be processed at native resolution without padding. The same architecture supports square 512×512 images and non-square images with a longer side of up to 1024 pixels. The image enters the network in two forms: a downsampled N×N density map aligned with the OT offsets, and a full-resolution image from which features are sampled at the continuous point coordinates.

    Training

    For each batch of size B, we pair each training image with an exemplar point set generated offline by a stippling sampler, whose point distribution the network learns to reproduce. Thus, the choice of exemplar sampler determines the point-distribution characteristics learned by the model, while the input image determines where points are placed.

    We train separate models using exemplars generated by Gaussian Blue Noise (GBN) [3] and Weighted Voronoi Stippling (WVS) [36]. We chose these samplers because they provide a good balance between generation efficiency and stipple quality, allowing us to generate training exemplars at practical computational cost while maintaining well-structured point distributions. The framework is not tied to these samplers and can similarly learn distributions produced by other methods, provided that their optimization converges reliably and can generate exemplars efficiently at the scale required for training.

    The BNOT sampler [10] also produces capacity-constrained stipples using an optimal-transport formulation. However, its relatively expensive iterative optimization makes it impractical for generating the large number of training exemplars required by our approach.

    We use GBN as the default for ablations and runtime evaluation because it produces visually pleasing stipples while providing a challenging distribution for the learned sampler to reproduce.

    Each model is trained at a fixed grid size determined by its dataset’s point budget (e.g., N=32 for 1024 points and N=40 for 1600 points). For each training image (Figure 2, orange), the exemplar points are converted once during data loading into an exemplar offset grid x₀ using the OT assignment described above. The image provides two conditioning signals: the full-resolution image, from which image features are extracted, and a density map downsampled to the N×N grid.

    For each batch element i, we sample a timestep tᵢ∼U(0,T) from the full training schedule (T=1000) and add Gaussian noise ε⁽ⁱ⁾ to its exemplar offset grid x⁽ⁱ⁾₀, yielding the noisy representation x̃⁽ⁱ⁾_tᵢ. The network then predicts the added noise conditioned on the corresponding spatial features.

    We optimize a combination of Min-SNR-γ weighted MSE [40] and a Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) loss:

    L(θ)= 1/B∑ᵢ₌₁^B[ w(tᵢ) ∥ε_θ(x̃⁽ⁱ⁾_tᵢ,tᵢ,c⁽ⁱ⁾)-ε⁽ⁱ⁾∥²+λ_KDE L_KDE(x̂⁽ⁱ⁾₀,x⁽ⁱ⁾₀)].

    Here, i indexes the batch, x⁽ⁱ⁾₀ denotes the exemplar offset grid, x̃⁽ⁱ⁾_tᵢ is its noisy version at timestep tᵢ with noise ε⁽ⁱ⁾, and c⁽ⁱ⁾ denotes the corresponding spatial condition. The predicted clean grid x̂⁽ⁱ⁾₀ is obtained from the network’s noise prediction.

    The first term is the standard noise-prediction loss, weighted by w(t)=\min(SNR(t),γ)/SNR(t), where SNR(t)=ᾱₜ/(1-ᾱₜ) and γ=5.0. This weighting balances the contribution of different diffusion timesteps [40].

    The second term operates on the predicted point distribution rather than the noise. Specifically, the predicted noise provides a closed-form estimate of the clean offsets,

    x̂⁽ⁱ⁾₀=(x̃⁽ⁱ⁾_tᵢ-√1-ᾱ_tᵢ ε_θ)/√ᾱ_tᵢ,

    which is decoded into point positions, as is the exemplar x⁽ⁱ⁾₀. For each point set, we construct a coarse density image on a fixed 32×32 grid, independent of the OT grid resolution. Each cell accumulates a Gaussian kernel with one-cell standard deviation centered at every point, and the resulting image is normalized to have unit mean. The KDE loss L_KDE is the mean squared difference between the predicted and exemplar density images. It therefore penalizes local regions that contain too few or too many points, providing a direct density constraint that the per-point noise loss captures only indirectly.

    We apply the KDE term only for tᵢ<0.4T, where the estimate x̂₀ is sufficiently reliable, and set λ_KDE=0.8, linearly ramped over the first five epochs.

    Inference

    Given a novel input image, we first draw the n points of the chosen point budget by density-weighted rejection sampling from the image (Figure 2, green), making darker pixels proportionally more likely to receive points. This provides a structural prior that accelerates convergence compared with initialization from pure Gaussian noise.

    The sampled points are converted to an offset grid on an N×N grid, with N=√n, using the same OT assignment as during training. Since N need not match the training resolution, a single checkpoint can support multiple point budgets.

    At each denoising step, the conditioning input is constructed exactly as during training (Figure 2), using the input image and the current noisy offsets.

    We use a truncated SDEdit-style diffusion schedule. The initial OT offsets are forward-noised to t=500, corresponding to 50% of the full T=1000-step schedule, and standard reverse DDPM sampling is then performed from t=500 to t=0. The resulting OT offsets are finally converted back to continuous point coordinates to obtain the stipple pattern (Figure 2).

    4. Experiments

    Datasets

    We evaluate our method on four datasets, converted to grayscale and paired with offline exemplar stipples generated by Weighted Voronoi Stippling (WVS) [36] and Gaussian Blue Noise (GBN) [3]. Each exemplar uses the point budget of the corresponding OT grid.

    Icons-50[15] is our first benchmark, comprising all 10K images split into 9K/1K for training/testing, resized to 512×512, with 1024 points on a 32×32 grid. CelebA[21] provides a natural-image benchmark using 5K images split 4.5K/0.5K, at the same resolution and point budget. The last two benchmarks are non-square, use 1600 points on a 40×40 grid, and hold out 10% of their images for testing. ShapeNet2D contains 4K renders of ShapeNet [7] objects from seven categories (cabinet, car, sofa, jar, trash bin, bottle, and bed) with the longer side at 1024 pixels, split 3.6K/0.4K; its renders are color-filtered before the exemplars are generated. Anime Chibi[16] contains 2,634 chibi illustrations, resized to a longer side of at most 1024 pixels with the aspect ratio kept, and split 2,371/263.

    Each dataset has its own point budget and image resolution. For each dataset we train two checkpoints, one per exemplar sampler (WVS and GBN), at the grid size set by its budget, eight checkpoints in total. Each is trained from scratch for 5000 epochs with batch size 16 and learning rate 10⁻⁴. All share the same architecture and differ only in their training exemplars, which isolates the effect of the imitated sampler. Each benchmark is evaluated with its own checkpoints on its held-out split.

    Qualitative Results

    Figure 1 illustrates capacity-constrained stippling with our diffusion model on diverse target images. The controlled denoising process progressively refines the initial point distribution while preserving local point repulsion and the prescribed density (left). Our resulting stipple patterns accurately capture the target shapes and spatial density across six target images (right).

    Figure 3 compares each learned variant with the sampler that produced its exemplars, WVS and GBN, on different targets, with BNOT as a reference. Further held-out examples are shown in Appendix D.

    In the top row, we evaluate the stippling distribution on a continuous quadratic density gradient, ρ(x)=x²+\tfrac1500 on [0,1]², partitioned into four equal-width vertical strips with target point masses of 1.7%, 11.0%, 29.7%, and 57.6%.

    We compare our model trained on Icons-50 with the WVS and GBN samplers. Both Ours-WVS and Ours-GBN produce visually comparable results across density levels and closely match the prescribed point-capacity percentages. Our 1024-point outputs closely track the target strip masses, staying within about one percentage point of each target, while using one model per exemplar sampler, without per-target optimization. Both learned variants slightly under-fill the sparsest strip (Ours-WVS 1.0%, Ours-GBN 1.3%, target 1.7%), and Ours-WVS is closer to the target than WVS in the first and the last strip. The density-weighted initialization allocates the mass per region, and the denoising preserves it to within about one percentage point.

    The remaining rows show results for target images from the Icons-50, CelebA, ShapeNet2D, and Anime Chibi test sets, respectively. Across these examples, our method preserves blue-noise-like point spacing while closely following the target density and image structure, using one checkpoint per dataset and exemplar sampler.

    Capacity Generalization

    Although our Icons-50 model is trained exclusively on 1024-point sets (32×32 grid), the OT-grid representation allows inference at different grid resolutions, with output capacities restricted to square numbers of points. Figure 4 shows results for two target densities using 576, 1024, 2304, and 4096 points.

    Across capacities, the generated patterns preserve the target density and structure, with higher budgets progressively recovering finer details. Thus, a single checkpoint generalizes across substantially different output capacities without retraining, unlike optimization-based methods that require separate optimization for each point budget. At 4,096 points, the icon stays clean, while the smooth density becomes mottled in its falloff zones, indicating the practical limit of capacity extrapolation beyond the training resolution.

    Spectral Analysis

    Blue-noise quality is commonly characterized by capacity adherence and spatial regularity, as well as by its frequency-domain signature. Because capacity-constrained stipples are inherently non-stationary, spectra of natural images are dominated by their target structure. We therefore evaluate a constant-density target (ρ=1.00) using 1024 points and 25 realizations. Figure 5 shows the resulting spectra; pair correlations at several densities are provided in Appendix C.

    All methods exhibit a principal blue-noise peak at approximately 1.05. Our models show spectral characteristics comparable to those of the optimization-based samplers, with Ours-GBN producing the cleanest high-frequency tail. The optimization-based samplers achieve lower low-frequency floors, indicating stronger suppression of low-frequency energy. The 2D spectra of the learned variants show a mild four-fold modulation aligned with the grid axes, which the radial average hides. We attribute it to the grid representation. Overall, our learned sampler preserves the characteristic blue-noise spectral structure, with modest differences in its frequency response.

    Comparison with Fixed-Target Base Model

    The optimal-transport diffusion model of [Doignies et al. [12]] (i.e., base model) can generate non-uniform point distributions when trained on examples from a fixed target density. In Figure 6, we qualitatively compare the base model with our conditioned model and verify that the conditioning branch preserves its ability to generate multiple samples from the same target distribution.

    In the top experiment, the target density is ρ(x,y)=0.2e^-20(x²+y²)+0.2\sin²(πx)\sin²(πy)[5]. This density is challenging due to its sharp localized wells, requiring both accurate global mass allocation and strong local point repulsion. We generate a 1024-point distribution by importance sampling from this density and use the resulting point set to generate GBN exemplars for training.

    When trained on the same GBN exemplars as the base model, our model captures the main density structure while maintaining regular point spacing. Multiple generated samples exhibit consistent density structure and point spacing, demonstrating that the conditioning branch preserves the stochastic generation capability of the underlying diffusion model.

    The bottom example extends this experiment to a natural image, again using GBN exemplars generated from the image to train the base model. Our generated point sets follow the image structure while maintaining a well-distributed pattern. Together, these results show that the conditioning branch preserves the base model’s ability to reproduce the prescribed exemplar distribution.

    Metrics

    We evaluate each point set using seven metrics grouped by the property they assess: relaxation (CVT, HOT), capacity (capacity deviation, centroid displacement), global agreement with the target density (EMD, Sinkhorn), and local spacing (spatial measure).

  • •

    CVT energy[13]. Measures point relaxation by integrating, over each point’s Voronoi cell, the density-weighted squared distance from every location in the cell to that point. It is minimized when each point coincides with the density-weighted centroid of its cell, as in Lloyd-based stippling [36]:

    E_CVT=∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ∫_Vᵢρ(x) ∥x-sᵢ∥² dx,

    where sᵢ is the i-th point, Vᵢ its Voronoi cell, and ρ the target density.

  • •

    HOT energy[25]. The analogous energy over power cells, whose weights are chosen so that all cells have equal mass [4]. This is the ⋆₀-HOT2,2 energy minimized by BNOT [10]:

    E_HOT=∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ∫_Vʷᵢρ(x) ∥x-sᵢ∥² dx,

    where Vʷᵢ is the power cell of sᵢ.

  • •

    Capacity deviation δ_c[5]. Measures how uniformly the target mass is distributed across Voronoi cells. It is zero when every cell contains the same mass:

    δ_c=1/n∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ((mᵢ)/(m̄)-1)²,

    where mᵢ=∫_Vᵢρ(x) dx and m̄ is the mean cell mass.

  • •

    Centroid displacement D. Measures the distance between each point and the density-weighted centroid of its power cell. It is zero when the BNOT centroidal optimality condition is satisfied [10]:

    D=1/n∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ∥sᵢ-bᵢ∥, bᵢ=(∫_Vʷᵢx ρ(x) dx)/(∫_Vʷᵢρ(x) dx).

  • •

    EMD and Sinkhorn. Measure global agreement with the target density by transporting the point distribution to the target distribution. EMD is the 2-Wasserstein distance [43]; Sinkhorn is its entropy-regularized approximation [9]. Both measure global density agreement without directly assessing local point arrangement.

  • •

    Spatial measure ρₛ[18]. Measures local point spacing after rescaling distances by the local density [45]. Higher values indicate more uniform nearest-neighbor spacing relative to the local density:

    ρₛ=1/n∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ(rᵢ√n ρ(sᵢ)/ρ̄)/(r_\max),

    where rᵢ is the nearest-neighbor distance of sᵢ, ρ̄ is the mean target density at the points, and r_\max=(2/√3)^1/2 is the reference spacing for hexagonal packing at unit density.

    • Quantitative Comparison

    In Table 1, we compare our model with the optimization-based samplers WVS and GBN on all four datasets: the 1K-image Icons-50 and 500-image CelebA test splits at 1024 points, and the 400-image ShapeNet2D and 263-image Anime Chibi test splits at 1600 points (subtables). Our model is trained separately on WVS and GBN exemplars, and both variants are reported. Bold and underlined values denote the best and second-best results, respectively.

    Compared with its own exemplar sampler, each learned variant improves HOT energy, centroid displacement and EMD on all four datasets (on Icons-50, the HOT energy is 4.059 for Ours-GBN against 5.204 for GBN), and falls short in CVT energy and spatial measure. The Sinkhorn values of all methods lie within 0.002 of each other on every dataset. Capacity deviation stays close to the exemplar sampler on the two square 1024-point datasets, but the gap grows on the two non-square 1600-point datasets (Ours-GBN 0.038 against 0.013 for GBN on ShapeNet2D, and 0.107 against 0.030 on Anime Chibi). These two datasets differ from the first two in point budget, aspect ratio and training-set size at once, and our experiments do not separate these factors.

    The learned variants inherit the ranking of their exemplar samplers. In 27 of the 28 dataset–metric pairs, the variant trained on the better of WVS and GBN is also the better of our two variants, and the remaining pair (Sinkhorn on Anime Chibi) is a tie for both. Within the table, our variants rank best or second-best on all but three pairs (CVT on ShapeNet2D and Anime Chibi, and capacity deviation on Anime Chibi), while requiring no optimization at inference. WVS minimizes the CVT energy directly and therefore has the best CVT energy, and with it the best spatial measure. GBN’s Gaussian-kernel objective promotes capacity preservation and gives the best capacity deviation.

    Relation to BNOT

    BNOT optimizes the HOT energy directly and sets the reference on the transport metrics. On HOT energy, centroid displacement and EMD, each learned variant lies between its exemplar sampler and BNOT on all four datasets. Ours-WVS has a better spatial measure than BNOT on all four datasets, and a lower CVT energy on the two 1024-point datasets. BNOT reaches its optimum by per-target Newton iterations whose cost grows by more than two orders of magnitude across our budget range (Figure 7). Our variants instead run at a cost that grows little with the budget, generalize to unseen images and budgets, and are differentiable. BNOT appears as an unranked reference in the figures and in Table 4 (Appendix E).

    Running-time Evaluation

    We report runtime measurements in Figure 7 across multiple point budgets. Ours-WVS and Ours-GBN share the same architecture and therefore have identical inference costs. For each method and point count, we report the mean time to generate one stipple pattern.

    The optimization-based samplers use their published default stopping criteria: 50 Lloyd iterations for WVS, up to 25 Newton iterations for BNOT, and 1000 optimization steps for GBN. Our runtime is determined by a fixed number of denoising steps, independent of the target.

    Our cost grows little with point count. It is slower than WVS at smaller budgets but becomes the fastest method from about 1024 points onward. It is faster than BNOT and GBN at every evaluated budget, with the gap to BNOT widening as BNOT becomes increasingly expensive. Hardware details and CPU/GPU profiling are provided in Appendix B.

    Ablation Study

    For the architectural ablations, we disable all inference-time modifications and use standard diffusion sampling from pure noise. We compare our full model with four simplified variants: Vanilla, a standard ControlNet applied to the frozen base model of [Doignies et al. [12]]; Unfrozen, which jointly trains the randomly initialized base U-Net and control branch; GECCO, which augments the frozen Vanilla model with continuous GECCO feature extraction; and Gated, which replaces zero-convolutions with transform-gated 1×1 projections. The Full model combines joint training with both GECCO and Gated augmentations.

    The architectural ablation results are summarized in Table 2, with qualitative comparisons shown in Figure 8. Full lowers capacity deviation from 0.0626 (Vanilla) to 0.0259 and also improves HOT energy, EMD and centroid displacement. Gating alone brings little over Vanilla; the gains come from joint training and the per-point features, and are largest when the two are combined. Figure 8 shows the same ordering: Vanilla and Gated leave uneven point density inside the contours, while Full is close to the final SDEdit sampler.

    We next evaluate the inference-time sampling strategy using the Full model. Following SDEdit [24], we replace pure-noise initialization with a density-weighted rejection-sampled prior and denoise only the final 50% of the diffusion schedule.

    As shown in Table 2, inference time decreases from 11.08 s to 5.65 s at comparable quality. Capacity deviation is essentially unchanged (0.0255 against 0.0259), centroid displacement and EMD improve slightly, and HOT energy is slightly worse. Qualitatively, SDEdit and Full produce similar results (Figure 8), and both look clearly better than Vanilla.

    Differentiable Tone Correction

    Because our sampler is a neural network, it defines a differentiable mapping S from a density map ρ to a point set. Thus, any differentiable objective on the generated stipple can be optimized with respect to the requested density by back-propagating through S. In contrast, the iterative optimization samplers provide no direct gradient; differentiating through WVS, BNOT, or GBN would require back-propagation through their respective Lloyd, Newton, or gradient-based iterations, or implicit differentiation at their fixed point, which we do not attempt here.

    We evaluate this capability on dot gain, where finite-sized stipple dots cause the rendered tone to differ from the requested density: isolated dots can appear too dark, while overlapping dots in dark regions saturate (Figure 9, left). We therefore optimize the requested density ρ so that the rendered stipple better matches the target darkness.

    The renderer R places each point as a Gaussian dot with standard deviation 2 pixels on a 256×256 canvas and converts accumulated ink a to darkness using Beer–Lambert saturation, 1-e^-κa. We calibrate the ink gain κ once on six images so that uncorrected stipples match their mean target darkness, and then keep it fixed. Given target image I, the target darkness, which is also its target density, is ρ₀=1-I. We parameterize the corrected density as ρ=sigmoid (logit(ρ₀)+φ), where φ is a 64×64 correction field bilinearly upsampled to the image resolution. We optimize

    φ^⋆=\arg\min_φ \lVertR(S(ρ))-ρ₀\rVert₂²+λ₂\lVertφ\rVert₂²+λₜᵥTV(φ),

    with λ₂=10⁻³ and λₜᵥ=10⁻². Adam is used with a learning rate of 0.05 for 300 steps. Only ρ is optimized; the network weights, remaining conditioning, initial points, and noise are fixed, making the objective deterministic.

    We validate the gradients using central finite differences with step 0.02 at 24 randomly selected entries of φ. The analytic and numerical gradients achieve a cosine similarity of 0.995, agree in sign at all 24 locations, and have a magnitude slope of 0.98.

    We compare four strategies on 24 held-out Icons-50 targets at 1024 points. uncorrected directly uses ρ₀. tone curve replaces φ with a global 17-knot transfer curve and is optimized using the same objective. random search optimizes the full 64×64 field using gradient-free (1+1) random search with the 1/5 success rule and 600 sampler evaluations, matching the computational cost of 300 forward-and-backward steps. ours performs the gradient-based optimization described above. We evaluate the rendered stipples using PSNR, SSIM, and mean absolute error (MAE).

    For efficiency, we compute gradients through the closed-form x̂₀ estimate after a single denoising step at t=120, which is already differentiated through during training. Full back-propagation through the reverse process is also possible, with memory proportional to the number of denoising steps. Although the dot-gain model is a simplified printer proxy, the results consistently show improvement across all targets and over gradient-free optimization at equal cost.

    Our correction improves all 24 targets, with an average PSNR gain of +0.83 dB, compared with +0.22 dB for random search at equal cost and +0.17 dB for the tone curve (Table 3, Figure 10). Gradients outperform random search on 23 of 24 images. The optimized density reduces point crowding (Figure 9, right), lowering RMS error from 0.0913 to 0.0700. Across a 16× range of ink gains, the PSNR improvement remains between +0.31 and +1.44 dB and consistently exceeds the tone curve (Appendix A).

    5. Conclusions and Limitations

    We present a learned stippling algorithm that learns the stippling process itself rather than a single point distribution. A single checkpoint per dataset and exemplar sampler generates high-quality stipple patterns for unseen images and a range of point budgets, with an inference cost that grows little with output size and a fully differentiable mapping from density to stipples. This shifts stippling from a per-target optimization problem to a reusable, image-conditioned generative process. It enables fast generation, capacity generalization, and downstream optimization through the sampler.

    Visual quality remains the main limitation. Gaussian Blue Noise produces smoother density transitions and preserves fine details and sharp edges more faithfully, while our spectra retain the blue-noise structure but suppress low frequencies less effectively than optimization-based methods. Our method is also slower than deterministic low-discrepancy samplers, and its OT-grid representation relies on regular grids and convolutions that do not readily extend beyond 2D, motivating non-grid alternatives. Nevertheless, differentiability enables capabilities unavailable to these optimizers, as demonstrated by our tone-correction experiment. Future work can optimize through the full reverse process, support richer objectives such as stylization, and use generated stipples in downstream learned models.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Differentiability: Sensitivity to the Ink Gain

    Figure 11 sweeps the ink gain of the renderer in the dot-gain experiment of Figure 9, to show that the advantage of optimizing through the sampler is not an artifact of the calibrated value.

item.title: 开放形态几何风格迁移：学到设计语言，而不是学到那一类形状 ｜ Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer
item.description:
一句话：用结构线稿 + 双 LoRA 解耦，把字母的几何风格迁移到人体姿态这类完全不同的形态。

要点：

  • 难点不在学风格，而在「学风格但别学下它所在的形状族」：目标形态用结构线稿表示，Geometry LoRA 管结构贴合、风格 LoRA 管风格实现。
  • 开放形态迁移要求 Geometry LoRA 通用，因此设计了几何富集策略：构造大量刻意多样的合成结构线稿，覆盖陌生几何。
  • 实验与消融验证了解耦与通用几何先验的必要性：字形、象形图等形状族学到的风格可以迁移到显著不同、未见过的形态。

为什么值得看：程序化建模与风格化资产最常被「只对同类形状有效」卡住。这套「结构线稿 + 双 LoRA」的做法，是让风格库真正复用到任意形态的一条可行路径。

中文摘要：从一类形状学到的几何风格通常只能应用到同类形状上。作者考虑更难的设定：学习一套风格化拉丁字母的几何设计语言，再把它应用到新形态上，从希腊字形到人体姿态这类完全不同的结构。他们提出开放形态几何风格迁移（Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer），即学到的几何风格可应用到不受原形状族限制的形态。这个设定的难点不只是学风格，而是要在学风格的同时不把风格所在形状族一并学进去。作者用结构线稿表示目标形态，并用 Geometry LoRA 与风格专用 LoRA 把结构贴合与风格实现解耦。关键是在开放形态迁移中 Geometry LoRA 必须是通用的，为此他们设计了几何富集策略，构造一个规模大、刻意多样、覆盖大量陌生几何的合成结构线稿集合。实验与消融表明解耦与这一通用几何先验都不可或缺，使从字形、象形图等形状族学到的几何风格能迁移到显著不同、未见过的形态。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-22

Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer

Abstract

A geometric style learned from one family of shapes is typically applied to new shapes from the same family. We consider a more challenging setting: learning the geometric design language of a stylized Latin alphabet and applying it to new forms, from Greek glyphs to entirely different structures such as human poses. We introduce Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer, where the forms to which a learned geometric style can be applied are not restricted to the shape family in which that style was observed. This setting is deceptively challenging: the difficulty is not merely learning a style, but learning the style without learning the shape family in which it was observed. We represent target forms by structural sketches and disentangle structural adherence from style realization using a Geometry LoRA and a style-specific LoRA. Critically, open-form transfer requires the Geometry LoRA to be universal. To achieve this, we devise a geometry-enrichment strategy that constructs a large and purposefully diverse collection of synthetic structural sketches spanning a broad range of unfamiliar geometries. Our experiments and ablations demonstrate the importance of both disentanglement and this universal geometry prior, enabling geometric styles learned from glyphs, pictograms, and other shape families to be transferred to substantially different, unseen forms.

††footnotetext: ∗Corresponding author

1 Introduction

Style transfer is a long-standing and intriguing problem in visual computing: given examples that contain both content and style, the goal is to capture the essence of the style, separate it from the particular content on which it is observed, and apply it to new content. The separation of style from content has been studied for decades [8, 7], and has more recently become central to neural style transfer and generative modeling [13, 27, 15]. At the heart of the problem lies the ability to distinguish what is represented from how it is expressed.

In this work, we focus on geometric style, where style governs how an underlying structure is geometrically realized. A canonical example is a font: different glyphs have different structures, yet their geometric realizations follow a coherent design language that makes them immediately recognizable as belonging to the same font. More generally, such geometric styles cannot be inferred from a single example; it is revealed through a collection of different shapes that share the same design language. Early work has considered related notions of separating style from content and transferring geometric style across shapes [25, 9].

Existing approaches [22, 29, 26] typically learn and apply such styles within a shared domain: a style observed on letters is transferred to other letters, and a style observed on human figures is applied to other human figures. We remove this restriction and consider transferring a geometric style to an open space of forms. As illustrated in Figure Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer, a style learned from a Latin alphabet may be applied to Greek glyphs, or more radically, to human poses; conversely, a geometric style learned from pictograms may be applied to glyphs. We call this new setting Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer, where the forms to which a learned geometric style can be applied are not restricted to the shape family in which that style was observed. We focus on forms whose underlying structure can be represented by a sparse structural sketch, which serves as the geometry to be styled.

The open-form setting, illustrated in Figure 2, is deceptively challenging. The difficulty is not simply learning a style, but learning the style without learning the shape family in which that style was observed. Existing font-generation methods can transfer styles to unseen glyphs [29, 26, 32, 18], and some explicitly separate character content from style. However, their structural component is learned and evaluated largely within the glyph domain, often within a single writing system. This distinction becomes critical when the target form leaves the source domain. A straightforward LoRA trained on a limited styled shape family learns an entangled style with the geometries observed at training (Sec. 4.2), causing it to drift toward familiar source-domain shapes when presented with substantially different target geometries.

Our approach addresses this entanglement by separating structural adherence from style realization. A Geometry LoRA is responsible for faithfully following the target structural sketch serving as a geometric-adherence prior, while a Style LoRA learns how that geometry should be realized in the desired style. Accordingly, the Geometry LoRA must be universal: generalize across the vast universe of styles, responding to structure rather than shape identity or residual stylistic cues. Acquiring such a universal geometry prior is itself non-trivial: a corpus of ordinary glyphs provides a limited and familiar geometry vocabulary, allowing the model to recognize known shapes rather than truly follow the input structure. We therefore introduce a geometry-enrichment strategy (GEE Sec. 3.2) that systematically leverages SVG font data to construct a large collection of unfamiliar synthetic geometries, untangled from their source style. This strategy proves vital for successfully learning a universal geometry LoRA.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We introduce Open-Form Geometric Stylization, where a geometric style learned from one shape domain is applied to universally arbitrary forms.

  • •

    We show that open-form stylization requires separating structural adherence from style realization.

  • •

    Finally, we introduce a geometry-enrichment strategy for constructing the broad and diverse structural training distribution needed to acquire this universal prior.

    • We evaluate these ideas through controlled ablations and increasingly challenging transfers, from held-out glyphs and cross-alphabet transfer to unrelated forms such as human poses, demonstrating that a geometric style can be extended well beyond the family of shapes on which it was observed.

    2 Background and Related Work

    Our work builds on three lines of research: the separation of style and content, font and glyph style transfer, and structurally conditioned generation. Below we review each line, clarify how our notion of geometric style relates to them, and how they relate to our approach.

    2.1 Style and Content

    Our work is closely connected to the seminal work of Tenenbaum and Freeman [25] on separating style and content. Using bilinear models, they showed that a common style can be inferred from multiple observations and applied to new content. Particularly relevant to our setting is their treatment of fonts, where style is shared across different letters and can be used to synthesize previously unseen characters. This provides an early and elegant formulation of style as a factor that can be learned across a family of shapes and separated from their individual geometry. Our work builds on this perspective, but considers an open-form setting in which the new content need not belong to the same family: a geometric style learned from one alphabet may be applied to another alphabet, or even to a different class of structures such as human poses.

    More broadly, style transfer has a long history in computer vision and graphics, with much of the literature focusing on style as visual appearance. Early example-based methods [8, 7] synthesized and transferred texture by sampling local neighborhoods or patches from example images. [13] later introduced neural style transfer, demonstrating that content and artistic style can be represented separately within a deep network and recombined to render new content in the appearance of a reference image. Recent diffusion-based methods such as StyleAligned [15], B-LoRA [10], InstantStyle [28], and ZipLoRA [24] substantially extend the quality and flexibility of reference-based style transfer. Across these works, style is predominantly expressed through visual appearance, including texture, color, material, brushwork, and shading.

    Our notion of geometric style is different. Here, style determines how an underlying structure is geometrically realized: how curves are formed, junctions are connected, strokes vary in thickness, gaps are introduced, and structural elements terminate or interact. Such a style is naturally revealed by a set of related shapes rather than by a single reference image. Glyphs provide a particularly clean instance of this setting: individual characters differ in structure, while together they reveal a consistent geometric design language. Related notions of transferring geometric style across shapes were also explored in early work by [9]. More recently, geometric stylization has also been explored for 3D shapes  [5].

    Closely related, Abstraction in Style (AiS) [19] also separates geometry from appearance using two specialized LoRA adapters. However, AiS learns style-specific geometric abstraction, whereas our Geometry LoRA is universal, enabling a learned geometric style to generalize to unseen structural sketches across shape families.

    2.2 Font and Glyph Style Transfer

    Modern font-generation methods provide the closest setting to our work, as they explicitly transfer a common style across glyphs with different structures. FontDiffuser [29] formulates one-shot diffusion-based font generation, using multi-scale content aggregation to preserve character structure and contrastive learning to capture style. It generalizes to unseen characters and also demonstrates cross-lingual generation. MX-Font [22] addresses few-shot font generation using multiple localized experts that disentangle content and style while capturing different local style characteristics. It also demonstrates cross-lingual generalization to unseen writing systems. VecFusion [26] approaches font generation in the vector domain, explicitly modeling glyph topology, paths, and Bézier control points, and supports applications including glyph completion and few-shot style transfer. Skeleton-Guided Diffusion [32] is particularly related to our structural representation, using character skeletons to guide diffusion and preserve structure during font generation. StrokeStyles [1] decomposes font glyphs into meaningful stroke structures and uses this representation for consistent geometric stylization across characters.

    FLUX-Font [18] is particularly close to our work architecturally. It adapts a pre-trained diffusion transformer using separate LoRA modules [17] for glyph content and style, explicitly separating the two factors rather than learning them through a single adapter. Our method shares this general motivation, but separates structural adherence from style realization hierarchically: a universal Geometry LoRA is first trained to follow arbitrary structural sketches, and each Style LoRA is subsequently learned with this geometry prior active and fixed.

    Despite their differences, these methods share an important restriction: their structural representations and learned priors are designed for the glyph domain. Their goal is to generalize from observed characters to other characters, possibly across writing systems, but the target remains a glyph. Open-form transfer removes this restriction. The target structural sketch may describe a character, a pictogram, a human pose, or another unrelated form. Consequently, separating content from style within the font domain is not sufficient; the geometry-following component must itself generalize beyond the shape family in which the style was observed.

    2.3 Structural Conditioning

    Spatially conditioned diffusion models provide a complementary line of related work. ControlNet [31] and T2I-Adapter [20] condition pre-trained text-to-image models on spatial signals such as edges, depth, segmentation, poses, and sketches, while Sketch-Guided Diffusion [27] focuses specifically on generation controlled by free-form sketches. These methods demonstrate that strong spatial adherence can be learned over broad image distributions.

    Our problem, however, is not spatial conditioning alone. The structural sketch specifies a form whose geometric realization must change according to a style learned from a separate set of examples. The challenge is therefore to preserve the target structure while preventing the learned style from carrying with it the shape distribution on which that style was observed. We use structural conditioning as a means toward this goal, learning a universal geometry prior that remains fixed while different geometric styles are acquired. At inference, we treat structure and style as independent conditions and adopt the dual-conditioning guidance of InstructPix2Pix [3], allowing their strengths to be controlled separately.

    3 Method

    Given a collection of shapes sharing a geometric style, our goal is to learn that style and apply it to a new target form specified by a structural sketch. We use the term sketch-glyph for a pair consisting of a structural sketch and its styled realization. The term originates naturally from fonts, where a sketch specifies the structure of a character and the glyph realizes it in a particular font. In this work, we extend this notion to pictograms, symbols, and other structured forms that are not letters. Given a small collection of sketch-glyph pairs sharing a style, we aim to realize arbitrary new structural sketches in that style, as illustrated in Fig. 2.

    Figure 3 provides an overview of the method. Our key design is to separate the two responsibilities involved in this task. A Universal Geometry LoRA (UGL) provides a general ability to faithfully follow the input structural sketch, while a Style LoRA learns how the conditioned geometry should be realized in the target style. The two adapters are learned hierarchically rather than independently. UGL is trained once (Fig. 3ii); each Style LoRA is subsequently trained on top of the frozen UGL (Fig. 3iii).

    For this separation to support open-form transfer, UGL itself must generalize far beyond any particular shape family. We therefore train it on a large and purposefully diverse collection of synthetic geometries constructed by our Geometry Enrichment Engine (GEE) (Fig. 3i).

    At inference (Fig. 3iv), UGL and the selected Style LoRA are applied jointly. Their contributions can be controlled independently through separate geometry and style guidance scales, allowing us to balance adherence to the target structure against the strength of its stylistic realization. The following sections describe UGL, GEE, and Style LoRA training in detail.

    3.1 Universal Geometry LoRA (UGL)

    The purpose of UGL is to fine-tune a text-to-image diffusion model to follow open-form geometries (i.e. sketches). Starting from a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion transformer (DiT), we fit LoRA parameters on the DiT’s weights using sketch-glyph data pairs constructed by GEE. The rich, diverse synthetic data produced by the GEE allows us to select a high LoRA rank without overfitting, giving the UGL significant learning capacity. After this one-time training, we freeze UGL and share it across all Style LoRAs, providing a common geometry prior beyond each style’s specific training examples.

    3.2 Geometry Enrichment Engine (GEE)

    Fonts are a natural starting point for data augmentation: they are available in a large variety of styles, and more importantly, their SVG native representation enables truly geometric augmentations compared to raster form. However, using real font glyphs directly presents two limitations. First, available fonts cover a relatively narrow set of languages and therefore a limited vocabulary of structures, which may hinder generalization to unseen scripts and, even more, to out-of-domain forms such as symbols or pictograms. Second, the geometry of a glyph is itself tied to the style of its source font, so the conditioning structure may carry unwanted stylistic cues. To address both issues, we introduce GEE: a data-generation procedure that expands the range of training geometries while reducing their dependence on font style. To increase structural diversity, GEE takes advantage of the native SVG parameterization of fonts and constructs novel geometric forms by applying random sequences of geometric edits. We refer to each such sequence as a geometric recipe. A recipe may, for example, repeatedly remove or merge SVG parts, producing coherent but unfamiliar structures (Fig. 4(a)). Recipes also allow the GEE to address the second problem. A recipe applied to one font can be re-applied to matching letters from another font, producing paired data with similar structure but different styles (Fig. 4(b)). During UGL training, we form mixed pairs by taking the conditioning sketch from one font and the target from another font to which the same recipe was applied (Fig. 4(c)). The sketch and target therefore remain aligned in structure while differing in style, encouraging UGL to learn the supplied geometry independently of its stylistic realization.

    We next describe the editing primitives that drive the geometry enrichment process, first motivating their design and then outlining each one (full details in Appendix C).

    Structural editing primitives.

    A glyph’s structure is determined by how its strokes relate: which strokes meet and where they branch or terminate. Smooth transformations such as warping, shearing, or scaling can change a glyph’s appearance, but they do not create new structural relations between its strokes. To generate genuinely new structures, we therefore need operations that modify these relations. We propose two elementary edits: component removal and merging. This builds on a broader principle: deleting and recombining existing parts can generate meaningful structural variation [11], and related cut-based augmentations have been shown to improve recognition performance [6, 30]. Repeating these edits produces novel structural relations beyond those found in existing alphabets.

    To make both edits transferable across fonts, we edit the glyph’s structure rather than its contour, which is more sensitive to stylistic variation. We therefore represent each glyph as a graph, with strokes as edges and intersections and endpoints as nodes. A recipe is then expressed as a sequence of graph edits, with component removal and merging each applied one to three times. The edit type and its structural parameters are sampled when the recipe is created, specifying which component to remove or where components should connect. Because the edits are defined structurally, the same recipe can be replayed across fonts to produce the same underlying structure in multiple styles. Structural correspondence across styles is further explained in Appendix C.

    Graph extraction.

    We represent each glyph as a graph that captures its dominant stroke structure (Fig. 5). Starting from the glyph (a), we compute its medial axis together with the local inscribed-disk radius, which provides an estimate of stroke thickness (b). We prune short branches caused by serifs and other stylistic details, leaving the main stroke structure (c). Pixel chains are then collapsed into edges, with junctions and stroke endpoints represented as nod es (d). Finally, we classify each edge by its structural role: an edge between two junctions is a bar, while an edge from a junction to an endpoint is a leg (e).

    Component removal.

    Fig. 6 illustrates the process. Our strategy is to perform the edit in the medial-axis representation and then reconstruct the glyph back in the SVG domain. Outline points unrelated to the removed component are preserved exactly. Only the region surrounding the cut is reconstructed, where additional processing is needed to obtain a clean, style-consistent boundary. Using the graph extracted in the previous step, we locate the component to remove from its structure, which lets us find the same component across styles (a). As seen in Fig. 6(b), simply removing the red branch can leave bulges where it connects to the remaining blue branches. We therefore trim these regions and reconnect the remaining blue branches. We then separate the pixels belonging to the removed region from those that should remain (c). This produces a pixel removal mask, which we convert to a smooth vector representation (d).Additional reconstruction steps are described in the appendix. The final removal result is shown in (e).

    Merging.

    Fig. 7 illustrates the process. We begin with two glyphs from the same style: a guest (a) and a host (b), and aim to combine them into a single coherent glyph. As in component removal, we perform the edit in the medial-axis representation and reconstruct the result in the SVG domain. Using the graphs extracted in the previous step, we identify where the guest should connect to the host based on their structural attributes. The process starts by randomly generating a candidate merging recipe, combining a set of simple augmentations, such as mirroring, rotation, and scaling, with a pair of connection points selected from the guest and host graphs, shown as red points in (c,d). To assess the result produced by the recipe, we apply the augmentations and connect the glyphs at the selected points. We approve only recipes that produce a clean, coherent shape (e). A merging recipe is retained only if it succeeds across a minimum number of styles. Additional implementation details are provided in the appendix. The final merging result is shown in (f).

    3.3 Style LoRA

    We train a separate Style LoRA on sketch-glyph pairs for each target style, as shown in Fig. 3(iii). The backbone and UGL parameters remain fixed, while UGL continues to guide the geometry throughout training. Only the Style LoRA is optimized, allowing it to focus on how that geometry is realized in the target style. Here we use a low-rank adapter, far smaller than UGL: its limited capacity helps keep the style update from re-learning geometry or competing with the shared geometry prior. Following previous work [12, 23], we associate each style with a unique rare token. This token and a short appearance description provide the textual conditioning during both Style LoRA training and inference.

    Geometry reinforcement.

    The few style examples also share a limited family of geometries, so the Style LoRA may still tie the learned style to those geometries despite UGL’s structural guidance. To preserve open-form transfer, we mix geometry-enriched sketch-glyph pairs into its training batches, shown by the connection from GEE to Style LoRA training in Fig. 3. These pairs expose the model to geometries outside the target style’s examples throughout adaptation, reinforcing its ability to follow new structures while learning the style.

    3.4 Inference

    After training, we apply UGL and the selected Style LoRA jointly to the base diffusion model to map structural sketches to styled outputs (Fig. 3iv). To control geometry adherence and style strength separately, we adopt dual classifier-free guidance following InstructPix2Pix [3]. During training, the structural sketch, the style caption, or both are dropped to their null conditions, so a single network learns all four conditioning combinations. During sampling, we combine three forward passes using two CFG coefficients to obtain separate geometry and style guidance strengths, balancing adherence to the input sketch geometry vs. the target style. Appendix B provides the guidance formulation and implementation details.

    This joint application supports transfer to new forms without further training: a pictogram style can depict new human poses, while a sculptural style can turn free-form strokes into tubular shapes (Fig. Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer). The same sketch can also be rendered in different learned styles (Fig. 2). Section 4 evaluates these capabilities through qualitative and quantitative comparisons and ablations of the method’s main components.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate our method across fonts, pictograms, and object-centric styles, using sketches of increasing structural novelty:

  • •

    In-domain, held-out test examples from the same source domain as the style training data

  • •

    Near-domain, semantically related but structurally unseen examples, such as non-Latin glyphs for fonts and everyday human poses for pictograms

  • •

    Out-of-domain, structures from unrelated shape families, such as non-glyph sketches for font styles or non-human sketches for pictogram styles.

    • We compare against prior methods and perform targeted ablations to assess both open-set transfer quality and the contributions of our main design choices.

    4.1 Training and Evaluation Data

    The training data for the universal geometry LoRA (UGL) is produced by the geometry enrichment engine (GEE) from 80 base glyphs (Latin letters, Latin Extended letters, and digits) shared across 16 fonts. Applying 6,000 random recipes yields 42,705 sketch–glyph pairs, on which UGL is trained once (Appendix D). Each style is represented by a small exemplar set with manually drawn structural sketches. We hold out six examples per style for evaluation and train the Style LoRA on the remainder, yielding roughly 20–70 sketch–exemplar pairs per style. During Style LoRA training, 10% of each batch is replayed from the UGL training pairs using their original style-free captions, helping preserve the learned geometry prior while adapting to style. For evaluation, we use a benchmark of 50 curated sketches per style category (fonts and pictograms). To analyze how well our method and the baselines generalize, the sketches span the in-, near-, and out-of-domain tiers defined above. We evaluate across twelve styles, and for each style all methods receive the same sketches and style references.

    4.2 Open-form Geometric Generalization

    We tailored our main technical contributions, the universal geometry LoRA (UGL) and the geometry enrichment engine (GEE), to open-form generalization and the challenges of fine-tuning large models.

    In this section, we demonstrate the necessity of both components; later in Table 12 we also present a quantitative evaluation that supports each claim.

    We begin with the most direct alternative: avoid the UGL by fine-tuning a single low-rank adapter on the few sketch-glyph pairs available for a given style. While this formulation preserves both the target geometry and the learned style on held-out examples from the same style family, it does not generalize to out-of-domain structures. Instead, the model takes a shortcut by producing results resembling the closest training example, best seen in the bottom rows of Fig. 8 (w/o UGL), where the model outputs styled examples similar to English alphabet letters rather than the desired geometry. Row w/o UGL in Table 12 quantifies this behavior.

    A natural hypothesis for this phenomenon is that each geometry is observed only through a single realization in the target style, providing too little variation to disentangle the geometry and style.

    An intuitive solution is to train a geometry adapter on ordinary glyphs drawn from a broad corpus of fonts, using the same training settings as UGL but without employing GEE, and then train the same Style LoRAs on top of it. Unfortunately, the failure persisted, now in an even more revealing form. The UGL is even more biased towards common geometries from the train set, e.g. alphabet letters, as again seen in the bottom row of the w/o GEE section of Fig 8. These results are again supported by data in Table 12.

    What is instead needed is a training distribution with fewer geometric correlations, preventing the model from capturing a specific shape identity. This is solved by our second technical contribution (GEE Sec. 3.2). The GEE’s immense augmentation strategy forces the geometry model to rely on the supplied structure rather than recognizing a known geometry. With this enriched corpus, completing our full method, the out-of-domain score rises to 0.94 (Ours in Table 12), with a geometry factor of 0.97 and style within 3% of the ceiling, and the characteristic substitutions largely disappear.

    4.3 Qualitative Evaluation

    We compare against FontDiffuser [29], MX-Font [22], Gemini 3.1 (Nano-Banana 2) [14], and gpt-image-1-mini [21]. All methods receive the same target sketch and style references, except FontDiffuser, which uses a single reference. We include the general-purpose models for completeness, as they require no per-style training. Additional comparisons, including the adapter-based methods B-LoRA and ZipLoRA as well as AiS, are provided in Appendix A.

    In the in-domain tier, we evaluate held-out sketches (Fig. 9). Our method closely matches the ground truth while preserving the requested geometry and fine stylistic details. Gemini and GPT often capture the overall style but drift toward familiar poses or glyphs and lose fine font details. FontDiffuser often deviates from the input structure, while MX-Font follows it more closely but transfers the target style less faithfully.

    In the near-domain tier (Fig. 11), we transfer styles to related but unseen forms: non-Latin glyphs. Baselines often distort these unfamiliar inputs toward known forms or lose structural or stylistic details, while our method follows the supplied geometry and preserves the target style. The zoomed examples highlight reference motifs retained in the outputs, demonstrating transfer beyond the forms seen during style adaptation.

    The out-of-domain tier (Fig. 10) provides a stronger test by applying pictogram and object-centric styles to structures from unrelated shape families. Across these sketches, our method retains the characteristic shapes and appearance of each style while following the new structure, demonstrating open-form transfer beyond the source domain.

    4.4 Quantitative Results

    We evaluate whether our method follows the structural sketch while realizing the target style, and how well both hold as the target geometry moves away from the style’s source domain. On the in-domain tier, where paired ground truth is available, we report LPIPS for perceptual similarity to the ground truth and SSIM for agreement in local image structure. For the near- and out-of-domain tiers, where paired ground truth is unavailable, we use VLM-as-a-judge [4]. The judge separately scores structural adherence to the sketch and stylistic fidelity to the references; we report their product, normalized by the score of real examples from the corresponding style (judge setup and prompt in Appendix F).

    Comparison and ablation.

    Table 12 reports judge scores by style family (Fonts, Non-Fonts) and by distance from the training domain (Near, Out), followed by LPIPS and SSIM. Our full method achieves the best results across all reported measures. In the upper block, the font generators closely follow the sketch but lack style fidelity, whereas the general-purpose models better capture the target style but drift from the input structure, as reflected in their lower Out scores. The lower block ablates our method. w/o UGL removes the UGL and trains the Style LoRA directly on the base model. Non-hierarchical trains the Style LoRA without the UGL and adds the UGL only at inference. w/o GEE trains the UGL, and applies geometry reinforcement, on original glyphs only, without GEE. w/o Reinforcement uses the GEE-trained UGL but omits geometry reinforcement during style training. Their performance shows that the importance of our design choices becomes more pronounced as the target geometry moves farther from the training domain. In particular, removing geometry reinforcement lowers the Near score from 0.975 to 0.966, but causes a substantially larger drop in the Out score, from 0.941 to 0.872. This suggests that preserving geometric adherence during style adaptation is particularly important for unfamiliar forms.

    User study.

    We complement these measures with user preferences collected from 32 participants, who compare our result against each baseline in terms of style, structure, and overall preference (Appendix G). Fig. 12 shows the same trend as Table 12: our results are preferred over every baseline on all three criteria, with the largest margins in style and overall preference.

    5 Conclusions, Limitations and Future Work

    We introduced Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer, where a geometric style learned from one family of shapes is applied to structures well beyond that family. We showed that learning geometric style requires separating how a shape is realized from the particular geometry on which that style is observed. However, disentanglement is necessary but not sufficient. To transfer a geometric language to unseen forms, the geometry component must itself be universal.

    These findings suggest an asymmetric view of geometry and style. Geometry should be learned broadly, across a large and diverse space of structures, and can be learned once as a reusable capability. Style, in contrast, can be learned from a much narrower collection of examples and specialized independently. Our Universal Geometry LoRA and Style LoRA instantiate this separation, while GEE provides the geometric diversity needed to make the former universal.

    As with many fine-tuned generative models, some challenges remain. Complex structures can expose a tradeoff between geometric and stylistic fidelity, while strong or recurring stylistic elements can occasionally interfere with the target structure or become overemphasized. Improving this separation, particularly for increasingly complex geometries and styles, is an interesting direction for future work. We believe this principle may extend beyond geometric style transfer, enabling learned visual languages to be applied outside the domains in which they were observed.
