More recent models make spatial prediction more explicit, using language models to reason about or directly generate 3D boxes, object identifiers, and structured scene layouts [(Cho et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Mao et al., 2026)]. A recent part-aware 3D MLLM further explores structured program generation for part-based reasoning, generation, and editing [(Wang et al., 2026b)]. However, such program-level outputs remain symbolic and coarse; they do not provide dense part segmentation masks that organize the surface geometry into a coherent part decomposition. In contrast, PartLLM bridges the generative capacity of language models with dense geometric prediction, using autoregressive generation not as a reasoning interface but as the decomposition mechanism itself, directly producing point-level masks tied to the generated semantic structure.

    3. Method

    Fig. 3 gives an overview of PartLLM. Given an input point cloud P={pᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N sampled from a 3D shape and a user intent u, such as “Please segment all parts” for the full-shape segmentation task, PartLLM first uses a 3D-aware MLLM to autoregressively generate a sequence of part hypotheses Y=(y₁,…,y_S). Each hypothesis yₛ=(lₛ,bₛ) specifies a part label lₛ together with a coarse 3D location bₛ, indicating what part should be segmented and where it is roughly located. Conditioned on these generated hypotheses, a decomposition-aware decoder then assigns each point to one of the hypotheses or the remaining region, producing a dense assignment q and the corresponding point-level masks.

    3.1. 3D-Aware MLLM for Part Hypothesis Generation

    3D Tokenization.

    To generate the part hypothesis sequence based on the input geometry, we attach a point cloud encoder [(Wu et al., 2024)] to the input token stream of an MLLM [(Bai et al., 2025)]. Given the input point cloud P, the encoder first extracts full-resolution point features for all input points. We then downsample the point cloud to K center points and gather their corresponding encoder features. A linear projector maps these sampled point features into the language hidden space, where they are inserted at the positions and serve as 3D visual tokens for the MLLM. The full-resolution point features are retained for the mask decoder, so the language model receives a compact token sequence while the decoder still has access to dense geometric evidence.

    Hypothesis Definition.

    The MLLM generates the hypothesis sequence Y=(y₁,…,y_S) in an autoregressive text format. Each hypothesis yₛ=(lₛ,bₛ) is serialized as a structured text span containing a semantic label lₛ and an axis-aligned 3D box bₛ, followed by a special token <|PART|>. For example, a generated hypothesis may take the form label=Backrest, bbox=[...] <|PART|>. Here, bbox denotes an axis-aligned 3D box [x_\min,y_\min,z_\min,x_\max,y_\max,z_\max] that serves as a spatial cue. The <|PART|> token acts as the terminal token of a part decision, rather than a generic separator. After the language model forward pass, the hidden state at each generated <|PART|> token is used as the representation of the corresponding part hypothesis. Through attention, the <|PART|> token summarizes the generated label, part location, user intent, input P, and previously predicted parts into a context-dependent representation of the part decision. This representation encodes what the part is, where it is, and how it relates to the current decomposition state. In addition to the <|PART|> tokens, the assistant response ends with a special <|BG|> token. Unlike the <|PART|> tokens, <|BG|> does not correspond to any generated part. Instead, its hidden state represents the context-dependent complement of the generated parts. Together, the <|PART|> token states and the <|BG|> token state serve as decoder queries for mask generation, as described next.

    3.2. Decomposition-Aware Decoder

    The generated token states are used as dynamic queries for mask decoding. Let hₛ denote the hidden state of the s-th <|PART|> token, and let h_S+1=h_bg denote the hidden state of <|BG|>. These states form the decomposition query set:

    (1)

    H=[h₁,…,h_S,h_bg].

    Let X denote the full-resolution point features provided by the point cloud encoder. Given H and X, the decoder first uses a two-way transformer [(Kirillov et al., 2023)] to contextualize the queries and point features jointly:

    (2)

    (H̃,Φ)=T_ψ(H,X),

    where H̃=[h̃₁,…,h̃_S+1] are the updated query features and Φ={φᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N denotes the point-wise geometric features used for mask prediction. This query-point interaction allows each generated part hypothesis to attend to the input geometry while injecting the current decomposition context into point-wise features.

    For each contextualized query h̃ₛ, s∈{1,…,S+1}, an MLP-based hypernetwork ρ_θ predicts a query-specific classifier wₛ. The compatibility between query s and point pᵢ is then computed as

    (3)

    wₛ=ρ_θ(h̃ₛ), z_i,s=wₛ^⊤φᵢ.

    For each point, this produces a logit vector zᵢ∈ℝ^S+1, where each dimension corresponds to one generated part hypothesis or the background query. The decoder predicts a categorical distribution over the generated query set:

    (4)

    p_θ(qᵢ=s|P,u,Y)=(\exp(z_i,s))/(∑ᵣ₌₁^S+1\exp(z_i,r)), s∈{1,…,S+1}.

    Here, qᵢ∈{1,…,S+1} is the assignment variable of point pᵢ. For s≤S, qᵢ=s indicates that pᵢ belongs to the s-th generated part hypothesis, while qᵢ=S+1 assigns the point to the background. The mask of each generated part is therefore induced by the points assigned to its corresponding hypothesis.

    Discussion.

    The key distinction from SAM-style decoders [(Zhu et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2025)] lies in the prediction space. Given S generated hypotheses, a SAM-style decoder would treat them as S independent binary mask predictions. PartLLM instead treats the generated hypotheses and the background query as a dynamic label set, and predicts an (S+1)-way assignment for each point. This is possible because the ambiguity of what to segment has already been resolved before mask decoding: the MLLM generates an explicit hypothesis sequence Y, leaving the decoder to ground this generated label set into dense masks. The shared categorical distribution explicitly couples all masks by forcing the generated parts and background to compete for the same points, yielding mutually exclusive assignments. This joint assignment is especially important for part segmentation, where neighboring or structurally related parts often have ambiguous boundaries and should be interpreted relative to each other within the same shape-level decomposition.

    3.3. Training Objective

    Training supervises both parts of the representation: the autoregressive hypothesis sequence and the dense point assignment. Let a^⋆ denote the target assistant response that serializes the part labels, coarse 3D locations, and special tokens. The language model is trained with the standard next-token objective:

    (5)

    Lₗₘ=-∑ₜ\logp_θ(a^⋆ₜ|P,u,a^⋆_

    This loss teaches the model to generate the semantic decomposition in language form, including the <|PART|> and <|BG|> tokens whose hidden states are used by the decoder.

    For mask supervision, let Z={z_i,s}∈ℝ^N×(S+1) denote the decoder logits over the S generated part hypotheses and the background query. The target assignment q^⋆∈{1,…,S+1}^N follows the response order: points belonging to the s-th target part are assigned to class s, and points outside the target parts are assigned to class S+1. The mask loss is a point-level cross-entropy over this dynamic label space:

    (6)

    Lₘₐₛₖ=-1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^N\log(\exp(z_i,q^⋆ᵢ))/(∑ₛ₌₁^S+1\exp(z_i,s)).

    Together with the decomposition-aware decoding strategy, this target construction turns mask supervision into a mutually exclusive point classification problem over the generated hypotheses. Unlike independent binary mask losses, each point contributes to exactly one class in the dynamic label space, forcing the generated parts and the background query to compete during training. As a result, the generated part hypotheses are optimized as a coupled decomposition of the shape, where the assignment of one part is learned relative to the others.

    The total training objective is a weighted combination of the sequence and mask losses:

    (7)

    L=Lₗₘ+λₘₐₛₖLₘₐₛₖ.

    3.4. Unified Task Formulation

    All part segmentation tasks reduce to the same problem: determining which parts to produce and where, conditioned on the user intent. The autoregressive semantic decomposition formulation reflects this shared structure by fixing the response format as a sequence of generated part hypotheses followed by <|BG|>. Here, <|BG|> represents the context-dependent complement of the generated hypotheses, rather than a fixed background category. Task differences are encoded in the input prompt, which determines both the generated part set and the meaning of its complement. By always including <|BG|> in the query set, the decoder performs the same softmax assignment over all points regardless of how many parts are generated, eliminating the need for task-specific decoding logic. This context-dependent behavior emerges from training with the same cross-entropy loss across all modes, allowing <|BG|> to learn a consistent role as the complement of whatever the current prompt requests. Table 2 summarizes the prompt-response interface for each task mode.

  • •

    Full-shape segmentation. The general full-shape prompt asks the model to generate all parts of the object. We further control the granularity with coarse, fine, and number-based prompt variants, so the same model can produce decompositions at different levels of detail. Besides this general open-ended prompt, these controlled prompt types provide an explicit interface for requesting different decomposition granularities. The construction details of these prompt variants are described in Sec. 4.1. In this setting, <|BG|> handles uncovered or unlabeled regions.

  • •

    Text-guided part segmentation. The prompt provides a list of queried part names, and the model generates only the requested parts, while <|BG|> absorbs non-queried parts.

  • •

    Interactive segmentation. The first interaction round provides a single 3D point, and the model generates the part containing that point. Subsequent rounds refine the previously predicted mask: we encode the previous mask as point colors in the input point cloud and provide an include or exclude point to refine the mask. In all interaction rounds, <|BG|> covers points outside the target part.

    • 3.5. Scalable Training with Heterogeneous Data

    Because task differences are expressed entirely through prompts and target responses, heterogeneous annotations can be converted into the same supervision format and mixed within one model. For semantic part annotations, each target hypothesis contains the annotated part label, its coarse 3D location, and a <|PART|> token. For category-agnostic decompositions, we retain the same response structure and simply use a generic label such as part. From the same annotated shape, we derive full-shape segmentation training examples by varying the granularity prompt, text-guided examples by sampling target part subsets, and interactive examples by sampling target points, with optional refinement rounds built from perturbed masks. Regardless of the original annotation type or task mode, we train the model on all resulting instances using the same autoregressive generation objective and decomposition-aware decoder. Training data construction details are given in Sec. 4.1.

    Viewed more broadly, this unified formulation turns task and data diversity into a scaling axis. As more datasets become available, the model can incorporate them through prompt and response design alone, without architectural changes or new training objectives.

    4. Experiments

    We evaluate PartLLM on three 3D part segmentation task families within our open-world formulation: full-shape segmentation, text-guided part segmentation, and interactive segmentation.

    4.1. Setup

    Training Data.

    We train PartLLM on a large-scale mixture of 3D part segmentation datasets. We first curate three public datasets with semantic part labels: PartNeXt [(Wang et al., 2026a)], 3DCoMPaT200 [(Ahmed et al., 2024)], and PartVerse [(Ding et al., 2026)]. We then use an MLLM to annotate 75K licensed 3D assets with semantic part labels. Together, these data provide full-shape, text-guided, and interactive supervision under a shared prompt-response interface. We additionally use a training subset of HY3D-Bench [(Hunyuan3D et al., 2026)] for category-agnostic geometric decomposition without semantic part names. For each shape, we construct training instances across all applicable task modes and granularity levels, yielding 1.1M training samples in total from 323K unique shapes. For full-shape supervision, granularity is defined according to the annotation structure. For the hierarchical datasets PartNeXt and 3DCoMPaT200, the shallowest valid decomposition is treated as coarse, the deepest valid decomposition is treated as fine unless it contains very few parts, and intermediate levels are grouped by part count, with at most 6 parts as coarse, 7–12 as medium, and 13 or more as fine. For all other datasets, granularity is determined directly by the same part-count thresholds. We then sample the full-shape prompt from a small family of general, coarse/fine, and number-controlled templates.

    Benchmarks.

    We evaluate on multiple benchmarks that cover different task settings. From PartNeXt [(Wang et al., 2026a)], we evaluate on 500 shapes covering 50 object categories. From 3DCoMPaT200 [(Ahmed et al., 2024)], we use about 2,000 shapes across 200 categories. Both datasets provide multi-level part annotations, allowing us to evaluate whether a model can handle different semantic granularities across categories. From HY3D-Bench [(Hunyuan3D et al., 2026)], we select 100 shapes with a roughly uniform distribution over part counts. This benchmark is challenging, with the most complex case containing up to 50 ground-truth parts. For full-shape segmentation, we additionally evaluate on PartObjaverse-Tiny [(Yang et al., 2024)], a common benchmark for category-agnostic part segmentation. For text-guided part segmentation, we additionally use PartNet-E [(Liu et al., 2023)]. All evaluation shapes are strictly held out from the training set, and all quantitative results are reported using mIoU-based metrics unless otherwise specified.

    Implementation details.

    Our 3D-aware MLLM is built on Qwen3-VL-4B [(Bai et al., 2025)]. The point cloud encoder is a PointTransformerV3 [(Wu et al., 2024)] initialized from Utonia [(Zhang et al., 2026)] pretrained weights, which takes an input point cloud of 81,920 points and produces per-point features of dimension 1386. We then select 4,096 points via farthest-point sampling and project their features to the language model’s hidden dimension through a linear layer. In the mask decoder, we use a two-way transformer with two layers, an embedding dimension of 512, and eight attention heads. Each layer contains self-attention on query tokens, cross-attention from queries to point features, an MLP, and cross-attention from point features back to queries. This transformer operates on the 4,096 downsampled point features together with the part-hypothesis hidden states. The updated point features are then interpolated back to the original point resolution and merged with the encoder’s full-resolution features to obtain the point-wise decoder features φᵢ used in Sec. 3. For autoregressive training, we serialize the target part hypotheses in ascending order of their bounding-box center coordinates along the x, y, and z axes. We apply random 3D rotation augmentation to each training sample. Bounding-box and point prompts are generated after augmentation in the transformed coordinate frame. We train all modules end-to-end on 48 H20 GPUs for 5 epochs with AdamW (β₁=0.9, β₂=0.95, weight decay 0.02), using 2% warmup followed by cosine learning rate decay to 0.1× the initial learning rate. All components are jointly optimized with differentiated learning rates: 1×10⁻⁵ for the point cloud encoder, 5×10⁻⁵ for projection layers, 1×10⁻⁵ for the LLM, and 1×10⁻⁴ for the mask decoder. The mask loss weight λₘₐₛₖ=1.0.

    4.2. Evaluation on Full-Shape Segmentation

    We first evaluate the central capability of PartLLM, i.e., decomposing a complete 3D shape into parts. We study this capability in two settings. Category-agnostic full-shape segmentation evaluates whether a method can predict the part structure of the whole shape without predicting the semantic label. Semantic full-shape segmentation further evaluates whether the method can produce a complete decomposition with meaningful part labels.

    4.2.1. Category-Agnostic Full-Shape Segmentation

    This protocol measures how well a method can recover the ground-truth part structure under its best operating granularity. We compare with PartField [(Liu et al., 2025)], P3-SAM [(Ma et al., 2025)], PartSAM [(Zhu et al., 2026)], SAMPart3D [(Yang et al., 2024)], and SegviGen [(Li et al., 2026)]. Following the evaluation protocol of PartField [(Liu et al., 2025)] and PartSAM [(Zhu et al., 2026)], we evaluate each method using decompositions generated at multiple candidate granularities. For PartLLM, we use the general, coarse, and fine full-shape prompts defined in Table 2 under a fixed random seed. We do not use number-controlled prompts in this evaluation and therefore do not provide the ground-truth part count at test time. For PartField, we use clustering results with the number of clusters ranging from 1 to 20. For PartSAM and P3-SAM, we adjust their post-processing parameters to obtain three sets of masks at different granularities. SegviGen does not support explicit multi-granularity control, so we sample three outputs using different random seeds. Each ground-truth part mask is then matched to the predicted mask with the highest IoU across all granularities, and we report the average of these best-matched IoU values.

    Results.

    Table 3 reports the quantitative results. PartLLM consistently outperforms all baselines across the evaluated benchmarks. The gains are especially large on 3DCoMPaT200, where PartLLM improves over the strongest baseline by 34.5 mIoU at the coarse level and 32.0 mIoU at the fine level. Fig. 5 shows qualitative comparisons. Existing methods often produce decompositions with unstable granularity: they may merge distinct functional parts, split a single coherent part into fragments, or miss small structures. In particular, promptable methods such as PartSAM and P3-SAM can recover many local regions, but their over-segmented masks are not associated with semantic part identities and are therefore not always meaningful as object parts. PartLLM produces more complete and coherent full-shape segmentations, with part boundaries that better align with the underlying object structure. Fig. 6 further shows examples on AI-generated meshes, where PartLLM produces plausible part decompositions for outputs from different generation paradigms, including dense meshes produced by geometry-based generative models and low-poly meshes produced by autoregressive topology generative models.

    We attribute these advantages to two properties of our formulation. First, autoregressive generation predicts parts as a coupled decomposition rather than as independent regions, which leads to more coherent full-shape segmentations. Second, granularity control is built into the generation process itself, so the model can produce decompositions that remain consistent with the requested level of detail. Fig. 7 further shows that the same interface also supports prompt-based number control: as the requested part count increases, the model produces progressively finer yet still semantically coherent decompositions.

    4.2.2. Semantic Full-Shape Segmentation

    Beyond category-agnostic mask quality, this setting further evaluates whether the predicted full-shape parts are assigned correct semantic labels. Existing open-world part segmentation methods do not directly support this setting, since they either produce category-agnostic masks or require queried part names. We therefore construct two semantic baselines by pairing category-agnostic full-shape segmentation methods with an MLLM-based naming stage. Specifically, we take the masks generated by PartSAM and P3-SAM, render each predicted mask as a highlighted region on the input shape, and ask an MLLM [(Bai et al., 2025)] to predict the semantic part name of the highlighted region. This yields PartSAM+MLLM and P3-SAM+MLLM, which add semantic labels to category-agnostic full-shape segmentations. To evaluate both geometry and semantics, we report semantic-aware mIoU (SA-mIoU). Let G and Ĝ denote the ground-truth and predicted part sets, where each part is represented by a mask and a semantic label. We define SA-mIoU as

    (8)

    SA-mIoU=(1)/(|G|)∑_(M,y)∈G\max_(M̂,ŷ)∈ĜIₛₑₘ(y,ŷ) IoU(M,M̂).

    Because part names may be ambiguous, we use an LLM-based matcher to decide the semantic match indicator Iₛₑₘ. The matcher is given the object context and the two part names, and determines whether the predicted name should be considered a correct match to the ground-truth name. Specifically, we use GPT-5.5 through the OpenAI API as the semantic matcher, which is independent of the Qwen3-VL backbone used by PartLLM. We use the following prompt:

    For a 3D object of category “{object_category}”, determine whether the predicted part name “{pred_name}” and the ground-truth part name “{gt_name}” are semantically equivalent part names. Answer only “yes” or “no”.

    This metric penalizes both geometric mismatch and semantic mislabeling: a mask receives credit only when it overlaps the target part and is assigned a compatible semantic name.

    Results.

    Table 4 reports the results. PartLLM obtains the highest mask mIoU and SA-mIoU in all three settings. More importantly, its performance drops much less when moving from mask-only mIoU to SA-mIoU. The two-stage baselines drop by 17.5–23.6 points after semantic matching, indicating that their masks are often not aligned with semantically meaningful part identities even when they overlap reasonable geometric regions. In contrast, PartLLM drops by only 11.1–14.2 points, suggesting that its predicted regions are already tied to the part names generated by the model. This supports our formulation: full-shape part segmentation should predict masks and semantics together, so that the output decomposition is not only geometrically accurate but also semantically meaningful.

    4.3. Evaluation on Text-Guided Part Segmentation

    This task evaluates whether a model can segment the requested parts in a 3D shape given queried part names. For this task, the input to PartLLM is a set of queried part names, and the model outputs masks for the requested parts. We compare our method with three state-of-the-art methods: Find3D [(Ma et al., 2024)], PatchAlign3D [(Hadgi et al., 2026)], and CoSMo3D [(Jin et al., 2026)]. For quantitative evaluation, we feed all ground-truth part names to the model at once and compute metrics from the corresponding output masks. We report category-averaged mIoU as the evaluation metric.

    Results.

    Table 5 summarizes the results. PartLLM outperforms all baselines on every benchmark by a large margin. The gains are particularly striking on PartNeXt (+40.8 over CoSMo3D) and 3DCoMPaT200 (+37.3 and +53.9 at coarse and fine granularities). Fig. 8 shows qualitative results. The first three rows query all parts of the object simultaneously, and the last two rows query only a subset. Baselines often produce fragmented or incomplete masks, while PartLLM produces consistently accurate masks with sharp boundaries in both cases. Non-queried regions are cleanly absorbed by the <|BG|> query (shown in gray), demonstrating that the proposed decoding strategy produces mutually exclusive masks with precise boundaries regardless of how many parts are queried. We attribute these advantages to the formulation of PartLLM. Existing methods treat each queried part name as an independent text-to-geometry matching problem, making them sensitive to ambiguous or compositional names whose interpretation depends on object context and on the other queried parts. PartLLM instead predicts all requested parts within a single semantic decomposition, so each mask is inferred jointly with the others and with the overall shape. This leads to more accurate part disambiguation, cleaner exclusion of non-queried regions, and more mutually consistent masks.

    4.4. Evaluation on Interactive Part Segmentation

    Interactive part segmentation evaluates whether a model can segment the target part indicated by sparse clicks. Following the experimental protocol of previous works [(Zhou et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026)], we evaluate with multi-round interactions and report mIoU after each round. For each ground-truth mask, the first point is sampled from its central region; subsequent points are iteratively selected from the error regions between the predicted mask and the ground truth. For the first click, the input prompt is “Please segment the part at (x, y, z) in ,” and the model outputs the corresponding part mask; for later clicks, the current mask is encoded as point colors in , and the prompt provides an include/exclude corrective point at (x, y, z) to produce a refined mask. We compare with Point-SAM [(Zhou et al., 2025)], P3-SAM [(Ma et al., 2025)], S2AM3D [(Su et al., 2025)], PartSAM [(Zhu et al., 2026)], and SegViGen [(Li et al., 2026)]. Point-SAM, PartSAM, and SegViGen are evaluated with the multi-round protocol; for the remaining baselines, we report the available one-click results.

    Results.

    Table 6 reports the quantitative results. PartLLM achieves the best mIoU on every reported dataset and at every interaction round. With only one click, it improves over the strongest baseline by up to 10.1 mIoU points; after seven clicks, the margin reaches up to 18.5 mIoU among methods with multi-round outputs. These gains show that PartLLM can infer the complete target part from a sparse prompt rather than treating the click as only a local geometric seed, and can use corrective prompts to refine the mask while preserving the semantic extent of the target part. Fig. 9 shows qualitative one-click comparisons. Given the same prompt point, baselines often either capture only a local region around the click or leak into adjacent structures with similar geometry. PartLLM instead recovers complete parts with cleaner boundaries, including thin or spatially extended structures where local geometric cues alone are ambiguous. These results suggest that the click is more effective when interpreted as part of a semantic decomposition rather than as an isolated geometric seed. This helps PartLLM separate the target part from neighboring regions with similar local geometry.

    4.5. Evaluation on Unseen Real-World Scans

    To evaluate generalization beyond synthetic assets, we conduct additional experiments on two benchmarks containing unseen real-world scans. FAUST contains human scans with part annotations adopted from SATR [(Abdelreheem et al., 2023)], while AKBSeg contains selected articulated-part annotations on scanned AKB-48 objects [(Liu et al., 2022)]. We evaluate category-agnostic full-shape segmentation on FAUST against PartSAM [(Zhu et al., 2026)], P3-SAM [(Ma et al., 2025)], and SegviGen [(Li et al., 2026)]. We further evaluate text-guided segmentation on both benchmarks against PartSLIP [(Liu et al., 2023)], ZeroPS [(Xue et al., 2025)], SATR [(Abdelreheem et al., 2023)], and PatchAlign3D [(Hadgi et al., 2026)]. As shown in Tables 7 and 8, PartLLM achieves the best performance in every setting. Fig. 10 further presents results on scans with sensor noise, partial geometry, and surface irregularities. PartLLM still produces coherent segmentation results despite these capture artifacts.

    4.6. Ablation and Analysis

    4.6.1. Method Ablations

    Table 9 evaluates the main design choices of PartLLM. The last two columns further report full-shape mask mIoU on PartObjaverse-Tiny and text-guided mIoU on PartNet-E. We test the decomposition-aware decoder by replacing it with an independent binary mask predictor and removing softmax competition among the part and background queries. This variant examines whether decomposition-aware point assignment provides benefits beyond SAM-style per-query mask prediction. As shown in the table, while this modification causes only marginal performance drops on text-guided and interactive segmentation, it substantially reduces full-shape mask mIoU and SA-mIoU. The result suggests that independent binary decoding can still handle a small number of prompted targets, but it is less suitable for complete shape decomposition, where all generated parts must compete for points under a globally consistent assignment. Fig. 11 further illustrates this effect qualitatively: independent decoding tends to produce ambiguous boundaries near adjacent parts, whereas the decomposition-aware decoder separates parts with sharper boundaries.

    We next ablate the information encoded in each part hypothesis. As shown in the table, removing the coarse 3D location leads to the largest degradation in most settings, indicating that semantic labels alone are insufficient for localizing parts within complex shapes. Furthermore, removing the semantic label also consistently harms all evaluable metrics, especially text-guided segmentation, because the model no longer receives direct supervision to align part names with their corresponding geometry. This degradation is naturally less pronounced in interactive segmentation, where the input click intrinsically serves as a strong spatial anchor. Overall, these results indicate that PartLLM benefits from generating part hypotheses that are both semantically grounded and spatially localized, and from resolving them through a decomposition-aware decoder.

    4.6.2. Robustness to Rotation

    To evaluate sensitivity to object orientation, we apply random rotations around all three axes at test time and compare performance under random rotations with that under the canonical orientation. As shown in Table 10, random rotations result in negligible performance degradation in both settings. PartLLM also maintains clear margins over PartSAM after rotation, indicating that its performance is not tied to a canonical object orientation.

    4.6.3. Robustness to Probabilistic Sampling

    PartLLM uses probabilistic autoregressive sampling, so different random seeds may produce different part-hypothesis sequences. In the main experiments, we use fixed sampling parameters and a fixed random seed for all reported comparisons. To assess sensitivity to the sampling seed, we repeat full-shape inference on PartObjaverse-Tiny using ten random seeds. PartLLM obtains 78.5±2.2 mIoU (mean ± standard deviation), close to the reported result, indicating stable performance across random seeds.

    4.6.4. Robustness to Prompt Variations

    We first examine whether text-guided segmentation requires the complete set of part names as input. Table 11 compares the standard all-part setting with a single-part setting in which only one target name is queried. Performance remains comparable across all benchmarks, showing that PartLLM can segment individual queried parts without requiring the full part vocabulary. We further test prompt paraphrases for full-shape segmentation on PartObjaverse-Tiny. Replacing “main parts” with “coarse structures” and “detailed parts” with “fine-grained components” yields 76.2 mIoU, compared with 78.8 using the default templates. This small difference indicates that the prompt templates are default formulations rather than strict input formats. Overall, these results demonstrate that PartLLM is robust to prompt variations and does not rely on a specific prompt formulation.

    4.6.5. Data Composition Ablations

    Table 12 studies the effect of multi-task data integration in our unified part segmentation framework. Under the same architecture and training objective, we progressively add training data from the four supervision sources. This ablation evaluates whether each data source only benefits its matched setting or transfers to other part segmentation tasks.

    Starting from full-shape segmentation data, we sequentially add text-guided data, interactive data, and category-agnostic geometry data. As shown in the table, adding text-guided data not only enables text-guided evaluation but also improves full-shape mask mIoU from 56.2 to 62.7 and SA-mIoU from 48.3 to 58.5, indicating that explicit part-name supervision promotes more semantically meaningful decompositions. Adding interactive data further improves both text-guided and full-shape segmentation. This suggests that point-conditioned supervision strengthens part localization and transfers to non-interactive settings. Finally, adding category-agnostic training data improves all metrics, with especially large gains on full-shape segmentation and interactive segmentation. Although these data do not provide semantic part names, they supply additional geometric decomposition supervision, improving the model’s boundary and shape priors. These trends support the motivation of our unified formulation: heterogeneous task data can reinforce a shared representation of 3D parts rather than merely improving performance on their corresponding tasks.

    4.6.6. Scaling Analysis

    Fig. 12 evaluates how PartLLM scales with the volume of unified training data. The scaling curve shows consistent gains across all three evaluation settings. Notably, scaling up solely the semantic part data yields steady improvements across all tasks, indicating that our unified formulation effectively capitalizes on both task diversity and expanded semantic supervision. Furthermore, holding the semantic data constant and introducing category-agnostic part decomposition data [(Hunyuan3D et al., 2026)] yields further performance boosts across the board. These gains are particularly pronounced in full-shape and interactive segmentation, where the influx of geometric decomposition examples directly refines boundary delineation and part-extent localization. Interestingly, text-guided segmentation also exhibits marginal improvements, suggesting that enhanced geometric part priors positively transfer to semantic understanding, even in the absence of explicit semantic labels in the added data. This result supports our data scaling argument: heterogeneous part data can be absorbed by the same formulation and converted into broadly useful 3D part understanding.

    4.6.7. Efficiency Analysis

    We report the running time comparison in Table 13. All runtime measurements in Table 13 are obtained on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU. While PartLLM relies on an autoregressive generation paradigm, modern LLM inference is highly optimized and benefits from inference acceleration frameworks [(Kwon et al., 2023)]. In practice, for typical 3D objects with a moderate number of semantic parts, PartLLM achieves inference efficiency competitive with or even superior to that of prior baselines, while attaining substantially higher full-shape segmentation accuracy. Although generation latency naturally scales with the requested part count, our framework maintains a favorable trade-off between computational efficiency and semantic segmentation quality.

    4.7. Application

    PartLLM exposes its unified 3D part understanding through a semantic decomposition interface, enabling practical use beyond standard benchmark settings. PartLLM generalizes to real-world scans, as demonstrated in Sec. 4.5, and supports part-aware editing, where the predicted masks serve as controllable handles for modifying 3D assets. Fig. 13 shows two editing workflows enabled by this interface. A target part can be localized either from an interactive click or from a semantic text query, after which the predicted mask is reused as a controllable editing region. This makes the output immediately actionable: the same part handle can support material replacement as well as structural edits that modify the part geometry.

    4.8. Limitations and Future Work

    As shown in Fig. 14, a representative failure mode arises when the object category is ambiguous from geometry alone. In such cases, PartLLM may produce a decomposition that is internally coherent but organized under the wrong semantic prior. For instance, misclassifying a router as a bed causes the model to hallucinate bed-associated sub-structures over the router’s topology. Providing the object category as an additional prompt cue can disambiguate the prediction and recover the correct part decomposition, including the router body and antennas. This suggests that stronger object-level context is important for precise semantic part understanding. Future work will explore integrating additional modalities, such as rendered images or multi-view visual features, to provide stronger category evidence. Furthermore, incorporating chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning could stabilize high-level semantic decisions prior to executing dense mask predictions.

    5. Conclusion

    We presented PartLLM, a unified framework that reformulates 3D part segmentation as autoregressive semantic decomposition and realizes this formulation through a multimodal large language model. By using language as the interface for part decomposition and mask prediction, PartLLM supports open-vocabulary and granularity-controllable part understanding within a single generate-and-ground pipeline. Experiments show that this formulation does more than integrate heterogeneous supervision: it turns task and data diversity into a new scaling axis for 3D part understanding, consistently outperforming strong task-specific baselines as training data expands. More broadly, our results suggest a path beyond task-specific 3D segmentation models toward a foundation model paradigm for part-level understanding, where parts serve as a general semantic and operational interface for open-world 3D assets.

item.title: SceneAE：把「3D 空间上下文」绑进潜空间的世界模型 ｜ SceneAE：绑定3D空间上下文的世界模型
item.description:
一句话：潜空间绑到稀疏点云上，同一份表示既能生成场景，也能查询任意视角。

要点：

  • 用 DepthAnythingV3 提深度与特征，先建全局点云再下采样；稀疏点经 deformable cross attention 聚合周围视觉特征，得到「带 3D 位置 + 区域纹理」的潜变量。
  • 解码按相机投影把潜变量 splat 到目标平面，再用 self/cross attention 查询出 RGBD，实现与视角无关的新视角合成。
  • 生成侧做几何/纹理解耦：stage1 由相机轨迹生成未来几何点云，stage2 用点云 (x,y,z) 的 3D RoPE 生成纹理，替掉 Wan 原本的 (u,v,t) RoPE。

为什么值得看：视频生成模型「只能沿一条相机轨迹看」是不可漫游的根因。这篇把潜空间绑到 3D 空间上下文上，是理解 Atlas / Gen3C 这一路线取舍的一手说明，也坦白讲了保真度与数据规模的局限。

中文摘要：作者介绍自己组的工作 SceneAE：用绑定 3D 空间上下文的潜空间表示，同时支持场景生成与场景重建。作者先论证视频生成模型还不是世界模型——它们本质上描述的是世界的一段轨迹观察，轨迹之外的视角无法查询，同一场景的另一条轨迹在几何上可能不一致，所以很多世界模型要外挂 3D memory 才能保证重访一致。SceneAE 的做法是把表示绑到 3D 上：用几何基础模型提深度与特征，构建并下采样全局点云，稀疏点通过 deformable cross attention 聚合周围视觉特征，得到带位置与区域纹理的潜变量；解码时按相机投影把潜变量 splat 到目标平面，再用注意力查询出 RGBD。生成侧利用几何与纹理解耦，stage1 生成未来几何点云，stage2 以点云 xyz 的 3D RoPE 指导内容生成，几何一致性更好。作者也说明局限：模型约 1B、数据仅 RE10K/DL3DV 与部分 ScanNet，保真度受解码渲染能力限制，且缺少环视数据导致「回头走」的漫游会失败。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：知乎·不知道起啥名字（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-22

作者系该工作作者，本文为方法自述（延伸阅读节选）。

为什么视频生成模型还不是世界模型

视频生成模型（Wan 系列、CogVideoX、MiniMax-H3）已经能产生非常逼真的画面，但它们描述的本质上是对世界的一段轨迹观察，而不是对当前世界的一个直接表示。对某个场景，它们只能输出一条连续的相机轨迹，轨迹之外的视角无法查询；同一场景的另一条轨迹渲染在几何结构上可能不一致，也可能描述不同的世界，于是无法实现真正的世界漫游。

因此「生成未知世界」与「对已有世界做新视角合成」的统一能力，是世界模型很重要的一环，可以称为「重建生成的一体化」。这也是很多世界模型要外挂一个 3D memory（Gen3C、Voyager、Mirage 等）来保证现在渲染和以前渲染的是同一个世界的原因，但那种做法只能保证历史重访的一致性。

可查询的潜空间 3D 表征

SceneAE 先构建一种潜空间 3D 表征：

  • 对输入视频用 DepthAnythingV3 这类几何基础模型提取每帧的深度图与特征图；
  • 根据所有帧深度构建全局点云并下采样得到稀疏点云；
  • 把稀疏点云与各帧特征图输入 Encoder，点云中每个点通过多层 deformable cross attention 聚合其位置周围的视觉特征；
  • 得到一个潜空间点云，每个点带位置与对应区域的纹理特征。

这种表征有三个好处：与视角无关（可以像 3DGS 那样支持新视角合成），稀疏（点云已去除多帧重叠，压缩率高于 Wan VAE），以及带空间上下文（每个潜变量都有 3D 位置，几何先验更强，对几何一致性与相机可控性有帮助）。

解码时因为稀疏，无法像 3DGS 那样直接投影渲染，但借鉴了其思路：对任意渲染视角，按相机投影关系把每个潜变量投到目标平面，平面上每个像素根据周围潜变量初始化特征，再以查询方式通过多层 self attention 与平面上的潜变量做 cross attention（Splat Cross Attn），解码出对应 RGBD。

作者也承认：3D 表征在输入重构的保真度上必然弱于 2D 表征，这也是这条路最大的问题；但考虑到它额外带来的新视角合成能力，以及受数据与算力规模限制，这条路仍值得继续探索。

几何纹理解耦的生成范式

最朴素的生成范式是把位置与内容潜变量拼起来过 DiT，但那样没有充分利用解耦的优势。作者的切入点是相机控制：相机表征的是几何变换，而 DiT 内部特征表征纹理信息，两者天然存在鸿沟，所以直接控制不够自然。

因此他们把表征天然分成的「位置几何」和「纹理内容」用在两条路径上：stage1 根据参考帧点云与相机轨迹生成未来场景的几何点云，作为 3D 布局影响后续纹理生成；stage2 再以几何点云构造 3D RoPE，告诉每个潜变量它负责空间中哪个物体的纹理。作者指出 Wan 自带的是 (u,v,t) 构成的 3D RoPE，同一物体在不同帧上的 (u,v,t) 不同，几何一致性较差；换成点云 (x,y,z) 的 3D RoPE 后，模型知道自己在渲染哪个空间位置的内容，与视角无关，一致性明显提升。

局限

  • 训练规模小：模型约 1B，为与同期工作公平对比；数据只用 RE10K、DL3DV 与部分 ScanNet。
  • 保真度：最限制生成性能的是最后解码阶段的渲染能力。
  • 世界漫游：训练数据基本是前向或单个转弯、没有环视，模型缺少补全各方向的能力，走过之后物体的背面没有生成，因此「回头走」的轨迹会失败。
  • 动态物体：固定 3D 坐标对动态物体不友好，是后续要扩展的方向。

item.title: 把 AI 生成的模型放进浏览器 3D 世界：九步流程与三个关键数字 ｜ AI 生成的模型怎么放进 3D 虚拟世界
item.description:
一句话：生成不是瓶颈，资产处理才是：场景资产集从 3.1GB 压到 390MB，服务端不渲染所以不需要 GPU。

要点：

  • 贴图重新压缩后单模型体积可降 68%–92%，整个场景资产集从 3.1GB 降到 390MB——决定用户等待时长的是资产总量，不是生成质量。
  • 服务端不做任何渲染，只发数据与静态资源，因此不需要 GPU，一台普通 VPS 够用，成本主要在资产存储与带宽。
  • 编辑端与访问端是两套界面、一份世界数据；多场景共享同一份世界、按范围加载，避免切场景时内存翻倍。

为什么值得看：最有价值的是那句边界：模型可以是 AI 生成的，世界仍然是人摆的。判断一个「AI 造世界」演示值不值得看，先看它有没有把资产预算与持久化这两件事做完。

中文摘要：作者用一座「从一张图生成、最后能在浏览器里走进去」的寺庙，串起 AI 资产进入实时 3D 世界的完整流程，并强调真正的瓶颈不在生成而在生成之后的资产处理。核心判断有两处：一是要看生成结果能否从多个角度都成立（屋顶看着对、做成模型可能缺内壁），二是面数与贴图尺寸必须按实时场景的标准重做——贴图重压后单模型可减少 68%–92%，整个场景资产集能从 3.1GB 降到 390MB。架构上，服务端只发数据与静态资源、不做任何渲染，因此不需要 GPU，普通 VPS 即可承载；编辑端与管理端分离，但共用一份世界数据，改动写回后访问端读到的就是新值。文章也明确划出边界：AI 现在能生成单个模型，但把几百个模型摆成空间上合理、走进去不别扭的世界，仍需人工完成布局与动线设计。文中提到的自部署系统采用订阅许可，源码开放但非开源软件。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：知乎·大志（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-22

原文为某自部署 3D 世界系统的落地流程说明（延伸阅读节选）。

一个反直觉的结论

一条从图到模型再到浏览器场景的流程里，真正花时间的是模型生成之后的资产处理，不是生成本身。

3D 场景在浏览器里卡顿，多数时候原因不在渲染管线，而在两件事：要让浏览器下载多少字节，以及每帧要提交多少次 draw call。这两件事和「模型生成得好不好看」没有关系。一个面数漂亮、材质精致的模型，贴图可能有几十 MB，在移动网络上光下载就要十几秒，这十几秒里用户看到的是空白页，渲染再快也没有意义。

九步流程与关键判断

  1. 生成：从提示词到图片。门槛不高，关键是判断这张图能不能落成结构完整的 3D 模型——看图要看「从多个角度是否都成立」，而不是「像不像」。
  2. 图片到模型：图片生成的模型多边形通常过量。实时场景能用的模型和展示用的模型，差的是面数、贴图尺寸、有没有多余内部空腔。贴图重压后单模型体积可减少 68%–92%，整个场景资产集可从 3.1GB 降到 390MB。
  3. 导入：模型文件被登记进世界的资产表，与场景数据建立引用关系，编辑端与访问端读同一份世界数据。模型进入资产库 ≠ 模型被放进场景，后者才涉及位置、朝向、碰撞与性能预算。
  4. 部署：自部署。服务端不做任何渲染，只负责发送数据与静态资源，因此不需要 GPU，一台普通 VPS 就能承载，真正占资源的是资产存储与带宽。这直接决定了成本结构与数据归属。
  5. 编辑端：位置、大小、朝向在同一界面调整；关键是改动必须写回世界数据，否则编辑器只是预览器。
  6. 保存并换到访问端：编辑端与访问端是两套界面、一份数据；权限分离做得不彻底，很容易退化成两套互不同步的数据。
  7. 走进世界：验收点——在编辑器里摆的东西真实存在于那个空间，位置、比例与地形关系在走进去之后依然成立。
  8. 多场景：多场景不等于多份世界。若切场景靠加载新世界，体验会中断、内存翻倍；共享同一份世界按范围加载，加载时间与内存才可控。
  9. 管理端：改一次、下次还是这样。修改可持久化，世界才是活的；做不到这一点的演示本质上只是模型查看器。

边界

让 AI 自己搭建一整个世界，目前尚未实现：生成单个模型已可行，但把几百个模型摆成空间上说得通、走进去不别扭的世界，涉及布局逻辑、动线设计、尺度一致性，这部分仍需人来做。所以这类演示里，模型是 AI 生成的，世界是人摆放的。

中文摘要：作者用一座「从一张图生成、最后能在浏览器里走进去」的寺庙，串起 AI 资产进入实时 3D 世界的完整流程，并强调真正的瓶颈不在生成而在生成之后的资产处理。核心判断有两处：一是要看生成结果能否从多个角度都成立（屋顶看着对、做成模型可能缺内壁），二是面数与贴图尺寸必须按实时场景的标准重做——贴图重压后单模型可减少 68%–92%，整个场景资产集能从 3.1GB 降到 390MB。架构上，服务端只发数据与静态资源、不做任何渲染，因此不需要 GPU，普通 VPS 即可承载；编辑端与管理端分离，但共用一份世界数据，改动写回后访问端读到的就是新值。文章也明确划出边界：AI 现在能生成单个模型，但把几百个模型摆成空间上合理、走进去不别扭的世界，仍需人工完成布局与动线设计。文中提到的自部署系统采用订阅许可，源码开放但非开源软件。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：知乎·大志（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-22

原文为某自部署 3D 世界系统的落地流程说明（延伸阅读节选）。

一个反直觉的结论

一条从图到模型再到浏览器场景的流程里，真正花时间的是模型生成之后的资产处理，不是生成本身。

3D 场景在浏览器里卡顿，多数时候原因不在渲染管线，而在两件事：要让浏览器下载多少字节，以及每帧要提交多少次 draw call。这两件事和「模型生成得好不好看」没有关系。一个面数漂亮、材质精致的模型，贴图可能有几十 MB，在移动网络上光下载就要十几秒，这十几秒里用户看到的是空白页，渲染再快也没有意义。

九步流程与关键判断

  1. 生成：从提示词到图片。门槛不高，关键是判断这张图能不能落成结构完整的 3D 模型——看图要看「从多个角度是否都成立」，而不是「像不像」。
  2. 图片到模型：图片生成的模型多边形通常过量。实时场景能用的模型和展示用的模型，差的是面数、贴图尺寸、有没有多余内部空腔。贴图重压后单模型体积可减少 68%–92%，整个场景资产集可从 3.1GB 降到 390MB。
  3. 导入：模型文件被登记进世界的资产表，与场景数据建立引用关系，编辑端与访问端读同一份世界数据。模型进入资产库 ≠ 模型被放进场景，后者才涉及位置、朝向、碰撞与性能预算。
  4. 部署：自部署。服务端不做任何渲染，只负责发送数据与静态资源，因此不需要 GPU，一台普通 VPS 就能承载，真正占资源的是资产存储与带宽。这直接决定了成本结构与数据归属。
  5. 编辑端：位置、大小、朝向在同一界面调整；关键是改动必须写回世界数据，否则编辑器只是预览器。
  6. 保存并换到访问端：编辑端与访问端是两套界面、一份数据；权限分离做得不彻底，很容易退化成两套互不同步的数据。
  7. 走进世界：验收点——在编辑器里摆的东西真实存在于那个空间，位置、比例与地形关系在走进去之后依然成立。
  8. 多场景：多场景不等于多份世界。若切场景靠加载新世界，体验会中断、内存翻倍；共享同一份世界按范围加载，加载时间与内存才可控。
  9. 管理端：改一次、下次还是这样。修改可持久化，世界才是活的；做不到这一点的演示本质上只是模型查看器。

边界

让 AI 自己搭建一整个世界，目前尚未实现：生成单个模型已可行，但把几百个模型摆成空间上说得通、走进去不别扭的世界，涉及布局逻辑、动线设计、尺度一致性，这部分仍需人来做。所以这类演示里，模型是 AI 生成的，世界是人摆放的。

item.title: Capcom 要把 RE 引擎改成「生成式 AI 引擎」？多数媒体读错了 ｜ Capcom's New AI Venture Gets Lost in Translation
item.description:
一句话：AI and Games 复盘 Capcom Open Conference RE:2026 的表述如何被翻译与转述带偏。

要点：

  • RE 引擎（REach for the moon Engine）是 MT Framework 的后继，自《生化危机 7》（2017）起用于生产，并非「为生成式 AI 新建的引擎」。
  • 作者认为争议既来自对游戏里 AI 如何工作的普遍误解，也来自跨语言转述的失真。
  • 同期的行业信号：PS5 基础款通过 QSSR 获得 AI 超分，Google 公布 Playground（自家的 AI 游戏引擎创作者平台）。

为什么值得看：做引擎的人最容易被这类标题带节奏。这篇的价值是把「引擎要重做」和「工具链里加 AI 辅助」区分开，顺便给了几条同周的行业动态。

中文摘要：这是 AI and Games 的一期周报，主线是澄清 Capcom 在自家技术大会 Capcom Open Conference RE:2026 上关于 RE 引擎未来的表述被大量游戏媒体与社媒误读的事件。作者指出，RE 引擎（全称 REach for the moon Engine，并非 Resident Evil）是 MT Framework 的后继，自 2017 年《生化危机 7》起就用于生产，外界「要把引擎变成生成式 AI 游戏专用系统」的说法站不住；这类误解一方面来自对游戏里 AI 实际如何工作的普遍不了解，另一方面来自翻译与转述的失真。周报还列了几条同期动态：SEGA 强调对创作环节使用 AI 非常谨慎、动视提到作弊已成 85 亿美元产业且 AI 在推波助澜、基础款 PS5 通过 QSSR 获得 AI 超分、Micron 因内存涨价创纪录利润、Google 公布 Playground（自家的 AI 游戏引擎创作者平台），以及 AI and Games Conference 的几场相关演讲预告。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：AI and Games（English）

原文发布：2026-10-07

本期推送：2026-10-22

Hello and welcome to this week’s edition of AI and Games. I’m feeling pretty under the weather this week sadly as some plague has descended upon our house somehow.

This week will be a little shorter than usual given I am propped up on a variety of drugs but still wanted to get something out to you. With a focus on the Capcom’s comments last week on their planned updates to their proprietary RE engine that were misrepresented by a lot of the gaming press and social media.

Follow AI and Games on:BlueSky | YouTube | LinkedIn | TikTok

Couple of quick announcements for you, including another Tommy sighting in the wild next week. Provided I shake off this horrid cough…

Very excited to say that this time next week myself and fellow AI and Games Conference founders Duygu Cakmak and Matthias Siemonsmeier will be at Game Republic New Horizons! Running from 14th-16th October in sunny Middlesborough, we’re doing something we’ve never actually tried before: speaking together on stage! We promise a fun panel as we dig into the current state of AI in the games industry in 2026. Expect some strong opinions, and a friendly bit of banter among friends.

Oh good grief we’re only five weeks out: five weeks! It’s all systems go here at AI and Games HQ as myself, Shraddha, Sally, and the rest of the team are all chipping away at the 101 things we need to do to get ready for this years event. Don’t forget to grab your tickets if you haven’t already. But for now, here’s more talk announcements!

Cheat Codes and Compliance Codes
The Legal Playbook for AI and Games in 2026
Rupam Davé / Lewis Silkin

We’re pleased to welcome back Rupam Davé to talk once again about the ever-evolving legal landscape surrounding Machine Learning and Generative AI and its adoption in the video games industry. Rupam’s presentations have continued to prove popular each year at the conference, and he now holds the record as the longest-serving speaker at the AI and Games Conference having presented in 2024 and 2025.

From Multiplayer to Single Player: Shipping Generative AI Temps in Dimensional Double Shift
Brian Tanner and Alex Kearney / Artificial Agency

Dimensional Double Shift is a co-op VR title released for the Meta Quest where players have to work together and coordinate around complex tasks. However, what would the circumstances need to look like for this to ship AI teammates? Alex and Brian from Artificial Agency dig into how this was achieved using small-scale Generative AI agents in the cloud, albeit capped to operate within a hard two-second window. With insight into how to operate three concurrent agents all while ensuring they run at significantly smaller inference costs than your typical GenAI models.

Perception and reaction systems for large amounts of NPCs
Alejandro Moya / Grip Studios

Last but most certainly not least for this week’s announcements we welcome Alejandro Moya from Grip Studios who in recent years have been co-developers on titles such as Subnautica, Mafia: The Old Country, and Marvel’s Midnight Suns.Moya will be sharing their insights into building perception systems for large numbers of NPCs in ways that scale in practical and sensible ways. Something of a spiritual sequel to the fantastic perception talk from Vadim Petrov of Warhorse Studios in 2025.

Some headlines in brief:

  • SEGA is insistent that they’re being “very cautious” around the use of AI in creative works.

  • Call of Duty creators Activision discuss how cheating is now an $8.5 billion industry and AI is certainly contributing to that issue. A point we need to discuss on our case study series in the future.

  • Base PS5’s are now getting their own version of AI upscaling courtesy of Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR) rolling out for Wolverineand Ghost of Yotei.

  • Micron celebrates higher prices for customers and record profits as RAM supply expected to worsen in 2027.

  • Google announces their new Playground platform, essentially their own AI game engine creator.

    • Thanks for reading AI and Games! This post is public so feel free to share it.

    Share

    Last week was Capcom’s own in-house tech conference Capcom Open Conference RE: 2026, and a big part of that event was discussions around the future of the RE engine. However, while the games industry has been enthralled by their releases in recent years ranging from Resident Evil: Requiemto Street Fighter 6, Pragmata, Monster Hunter: Wilds and more recently Onimusha: Way of the Sword, folks were up in arms about the suggestion that they’re transforming the engine into a system built for Generative AI games. An issue that stemmed both from again misunderstandings of how AI works in games, but also a fundamental issue of translation.

    The ‘REach for the moon’ Engine - that’s right kids, it doesn’t stand for Resident Evil - is the successor to the MT Framework and has been used in production since Resident Evil 7: Biohazardreleased in 2017. It’s since been used for virtually all of Capcom’s titles in recent years, including all of the titles mentioned above as well as the modern reboots of classic Resident Evilgames. During the conference there was a presentation by programmer Satoshi Ishida entitled “The Outlook and Future of the ‘REX’ Project”. REX is the codename given to the next generation version of the RE engine (dubbed ‘RE neXt Engine’) which has been in development since at least 2023.

    During the presentation Ishida gave a brief discussion of some of the major challenges faced by developers at the studio. Notably that many simple tasks can prove time consuming and onerous, and that the engine needs to become easier to use as the number of devs on a given project increases. Hence their solution is to integrate AI tooling into future workflows. The intention being to update the engine to allow for more effective integration of AI models for areas such as editor tools, development support, and quality assurance.

    This has led to the creation of new components to the RE engine, all of which integrating AI in some form or another. Note that none of these components are AI modules in themselves, but are described as potentially integrating AI models in their efforts to be more efficient. Now this all makes sense. Both given there are a variety of machine learning models already used in some aspects of game development, but there is also potential for them to integrate LLMs to support in specific tasks. Ishida gave some examples in the talk such as translating data from various file formats and syntaxes, to performant code generation based off visual editing workflows.

    While Capcom remain cagey about embracing Generative AI for assets, the integration of machine learning and potential generative models to support common tasks of the dev team sounds like a much more reasonable and sensible approach - even compared to some of the more egregious examples of public engines like Unreal Engine 6. This strikes me as a more sensible adoption of AI into workflows given it appears to be driven by their own experiences of actually shipping content with their engine.

    Now I first caught wind of this while on a short vacation and seeing the IGN story being bounced around with a lot of sensational rhetoric around this being how Capcom now embraces GenAI in their games. Though I really read this as far removed from such an assessment. What Ishida describes is changing parts of a workflow to now integrate AI tools to support an existing process, rather than merely supplant it - and the humans involved - with AI tooling.

    But perhaps the other key aspect of what drove this misunderstanding outside of the most folks lack of understanding of AI’s use in games, is a sentence in the report by GameBiz which when machine-translated into English reads like this:

    Ishida commented that these technological advancements will ultimately lead to the larger goal of evolving into an "AI-generation game engine."

    This appears to be where many a headline such as those by Eurogamer and IGN emerged from, but I think this has been misread as ‘an engine that generates games with AI’ rather than simply ‘an engine updated to reflect the current era of AI technologies’.

    This was later corroborated by folks more fluent in Japanese than I am. Notably John Linneman over at Digital Foundry who pointed out that the term ‘generation’ in this translation is in reference to an epoch. This is an ‘age of AI’ - a generation if you will - and not referring to the use of AI as a means to generate content. 

    Note: Eurogamer has since amended the story and removed the original social media post implying that the engine is focussed on AI-generation.

    So what this means in the future we’ll still waiting to see. But I do believe that this is a headline that’s been blown out of proportion once again as a result of a lack of understanding of AI integration. Though admittedly there was a language barrier this time around!

    Okay, yup… that’ll do. I need more drugs. Catch you next week!

    Discussion about this post

    No posts

    Ready for more?

item.title: Epic 用「vibe coding」重写了启动器，只为比 Steam 快 ｜ Epic throws shade at Steam, admits to vibe-coding the new Epic Games Launcher with AI
item.description:
一句话：Epic 官方承认新版启动器是 vibe coding 产出，主打开机比 Steam 快（约 5 秒）。

要点：

  • Epic 在社媒上直接说「我们 vibe coded 了 Epic Games Launcher，就为了比另一个更快」，并贴出与 Steam 的启动耗时对比。
  • 官方同时承认会有 bug，请用户用启动器内的反馈按钮上报，说明这条路线是在预览版里边发边修。
  • 背景是 Epic 近期在生成式 AI 上的连续表态（含此前对 AI 生成内容与商店策略的立场），以及 Fortnite 生态的 AI 化推进。

为什么值得看：这是一条工程组织层面的信号：AI 辅助编码已经进入大型客户端工具链，代价是「先上线再修」。做引擎/工具的人更该关注它的发布与质量流程，而不是当成八卦。

中文摘要：Eurogamer 报道，Epic Games 在生成式 AI 上没有收手：公司公开表示新版 Epic Games Launcher 是用「vibe coding」方式做出来的，目标就是「比另一个（Steam）更快」，并配了一张启动耗时对比图，称可快约 5 秒。Epic 在社媒原文里也承认「会有一些 bug」，请用户遇到问题就用启动器内的反馈按钮上报，等于把预览版当成公开测试渠道，边发边修。报道把这当作 Epic 近期一系列 AI 相关动作的延续：从对商店与 AI 生成内容的态度，到 Fortnite 生态里的 AI 功能推进。对工具与引擎团队来说，这条新闻的重点不是口水战，而是大型客户端软件已经开始用 AI 辅助编码重写，并把质量保证的压力转移到线上反馈循环。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：Eurogamer（English）

原文发布：2026-10-14

本期推送：2026-10-22

Epic Games isn't lifting its foot off the gen-AI pedal. The company behind Fortnite and Unreal Engine has now vibe-coded a new Epic Games Launcher in an attempt to outrun Steam, by far the most popular digital games marketplace on PC.

The Epic Games Launcher is the platform that grants players access to the Epic Games Store, their game libraries and a host of social features - and the app's newest version was prompted into existence with the use of generative AI, according to the company.

"We vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy," Epic tweeted alongside a graph (below) comparing how much faster the EGS Launcher is to boot than Steam (Five seconds!) "Is this bad boy faster? Yes. Will it have some bugs? Yes. Do we want to hear about them? Hell yes. When you find something that’s off, hit the 'Send Feedback' button in the Launcher so we can tackle on the road to release."

We vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy. Don't believe us? Test it out for yourself in Preview: https://t.co/pdtAeEIri4 https://t.co/aMxojUUVPV

— Epic Games Store (@EpicGames) October 14, 2026
To see this content please enable targeting cookies.

A follow-up blog post attempts to justify the gen-AI usage: "Programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that's way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look. The first release is light on features. Think of it as a speedboat and not a yacht!" (Is that more Valve shade I see?)

Vibe coding is a colloquial term often used to refer to code generated or prompted with gen-AI. Speaking to IGN, EGS' vice president and general manager Martin Keely acknowledged it's an "issue that's of high visibility" across the games industry at the moment - countless games have been recompiled and decompiled in recent weeks by vibe coders - but Keely reckons it's "made us more efficient and allowed a small team to rewrite the code base and be able to launch it faster across platforms."

This comes just a day after a Bloomberg report claimed Epic Games is fully embracing an "AI first" development pipeline, starting with a Marvel and Star Wars shooter that was internally delayed. Developers were allegedly told that "no more hand-written code" should be used while making the Disney crossover project from here on, and even art should be "generated with full AI workflows".

In an online post, CEO Tim Sweeney also suggested the gen-AI pivot could seep into Unreal Engine, the widely-used game development tool behind everything from Gears of War: E-Day to Final Fantasy 7 Revelation: "The aim isn't to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build more and better stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal."

The Epic Games Store has long struggled to pull the vast majority of PC players away from Valve's Steam platform. We'll see if a controversial AI spin can move the needle in any way.

item.title: Inworld Inference：为消费级 AI 应用重做的推理栈 ｜ Introducing Inworld Inference
item.description:
一句话：首 token 最快 7.8 倍、同硬件 1.8 倍吞吐、90% 提示命中缓存——算的是消费级应用的账。

要点：

  • 为每个开源模型单独做服务构建：新的注意力 kernel、小模型起草 + 全模型一次校验的实时解码、评测允许处降精度，以及把每一轮送回已持有上下文的服务器。
  • Gemma 4 26B 上首 token 比 OpenRouter 中位提供商快最多 7.8 倍，同硬件吞吐是 9 月的 1.8 倍；三个模型上输入价格在不训练用户数据的前提下最低。
  • 消费级场景的账本：每轮都要重发全部历史，提示长度是回复的 13–36 倍，一次交互会扇出到审核、记忆、排序等多个模型调用，而用户只付 5–20 美元/月甚至不付。

为什么值得看：游戏里的 NPC 对话是典型的消费级 AI 负载：延迟即留存、单价极低。它给出的成本结构（cache 命中率、提示/回复长度比、扇出次数）可以直接用来判断一套 NPC 运行时在商业上是否成立。

中文摘要：Inworld 发布 Inworld Inference，一个面向消费级 AI 应用的推理服务。作者的论证是：大模型厂商与多数推理服务商都在押注企业与编码场景，而消费级应用的需求正好相反——延迟就是收入，用户慢一次就退回按钮操作；每一轮都要重发全部历史，提示长度是回复的 13 到 36 倍；一次交互会扇出成审核、记忆、排序与回复等多个模型调用；而用户每月只付 5 到 20 美元甚至不付。因此他们不列上千个模型，而是对消费级应用会选的每个开源模型做单独的服务构建：新的注意力 kernel、小草稿模型先行 + 全模型一次校验的实时解码、在评测允许处使用更低精度权重，以及把每一轮路由回已经持有其上下文的服务器。官方数据：Gemma 4 26B 上首 token 比 OpenRouter 中位提供商快最多 7.8 倍，同硬件承载请求量是 9 月的 1.8 倍，最多 90% 的提示由缓存提供且缓存输入价格最多便宜 99%。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：Inworld AI（English）

原文发布：2026-10-14

本期推送：2026-10-22

Key resultsup to 7.8×faster first token than the median provider on OpenRouterup to 48%lower input price than the median provider, and the lowest of any that doesn't train on your data1.8×more requests served on the same hardware, while median time to first token improvesup to 90%of each prompt served from cache, at up to 99% off99.999%of requests completed without an error

AI's first wave was built for companies. Developers have felt it, and so have finance teams, but most people haven't yet seen AI change their lives. The bigger wave is built for people: a tutor on the commute, a coach mid-run, a language partner who waits for you to finish your sentence, someone to talk to after a hard day. Today only 2% of US households, and 3% of US consumers, spend anything on AI.[7] Consumer AI is where the internet was in 1995.

Building for people is a different engineering problem. In consumer AI, latency is revenue: when a reply is slow, people go back to tapping buttons. Every turn resends the whole history, so prompts run 13 to 36 times longer than replies. One interaction fans out into many model calls, from moderation and memory to ranking and the reply itself. People pay $5 to $20 a month, or nothing, so each of those calls has to cost almost nothing. And when a consumer app goes down for ten minutes, its users leave for another one, while an enterprise workflow just waits.

The big labs and most inference providers have doubled down on enterprise and coding. Consumer AI needs the opposite on every count. So we built Inworld Inference, the first inference service designed for consumer AI, and today it is open to every developer.

Rather than list thousands of models, we go deep on the open models consumer apps choose. Each one, from Gemma 4 to GLM, DeepSeek and MiMo, gets its own serving build: new attention kernels, realtime decoding where a small draft writes ahead and the full model checks it in one pass, lower-precision weights wherever the evals hold, and a router that sends every turn back to the server that already holds its context.

The same research gives lower latency, lower cost and higher reliability. On Gemma 4 26B, first tokens arrive up to 7.8 times faster than from the median provider on OpenRouter, and the same hardware serves 1.8 times the requests it did in September, with a faster median first token. Input prices are the lowest of any provider that doesn't train on your data, on three of the five models we feature. Up to 90% of each prompt is served from cache, and cached input costs up to 99% less. On GLM 5.3 Flash, 99.999% of more than 20 million requests in 30 days completed without an error. Every build ships only if it matches the eval scores of the build it replaces.

Consumer AI is all we do, so being good at this is existential for us. Almost every token we serve comes from an app people use in their own lives, tens of trillions of tokens a month, 25 times what we served in March. Use the hosted models with no rate limits and a service tier per request, route across them with automatic failover, or bring your own model for a dedicated deployment.

01Consumer vs. enterprise inference

For an enterprise task that replaces expensive manual work, a single result can justify a lot of compute, and the result can wait. A consumer app has to deliver interaction after interaction inside one subscription or one free session, while a person waits for each reply. So the number to optimize is the cost of one completed interaction, at the quality and response time the product needs.

Our goal is to get this down to a few cents per user per day, and that's something that you can only do with true experts and an ML team that really understands the trade-offs and techniques for accomplishing that.

FaiStatus by Wishroll

The table below sets the two workloads side by side, with what we built for each.

The tightest constraint is time. In conversation, people leave 0 to 300 ms between turns.[7] The model's first token is only part of that window, because the network and, in a voice app, speech synthesis use the rest. So the first token has to arrive well inside 300 ms, at production load. On Gemma 4 26B, the median first token now lands in 117 ms, which leaves most of the window for the voice.

The second difference is the size of each request. A consumer turn sends the whole conversation as the prompt and gets one short reply back. Across the apps we served in the 28 days to 23 September, median prompts were 13 to 36 times the length of replies. Enterprise work leans the other way, toward long outputs such as code and documents.

That workload already runs on Inworld at scale. On the most-used Gemma 4 models, we process up to 1.8 times the daily tokens that OpenRouter publicly reports across every provider on its platform combined.

We also serve those models faster. OpenRouter publishes first-token latency for every provider of a model. Against those measurements:[6]

  • Gemma 4 26B: the lowest median (0.17 s) and p95 (0.31 s) first token of the providers compared. That is 3.6 times faster at the median and 7.8 times faster at p95 than the median provider, at an input price nearly 40% below the median provider's.
  • MiMo 2.6 Pro: the lowest input price of the providers on OpenRouter, with the lowest median (0.39 s) and p95 (0.91 s) first token. That is 2.6 times faster at the median and 4.6 times faster at p95 than the next-fastest provider.

    • The sections below cover the calls a consumer app makes, then each technique and what it changes for the app.

    02Consumer inference tasks, and how we serve each

    A consumer app doesn't make one kind of model call. A single turn can check the message for safety, classify what the person wants, read their memory, write the reply, call a tool and update the memory afterwards. Each of those calls has a different size, a different deadline and a different budget, and a provider built around one of them leaves the rest slow or expensive.

    TaskWhat it needsHow we serve itWhat you get
    Conversation repliescompanions, tutors, assistantsFast first token responses, even as the conversation gets longerRealtime decoding speeds up generation, and KV-aware routing reuses the conversation history already processedup to 7.8× faster first token than the median OpenRouter provider; up to 90% of the prompt from cache
    Voice turnsthe reasoning inside speech to speechText fast enough for speech to start, and a fallback when a model is slowThe same serving path inside speech to speech, with a first-token timeout that moves to the next modelfirst audio as fast as 204 ms after the turn ends
    Intent, safety and moderation checksrun before every replyFast checks on every message, before the reply startsSpecialized decision models such as Clef on an optimized serving path, along with lightweight Flash models for quicker checks11.5× the throughput of Clef's reference code for high-volume checks
    Ranking and next-action decisionswhat to show or say nextStructured output, cheap at high volumeStructured outputs, with Flex for lower-cost background work or Priority for faster decisions while users waitfrom $0.07 per million input tokens
    Memory and summariesupdating what the app remembersLong input that can wait a few seconds, at the lowest priceThe Flex tier for background work, with the cached conversation reusedcached input at up to 99% less
    Stories and long repliesbedtime stories, interactive fictionA long answer that streams faster than people readDraft-and-verify decoding and fused mixture-of-experts kernelsup to 3× faster first token and 1.6× faster streaming on large MoE models
    Model failoveroutages, timeouts, failed requestsKeep the app responsive when the primary model fails, without building separate recovery logicConfigure a primary model and compatible fallback models once. The router automatically tries the next model when a request meets the failure conditions you setautomatic recovery through one API, with each attempt reported in the response
    Many model calls per turnrules, state and story in one turnSeveral model calls within one turn's latency and cost budgetOne API for every call, with a service tier per request and routing matched to each taskLatitude: tens of millions of calls in six weeks, about 20 per turn
    Your own modela fine-tune for your appBetter quality for your app's agents, at lower cost and lower latencyPost-training with app-specific evals, served on a dedicated deployment with lower-precision weights and a draft trained on your trafficbetter efficiency at your quality targets, with quality measured against your existing model; +35% throughput on one customer's fine-tune

    The same work sits underneath every row: kernels and decoding built for each model, a router that keeps each conversation's cache warm, precision checked against the evals, and a service tier per request so each call gets the speed or price it needs.

    03The serving challenge: long context in, short reply out

    Consumer apps have a distinctive traffic pattern. They send very long context to get a short reply, so processing and reusing the input matters as much as generation speed. And the calls one user action triggers each have their own size and deadline, as the timeline below shows.

    A dialogue turn with 3,500 tokens of history and a 200-token reply puts most of the work on the prompt. Long conversations pull the average far above the median: on GLM 5.3 Flash, the average request is 13,433 tokens in for 309 out.

    A story with a longer answer shifts the weight to decoding. The two phases hit different limits. Prefill, the work of processing the input, is bound by compute and gains from cache reuse and batching. Decode, the work of generating the output, is bound by memory bandwidth and gets faster when each step is cheaper or produces more than one token.

    So we work on both sides of the turn. On the prompt side, we avoid recomputing context the model has already seen, and chunked prefill processes a long prompt in pieces so it never holds up the replies streaming to other users. On the output side, we make every decode step cheaper and let each step produce several tokens. And because a background summary can wait while a reply cannot, every request carries a service tier. The next two sections cover the prompt side first, then the output side.

    04KV-aware routing for long conversations at scale

    Each turn resends the conversation so far. Prefix caching keeps the attention keys and values (the KV cache) for context the model has already processed, so the engine computes only the new part of the prompt. Every reply is still generated fresh.[2]

    At fleet scale, the hard part is placement. A conversation's cache lives on the replica that served its last turn, while another replica may have more free capacity. Our router is KV-aware. It hashes each block of the prompt, tracks which replica holds which blocks, and scores every replica on two things: how much of this request's prefix it already holds, and how busy it is. Sending every turn to the warmest cache would overload it, so the score trades reuse against load, tuned on representative traffic. KV that doesn't fit in accelerator memory spills to host memory instead of being evicted and recomputed.

    Built into each engine, model by model

    Cache-hit rate is one of the numbers we watch most closely, because it sets both how soon a reply starts and what the turn costs. Getting it high on real traffic takes more than turning prefix caching on. Different models and engines represent cached context differently: draft modes for realtime decoding, hybrid attention layouts, recurrent state and data-parallel ranks each change how prompt tokens become cache blocks, and the router finds a match only when its view agrees with the engine's.

    So we integrate the router with every model's serving path and measure the hit rate on production traffic. That work roughly doubled cache hits on GLM 5.3 Flash, from 25% to 47% on a replay of 5,000 production requests, and tripled them on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Our stack holds high hit rates on mixed traffic from many apps at once, and on one customer's dedicated deployment, cache hits reach 80% in production.[1]

    For your app. MiMo 2.6 Pro lists cached input at $0.0036 per million tokens and uncached input at $0.43, so every cached token costs 99% less. When 90% of a prompt comes from cache, the input cost of that turn falls by about 89%, and only a tenth of the prompt has to be processed before the reply can start.

    Under the hood. Each cached block skips its share of prefill. With more of every prompt coming from cache, each replica can carry more conversations at once, and time to first token grows far more slowly as a conversation gets longer.

    05Faster replies through model-specific decoding and precision

    People experience latency twice: while waiting for a response to begin, and while waiting for it to finish. Time to first token (TTFT) measures the first wait. Inter-token latency (ITL) sets the pace of the stream. A serving configuration has to handle both at the app's production concurrency.

    Draft-and-verify, tuned for each model

    Realtime decoding is our draft-and-verify serving approach, based on speculative decoding. A lightweight draft model proposes several tokens, and the target model verifies them together in one forward pass, accepting consecutive tokens until the first rejection. With exact acceptance and correction, generation can advance by multiple tokens per target-model step while preserving the target model's output distribution, with the same quality.[3]

    We optimize the drafts and the verify step for each model. Gemma 4 uses the draft models Google publishes for it, and GLM and DeepSeek use their own multi-token prediction layers. On a dedicated deployment, with the customer's approval, we train the draft on a sample of that app's traffic. A draft that predicts that app's outputs more accurately gets more tokens accepted per verification step, and we measure the gain at production load, because draft overhead, acceptance rate and concurrency all affect it.

    Verify attention on split-KV: up to 7.5× faster

    On Gemma 4 26B, a mixture-of-experts model, the verify step turned out to be the bottleneck. Verifying a 7-token draft sends 8 query tokens per sequence through attention, and the stock kernel only uses its faster split-KV path for single-token decoding. Verify fell back to a 2D kernel that split the work into about 60 blocks and left most of the chip's compute units idle.

    We changed the kernel so verify batches of up to 16 query tokens take the split-KV path. On the model's global (full-context) attention layers, verify attention ran 3.4 to 7.5 times faster, and attention fell from 27.5% to 16.5% of each decode step. The full build, which also runs the whole verify step as one captured graph and sets the draft length to 7 tokens, took ITL p50 from 6.4 to 5.2 ms and TTFT p50 from 154 to 117 ms on replayed production traffic, with the same math and reasoning scores.[1]

    For your app. ITL sets how fast a reply streams: at 5.2 ms per token, a 200-token reply finishes in about a second after it starts. Faster decode steps also let each accelerator serve more requests, which is what keeps prices low.

    Under the hood. Decode is bound by memory bandwidth: every step reads all of the weights to produce one token per sequence. A draft lets one read of the weights produce several tokens, so the speed of the verify step sets the gain. When attention dropped from 27.5% to 16.5% of the step, every request in the batch got faster.

    Same eval scores, fewer bytes per token

    A cheaper build ships only if it scores the same. Every build has to match the production build it replaces on our evals, including MATH, MMLU-Pro and GSM8K. Within that gate, each layer runs at the lowest precision its evals allow. On Gemma 4 31B, the MLP, which holds most of the weights, runs in 4-bit floating point (NVFP4), while attention and the KV cache stay at FP8.

    The gate catches regressions before they ship. It found a scaling bug in FP8 attention, and the fix brought MATH back from 87.4 to 89.6. It also blocked a build that was 80% cheaper to serve, because that build lost 5 points on MATH.

    For your app. Fewer bytes per weight keeps inference affordable as your app grows, at the same latency and quality. That is part of how Gemma 4 26B lists at $0.07 per million input tokens and $0.34 output.

    06Continuous optimization, model by model

    Our work doesn't stop when a model goes live. We continually profile production traffic to improve response times, serving efficiency and reliability, from new attention kernels that accelerate generation to resolving memory leaks that require periodic restarts. Each change is evaluated against our quality benchmarks before release. The table below shows a selection of these improvements and their measured results.

    Measured serving improvements

    ModelWhat changedResultBasis
    Gemma 4 26BRealtime-decoding verify moved onto split-KV attentionup to 7.5× faster verify attentionmicrobenchmark and replay, Oct
    MiMo 2.6 ProFused expert kernels and a custom collective3× faster first token (1.93 → 0.63 s)replay, pre-release build
    DeepSeek V3.2Turned on the model's own multi-token prediction1.6× faster token generation (62.4 → 39.9 ms/token)replay, Jul
